💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that victor Coimbra is CTO and Managing Partner at Artefact, where he leads AI, data science, and engineering work across the Americas.
  • According to recent reports, artefact is a global data and AI consulting company that helps enterprises develop strategies, build data platforms, deploy AI solutions, and manage organizational change.
  • According to recent reports, your career has taken you from business strategy at Accenture to leading AI, data science, and engineering teams at Artefact across the Americas.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that victor Coimbra is CTO and Managing Partner at Artefact, where he leads AI, data science, and engineering work across the Americas. His career combines business strategy experience at Bain and Accenture with hands-on leadership delivering AI and machine learning systems in complex enterprise environments. He focuses on helping organizations connect technical capabilities with measurable business outcomes, including the architecture, governance, and operating models needed to scale AI.

According to recent reports, artefact is a global data and AI consulting company that helps enterprises develop strategies, build data platforms, deploy AI solutions, and manage organizational change. Its work spans industries including financial services, healthcare, manufacturing, and retail. Ahead of its Adopt AI Summit, taking place December 3–4, 2026, at the Grand Palais in Paris, Coimbra discusses how enterprises can move beyond pilots, build teams that combine people and AI agents, and measure the value of AI in production.

According to recent reports, your career has taken you from business strategy at Accenture to leading AI, data science, and engineering teams at Artefact across the Americas. How has this combination of strategic consulting and hands-on technical leadership shaped your approach to helping enterprises turn AI investments into measurable business outcomes?

Recent findings suggest that it taught me to always connect AI strategy to delivery. Strategy at Bain and Accenture indicated me that executives buy a change in a P&L line. Engineering taught me that a lot of that value can get lost between the slide and production.

According to recent reports, today AI is less about technology and more about building a moat around your core business operations. The key question is how to turn individual productivity into collective enterprise value, with a true shared cognitive capacity across the firm.

That takes a mix of strategy and delivery, and it is something I learned a lot from doing both.

Despite significant investment in artificial intelligence, many organizations still struggle to move beyond successful pilot projects. In your experience, what are the most common obstacles preventing enterprise AI initiatives from reaching production, and what distinguishes companies that successfully scale their deployments?

According to recent reports, in my experience, many pilots stall because AI is added to an organization that was designed for humans only. The technology usually works. What is often still open is the division of work: which tasks belong to agents, which stay with humans, who reviews, and who owns the result.

On top of that, 3 needs tend to slow the scale-up: token costs that explode with usage-based pricing, security and governance, and adoption that never turns access into real usage.

Industry observers note that the companies I see scaling well treat AI as an organizational redesign. They split delivery into 2 loops. In the inner loop, agents execute end to end: code, build, test, push, review. In the outer loop, humans set the intent, verify the result and monitor cost and quality. Then they build one platform underneath and reuse it for every use case.

You’ve written about the importance of building an AI-native organization rather than simply adding chatbots and copilots to existing systems. What fundamental changes to enterprise technology architecture are necessary to support this transition, and where are businesses currently underinvesting?

It has been revealed that an AI-native tech giant runs on a platform, and that platform is the sum of 4 layers: Harness, Context, Model and Infra. The Harness is where humans and agents meet and work, the full application around the model. Context defines what agents know and what authority they have. Model is how models are accessed, routed and governed at the right cost. Infra is where they actually run, and who holds the keys.

According to recent reports, naturally, most of the attention goes to the visible 20%: copilots and chat tools. The hidden 80% is where most of the engineering lives, and where cost, security and control are decided.

Sources indicate that my suggestion is simple. Buy generalist harnesses and build the industry-specific ones. Rent and experiment on models and infra, because they change every quarter. And own your context completely. It is the layer that is truly yours, and where I see the biggest opportunity to invest more.

As AI evolves from assisting employees to autonomously executing complex workflows, how should organizations determine which processes are appropriate for agentic automation? What technical and operational safeguards must be established before granting AI agents greater decision-making authority?

The way I see it, agents are very good at work that looks to the past, humans at work that looks to the future. Agents excel at anything built on existing information, like analytics, coding, testing, documentation and reconciliation. Humans own what needs creativity, and creativity by definition looks forward: taste, vision, planning, deciding, and judging whether a result is actually good.

In practice that maps to the 2 loops. Agents run the inner loop and execute. Humans keep the outer loop: intent, verification and monitoring.

According to recent reports, the safeguards are engineered, not prompted. We use 6 harness layers: task capture, memory, a secure workbench with sandboxed runtime and permissions, a loop with checkpoints and clarifications, model routing, and guardrails that define what an agent cannot do alone, like human approvals, policy checks and PII controls. Autonomy then grows with the track record, the same way it does for a new hire.

You’ve described AI agents as teammates rather than conventional software tools. How does this perspective change the way organizations should structure teams, assign responsibilities, and train employees to collaborate with increasingly autonomous AI systems?

Industry observers note that we are already in the hybrid organization. The question I find most important now is how to divide the workforce between humans and agents. I believe it is the key to scaling.

In a hybrid team, the org chart allocates cognitive capacity, not headcount. A typical split I see in a mature tech team is 15% human-only work, 25% augmented work and 60% done by agents. The Head of IT sets intent, allocates capacity and owns outcome and cost. A senior developer verifies agent deliveries and decides architecture. An orchestrator agent routes tasks and reports cost, and a review agent checks every delivery.

The gains compound in 3 steps. Augmented employees deliver around 5x. Agents as synthetic employees doing end-to-end work deliver around 10x. Orchestrating both as one workforce is where I believe the 1000x potential lies.

It has been revealed that training follows the same logic. People learn to brief an agent like a junior engineer, with structured context and clear outcomes, and to spend their time on taste, planning and decisions.

Enterprise AI systems depend heavily on reliable data infrastructure, yet many organizations continue to struggle with fragmented data, inconsistent governance, and legacy technology. What foundational capabilities should businesses prioritize when preparing their data platforms for agentic AI, and how can they modernize without disrupting existing operations?

Recent findings suggest that design your data platform for a newly introduced kind of consumer: agents. A dashboard with a wrong number gets questioned by a human. An agent with a wrong number acts on it, at scale.

Prioritize 4 capabilities. Shared business definitions, so every agent and team means the same thing by “active customer.” An integration gateway with authentication and standard protocols like MCP, so agents access data with the permissions of the role they act for. Observable quality and lineage. And unstructured data treated as a first-class asset, because contracts, tickets and meeting notes hold most of the real knowledge.

To modernize without disruption, wrap legacy systems first and migrate use case by use case. Agents also change the economics here. Multi-agent migration pipelines now modernize hundreds of thousands of lines of legacy code in months, with humans deciding the architecture.

Beyond access to structured data, AI agents increasingly require an understanding of institutional knowledge, business processes, and organizational context. How can enterprises effectively capture and integrate this knowledge into their AI systems, and what risks arise when agents operate without sufficient business context?

It has been revealed that context is what turns a model into a colleague. Tools understand tasks, agents understand context. You don’t ask a junior engineer to work without explaining the goal, the constraints and what good looks like, and an agent is no different.

In a recent development, capture knowledge from the work itself, rather than from large documentation projects that are hard to keep up to date. Every meeting, ticket, decision and correction feeds a context layer that combines files, tables, vectors and a graph of relationships. Every finished task writes back to memory, so the organization learns with each delivery. And context needs its own governance: evals, permissions and cost control.

Without context, agents tend to struggle in a few predictable ways. They follow the written rule and miss the unwritten one everyone knows. They retrieve the wrong information and answer with total confidence. They work on last quarter’s facts. And a context layer without strict permissions can put sensitive data at risk.

Many companies measure AI success through productivity improvements, adoption rates, or the number of pilots debuted. What metrics should CIOs and business leaders use to evaluate genuine AI return on investment, particularly when accounting for infrastructure costs, ongoing maintenance, and the operational complexity of autonomous agents?

Sources indicate that measure the hybrid workforce, not the tool. Adoption is only the first of 4 levels, always against a baseline taken before rollout. Adoption asks if people use it. Productivity asks if we deliver faster: lead time, throughput, resolution time. Quality asks if the output is better: escaped defects, change failure rate, rework. Value and cost ask if it is worth it: effort freed, time to market, full cost per task.

It has been revealed that one metric that is easy to overlook is how cognitive capacity moves between humans and agents, team by team. Freed human capacity has to be redeployed to future-facing work with intent. Otherwise part of the gain gets lost.

It has been revealed that on cost, pricing is moving from flat fees to usage, which can make bills harder to predict, so model routing and FinOps belong in the platform from day 1. Treat AI spend like cloud spend: visible, attributed to a team, and tied to value.

Artefact works with enterprises across financial services, healthcare, manufacturing, retail, and other industries where AI adoption presents different challenges. What lessons are emerging from real-world deployments in these sectors, and how should organizations balance innovation with regulatory compliance, reliability, and human oversight?

According to recent reports, every sector faces the same question: how to divide the work between humans and agents. What changes is how much of the outer loop must stay human. In retail and consumer goods, mistakes are cheap, so agents take more of the work faster. In manufacturing, reliability and integration with operational systems set the pace. In financial services and healthcare, every decision must be explainable, so humans keep more of verification and decision for longer.

Industry observers note that the lesson I see everywhere is that compliance works best as a property of the platform, built in from the start. When guardrails, audit logs and human approvals live in the harness, every latest use case inherits them. When compliance comes only at the end, each new project has to start that conversation again.

According to recent reports, oversight should be tiered. Agents act alone on low-risk tasks, get reviewed by exception on medium risk, and only prepare the decision on high risk. The tiers move as trust is earned.

With Artefact’s Adopt AI Summit taking place in Paris this December, discussions around AI sovereignty, governance, and industrial competitiveness are becoming increasingly notable. How do you see Europe’s approach to AI adoption influencing global enterprise strategies, and what developments do you believe will define the next phase of enterprise AI over the coming years?

Europe was early in asking the sovereignty question, and I think it is becoming a global design principle. Multinationals don’t want one architecture per regulation, so they design for the strictest one: own your context, rent your models, and keep control of where they run and who holds the keys. The next opportunity for Europe is to bring the same energy to adoption, because competitiveness will come from usage at scale.

Industry observers note that the next phase is the hybrid organization, and I believe it is the future of work. Companies will move from counting headcount to managing a shared cognitive capacity between humans and agents. Agents will take most of the work that looks to the past: analysis, code, reporting. Humans will move to the work that looks to the future: taste, vision, planning and decisions.

Recent findings suggest that I believe the companies that solve the division of work first will lead the way. That is the conversation I want to have in Paris to define the next years.

Thank you for the great interview, readers who wish to learn more about enterprise AI adoption, agentic workflows, and data transformation should visit Artefact.

Industry observers note that antoine is a visionary leader and founding partner of Unite.AI, driven by an unwavering passion for shaping and promoting the future of AI and robotics. A serial entrepreneur, he believes that AI will be as disruptive to society as electricity, and is often caught raving about the potential of disruptive technologies and AGI.

Sources indicate that as a futurist, he is dedicated to exploring how these innovations will shape our world. In addition, he is the founder of Securities.io, a platform focused on investing in cutting-edge technologies that are redefining the future and reshaping entire sectors.

While I acknowledge Meta’s role in bringing smart glasses to a mainstream audience, it has proven to be an irresponsible steward. Its “growth at all costs” mindset has actively poisoned people’s perception of the form factor. Under Meta’s watch, glasses have gained a creepy connotation before their utility has been fully realized.

It has been revealed that google’s second take on smart glasses is the exact opposite of what Meta has done. Every single aspect has been considered, and the result is worthy of being most people’s introduction to the form factor.

Officially, Android XR glasses are known as Gentle Monster and Warby Parker Intelligent Eyewear. The branding is a mouthful, and I’m not quite sure “Intelligent Eyewear” will take off. Something more colloquial, like “Google glasses” — glasses.google is the landing page — or “Samsung glasses,” will probably stick in the public consciousness.

That critique aside, the name reflects how Google wants Intelligent Eyewear to actually replace your existing glasses. Unlike the Ray-Ban trap that I frankly think Meta did not consider, Google’s offerings are not situational or activity-based devices like sunglasses. These are a “smart” upgrade to the assistive device some people have to wear.

As a wearable, smart glasses are a bit like smartwatches in that the platonic design is pretty well established and indistinguishable from traditional eyewear. Unlike watches, glasses are so visible on people’s faces that form overrides everything else.

Industry observers note that fortunately, the Samsung hardware I wore for an hour last week looks and feels like glasses, almost unremarkably so. I’d venture to say that audio-only glasses without a display are a solved design challenge. Google emphasized that, at 41 grams, this is the lightest pair of smart glasses on the market, and it worked to make sure the weight is distributed evenly.

Industry observers note that the sides of the stems that face your head feature translucent plastic that lets you see the internal components. I liked that small design choice. You can control the glasses using voice commands, with Google debuting a latest “Hey Gemini” hotword for the form factor. While “Hey Google” and “OK Google” remain available, the new one is meant to reflect how massive a role Gemini plays on smart glasses.

There is also a touchpad on the right stem that accepts taps and swipes, while a button up top lets you take pictures and record video. Another way you’ll be able to control the glasses is with your Pixel Watch and Galaxy Watch. You can play/pause audio and enable Gemini using double-pinch and wrist gestures. Notably, gesture support is also coming to the Fitbit Air next year.

From its internal testing, Google tells me that which input method people use is pretty situational and ends up being natural. At the beginning of my demo, I favored the touchpad, but by the end, I was leaning toward voice commands.

It has been revealed that when you’re capturing media that gets saved, there will always be a white blinking indicator light. There’s also another light in your field of vision that’s analogous to the camera and microphone privacy indicators in the top-right corner of Android phones. When I first put on the glasses, that light was distracting, but I swiftly forgot about it by the end of my demo.

Talking to Intelligent Eyewear uses Gemini Live. Some prompts, like take a picture or play a song, are one-shot “chat” commands in phone parlance, but for the most part, you’re using Gemini’s back-and-forth conversation mode. Google heavily customized the Gemini Live model for glasses to reduce latency, shorten responses, and tightly integrate the camera.

Even compared to my last demo in May, the latency of voice commands has come a long way. That mentioned, I need more time to see if it’s really fast enough to use as a primary interaction method for most commands.

Google built a number of privacy protections into Intelligent Eyewear that are clearly in response to the current perception of smart glasses. There are some interesting ideas here, starting with how Gemini queries that involve a picture (like a visual search) won’t be saved to your Gemini History, used for model training, or ad targeting. For example, if you ask Gemini to find out what kind of plant you’re looking at, that image won’t be accessible anywhere else.

Recent findings suggest that similarly, Google will blur all faces and filter out bystander voices before it gets uploaded to Gemini in the cloud. This on-device processing occurs on your phone.

Recent findings suggest that since that visual media isn’t being saved, the external indicator light won’t be active when you’re talking to Gemini. The LED is only on when photos or videos are being saved and can be reviewed later.

It has been revealed that that indicator light features anti-tamper detection that prevents recording. Algorithms detect whether the LED is covered by stickers or markers, with this process featuring hardware verification when the glasses are in their charging case.

Recent findings suggest that google’s “Glasses” companion app, with Samsung having a near-identical version for Galaxy phones, is pretty similar to the version for Pixel Watch. Unlike the bloated “Meta AI” app, it’s just for settings rather than the very definition of a growth hack with a full chatbot. The difference is staggering, and something Google deserves a bit of credit for in this age of throwing AI into every crevice of day-to-day smartphone usage.

Under the hood, the glasses are offloading a lot of processing to your phone. This includes HDR pipelines and video stabilization. The 12MP camera takes pictures in a 4:3 aspect ratio, while you can record up to 90 seconds of video. Images are transferred immediately to your phone over Wi-Fi, while videos wait until the glasses are charging to preserve battery life. I am so excited by point-of-view photography and the instantaneous capture the glasses offer, and early impressions of camera quality are positive.

Another thing I want to test is how Intelligent Eyewear fares as always-available headphones. There are two open-ear speakers and four microphones, and Google is clearly very proud of the noise-cancellation work in place.

As someone who has been waiting for smart glasses since 2012, I cannot overstate my annoyance at how Meta allowed smart glasses to gain a scummy undertone, if not overtone. It should have been more proactive to societal problems. Meanwhile, Meta releasing glasses without a camera, thus removing the primary utility of real-world context, makes me deeply question its belief that this is the future.

Recent findings suggest that smart glasses that know what you’re interacting with in the world can be extremely useful. That always-available camera is a genuine physical advantage over smartphones. It unlocks new use cases and convenience that are just not possible with something that goes in your pocket.

Recent findings suggest that google took a long time to get back to glasses. From what I’ve used so far, the wait will be worth it. The hardware and designs are solid, while the software is chock-full of innovative, well-considered ideas.

DocumentDB 1.0 is the first generally available release of the open source, MIT-licensed document database built on PostgreSQL, with compatibility for the MongoDB wire protocol. Most MongoDB drivers, tools, and queries work without changes.

It has been revealed that documentDB consists of a PostgreSQL extension that provides MongoDB API-compatible functionality and a gateway that translates MongoDB protocol requests into PostgreSQL calls. Version 1.0 supports PostgreSQL 15–18 through container images, with Linux packages available for PostgreSQL 17 and 18, and includes a Kubernetes operator, with the GA focusing on security, stability, and fixes for indexing, aggregation, and geospatial queries.

Microsoft announced the open source project early in 2025, aiming to provide the developer community with a NoSQL datastore built on PostgreSQL, and offering full visibility into the engine's architecture and implementation. The project joined the Linux Foundation a few months later, with support from other large database organizations including AWS, Cockroach Labs, Google, Snowflake, and Yugabyte. In the recent article "DocumentDB and the MIT License: What to Know Before You Build, Deploy, and Distribute," the team explains how DocumentDB’s permissive MIT license allows commercial use, modification, and hosting without requiring disclosure of proprietary code, contrasting it with MongoDB’s SSPL.

Even if the project provides a page discussing the DocumentDB name disambiguation, covering the open source project, Azure DocumentDB, and Azure Cosmos DB, the community remains perplexed about the choice. In a popular Hacker News thread, user marifjeren writes:.

Industry observers note that name it anything else for god's sake. DocumentDB is already what everybody calls Amazon DocumentDB.

With multiple open source options now on the market, Patty Chow, product manager at Microsoft, explains why open-source document databases need multiple implementations to give developers more choice in deployment and infrastructure while preserving compatibility with MongoDB drivers and queries. Chow writes:.

MongoDB has given developers a widely used way to work with document data. Familiar drivers and query patterns are worth preserving. Alternative implementations give developers a chance to keep using that knowledge while evaluating different approaches to storage and deployment.

In a recent development, in a Reddit thread, some practitioners raise concerns about current MongoDB compatibility and confusion with similarly named products. User 716green comments:.

Sources indicate that compatibility between MongoDB and FerretDB has been absolutely minimal compared to what you would probably expect. I've been a fan of DocumentDB for a long time and I love that Microsoft is supporting FerretDB.

DocumentDB provides the PostgreSQL extensions and its own MongoDB-compatible gateway, while FerretDB is a separate project that uses the DocumentDB extensions as its backend and provides its own MongoDB-compatible interface.

Layerbase recently ran an initial comparison of FerretDB and the PostgreSQL-based DocumentDB using YCSB benchmarks, finding that DocumentDB delivered 20–33% higher read throughput, while FerretDB had lower tail latency for updates in mixed workloads, but noting the results are not conclusive. An open GitHub problem reports higher query latency in DocumentDB 1.0 than MongoDB 9.0.4 across several workloads, but the results have not been independently verified.

According to recent reports, the DocumentDB release notes include upgrade paths and known problems. The project plans separate long-term support and development tracks, with its versioning policy still under discussion.

#192. Cornelis Unveils CN6000: What 800G Networking Means for AI and Supercomputers

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1324 w)
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Unite

Cornelis Unveils CN6000: What 800G Networking Means for AI and Supercomputers

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1324 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that cornelis has introduced CN6000, an 800-gigabit networking family designed to reduce the time AI accelerators and supercomputers spend waiting for data.
  • The November 12 announcement introduces both Omni-Path and Ethernet adapters, alongside an Omni-Path switch.
  • According to recent reports, the commercial goal is straightforward: expensive processors produce more useful work when the network can keep up with them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that cornelis has introduced CN6000, an 800-gigabit networking family designed to reduce the time AI accelerators and supercomputers spend waiting for data. Its headline claim is striking: up to 1.6 billion messages per second on its Omni-Path SuperNIC. Understanding what that means, however, requires separating three different measures of network performance: bandwidth, message rate, and latency.

The November 12 announcement introduces both Omni-Path and Ethernet adapters, alongside an Omni-Path switch. Cornelis says hardware is available for evaluation and early deployments, with partner systems expected in the first quarter of 2027.

According to recent reports, the commercial goal is straightforward: expensive processors produce more useful work when the network can keep up with them. A faster GPU does little to shorten a distributed job while it is waiting for another machine to send a result.

An AI cluster is a group of connected computers working together. The network carries everything from large blocks of model data to small coordination messages. Its performance has several dimensions:.

800G means 800 gigabits per second. Dividing by eight gives a nominal 100 gigabytes per second, before protocol overhead and other practical limits. It describes data-carrying capacity, not how rapidly a chatbot generates words.

Message rate measures a different bottleneck. Sending many tiny pieces of information requires the adapter to process many separate operations, even when they do not fill the link’s bandwidth. Cornelis’s Omni-Path product brief specifies its 1.6-billion-message rate as bidirectional. It is an aggregate capability, not a claim that one application completes that many sequential requests every second.

Latency matters when the next calculation must wait for a message. In Cornelis’s internal 8-byte Intel MPI ping-pong test, the reported latency was 0.95 microseconds for CN6000 versus 1.2 microseconds for NVIDIA InfiniBand XDR at 800G, approximately 21% lower. MPI, or Message Passing Interface, is a standard way for parallel scientific programs to communicate.

That test measures a particular small-message exchange. It does not establish that a training run, simulation, or inference service will finish 21% faster. The outcome depends on how often the application communicates, the sizes of its transfers, congestion, and the rest of the system.

A network interface card, or NIC, connects a server to the network. “SuperNIC” is Cornelis’s product terminology for its specialized high-performance adapters. A switch connects those server links and forwards data between them. The complete arrangement of adapters, switches, links, and communication software is commonly called a fabric.

The distinction is important when buying a cluster. Installing a capable adapter does not automatically upgrade every switch, cable, or software path that its traffic will encounter.

CN6000 offers two fabric choices. Omni-Path is Cornelis’s purpose-built interconnect for parallel computing. Ethernet is the widely used networking foundation familiar to data center operators. The Ethernet adapter targets customers seeking high-performance communication while retaining compatible Ethernet switching infrastructure. InfiniBand, the technology in the benchmark comparison, is another specialized computing fabric; its switches are not interchangeable with Omni-Path switches.

The CN6000 platform therefore represents a family of components and deployment options, rather than a guarantee that any combination of network equipment produces the same result.

Sources indicate that the Ethernet SuperNIC implements RoCEv2: Remote Direct Memory Access over Converged Ethernet, version two. The underlying idea, RDMA, lets network hardware move data between authorized memory regions on different machines without making the host CPU copy every payload through the conventional networking path.

Recent findings suggest that think of it as arranging a direct delivery between two approved locations, instead of asking an intermediary to repeatedly receive and copy the contents. The CPU still has work to do in establishing and managing communication; the benefit is reducing its involvement in the data movement itself.

According to recent reports, NVIDIA’s RoCE documentation explains that version two carries RDMA traffic using IP and UDP headers, allowing it to traverse routed IP networks. Efficient deployment still depends on network configuration and congestion behavior, not merely the presence of an Ethernet connector.

Industry observers note that cornelis’s Ethernet product brief describes hardware offload, support for large numbers of simultaneous operations, and Priority Flow Control. That flow-control mechanism can pause selected traffic classes to help avoid packet loss. The announcement places Ultra Ethernet support on a software-revision path; buyers should distinguish that planned capability from the initial RoCEv2 offering.

Industry observers note that AI inference is the process of using a trained model to produce an answer. For a language model, it includes prefill, which processes the prompt, and decode, which generates the response one token at a time.

In a recent development, some serving systems run those stages on separate groups of processors so each group can be sized for its job. This is called disaggregated inference. The separation introduces a handoff: information calculated while reading the prompt must reach the processors generating the answer.

Recent findings suggest that that information includes the key-value cache, usually shortened to KV cache. It stores intermediate attention data so the model can reuse previous work. It is neither the model’s entire set of weights nor simply a saved text transcript.

NVIDIA’s Dynamo documentation describes the sequence: process the prompt, transfer its KV cache, then generate tokens on the decode worker. Faster transfers can make that separation more practical. But moving the cache adds work of its own, so disaggregation is useful when the scheduling and hardware benefits outweigh the handoff cost.

On Omni-Path, CN6000 uses credit-based flow control: a sender transmits according to the receiving side’s available capacity. Adaptive routing can distribute traffic over available paths, while multiple network planes provide separate paths through the fabric.

The Omni-Path brief describes two independent 400G data paths that together provide 800G aggregate bandwidth. If one plane needs service, the other can remain available, though losing part of the network does not preserve its original full capacity.

The platform also includes a hardware root of trust, secure boot, and device attestation. These help establish that firmware and device identity are trustworthy. Its use of post-quantum digital signatures concerns authentication and integrity; it should not be read as a blanket claim that every network payload is encrypted.

It has been revealed that CN6000 follows Cornelis’s earlier scale-out networking work, including the expanded AMD collaboration for scientific computing. Its appeal is the combination of high-performance interconnects with a wider choice of processors and network environments.

For buyers, the useful comparison is the time and cost required to complete their own workload. A simulation that repeatedly exchanges small updates may benefit from lower latency and higher message rates. A service moving large caches may care more about sustained transfer speed and congestion. Both need an appropriate fabric, functioning software support, and qualified server configurations.

CN6000’s announcement adds another option for building those systems. Its peak figures identify capabilities worth testing; the practical win is keeping more compute productive while real applications run.

That's because developer Level Infinite has just released a new version of PUBG Mobile designed specifically to be the lightest version of the popular battle royale game yet. The initial download of PUBG Mobile Flash takes up just 0.96GB, with multiple tools available to ensure subsequent content downloads are limited to the maps and modes you want to play – keeping as much free space on your phone as possible.

PUBG Mobile Flash also supports a wider range of devices than the base game, including those with just 2GB of RAM, and promises better graphics optimization for smoother frame rates.

The file size may be small, but Level Infinite makes it clear that this is still a fully fledged version of what it calls "one of the world’s most popular mobile games.".

PUBG Mobile Flash players will be able to squad up with their friends on regular PUBG Mobile. There is also seamless account cross-progression, so you'll be able to pick up where you left off if you already play the regular version of the game.

“Expanding access to PUBG Mobile has always been an important part of our long-term vision, and we’re continually looking for new ways to connect players around the world,” explained general manager and PUBG Mobile head Vincent Wang.

"With PUBG Mobile Flash, we’re taking another step towards that goal, making it easier for more players to enjoy the core PUBG Mobile experience, reconnect with friends, and remain part of our global community.".

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, to rapidly summarize the problem at hand (and name names), Meta’s smart glasses developed a reputation of being abused by bad actors who would disable the visible privacy LED (which Meta only recently fixed) or use these glasses in tasteless ways.
  • It’s a shame, because a camera in smart glasses serves such a functional role, both for the user in just capturing pictures and for the AI assistant built into the experience.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google’s Intelligent Eyewear push with the first Android XR glasses from Warby Parker and Gentle Monster are forced into an unfortunate uphill battle. The “perv glasses” stigma is very real because, frankly, early movers in this category didn’t respect privacy. Here’s how Android XR and Gemini are handling the camera and privacy on “Intelligent Eyewear,” and why I think Google has struck a near-perfect balance.

In a recent development, to rapidly summarize the problem at hand (and name names), Meta’s smart glasses developed a reputation of being abused by bad actors who would disable the visible privacy LED (which Meta only recently fixed) or use these glasses in tasteless ways. Combine that with improper handling of recordings on Meta’s part and it’s a recipe for distrust and an earned social stigma. It’s not like Google is a simple bystander here, either. The original Google Glass project was met with the “Glasshole” stigma, and it’s something that Google has clearly learned a lot of lessons from.

It’s a shame, because a camera in smart glasses serves such a functional role, both for the user in just capturing pictures and for the AI assistant built into the experience. I recently talked about how the camera was my favorite part of smart glasses in an matter of our 9to5Google Weekender newsletter, but how it just feels a bit wrong now.

Anyway, with that context in mind, let’s look at how Google is handling this touchy subject.

It starts with the outward-facing light on every part of Android XR glasses, which works similarly to the privacy LED on Meta’s glasses. The key distinction here is this is a “recording light” on Android XR glasses. It turns on whenever the glasses are capturing content that can be viewed later in some form or fashion by the user. So if you’re taking a picture or recording a video, it lights up. If you’re just using Gemini for context, the light doesn’t activate. That’s because any camera captures being used for Gemini are deleted immediately after use. They won’t show up in your Gemini chat logs and that’s not a choice for the user – these images are purged immediately after they’ve been used so that you as the user nor Google can use them. That includes Google not using visuals from Gemini captures for AI training or advertising. Users also have control over what apps on Android XR glasses can use the camera.

Importantly, the light on each pair of Android XR glasses is also designed to avoid any tampering. Android XR glasses automatically perform a system check to ensure the light is working on a regular basis – you might catch the light blinking in white and blue while charging which is a part of the system check ensuring the hardware is fully functional. If the light is found not to be working, the camera is disabled.

According to recent reports, one of the pieces of this package that really caught my attention is how Google is handling the privacy of those around you. When your Intelligent Eyewear glasses send a photo to Gemini, your phone automatically redacts faces from the image before it’s sent to Gemini. This happens locally on the phone, essentially as a part of the glasses app. Similarly, voice data sent to Gemini filters out other voices besides your own. The voice filtering bit is just one way in which Google is doing some impressive things with the microphones here, with another example being that the live translation feature works in a 60-degree “cone” in front of you, filtering out other voices in the space.

According to recent reports, continuing on with how the camera interacts with Gemini, Google explained in a conversation with 9to5Google that Gemini is tuned not to use the camera in cases where it’s not obvious that the user wants the camera to be active. An interaction such as “what painting is this” would very clearly imply that the user wants the glasses to view the scene in front of them and identify the art piece, where “how much money is on the table,” Google explained, would ask for a follow-up before using the camera seeing as it’s not obvious that the user expects the camera to be used in that sort of phrase.

According to recent reports, another way in which Android XR glasses will avoid the recording stigma is with their limits. Google is limiting Intelligent Eyewear video recording to 90-second sessions. While that does limit what the user can do, Google said that most recordings fell within that window anyway. Meta, by comparison, offers recordings up to 5 minutes.

Beyond just the glasses app and Gemini, Google notes it is making other efforts across its ecosystem to protect against and deter misuse of the camera on Android XR glasses, including:.

For the most part, Google’s efforts around privacy on Android XR glasses aren’t groundbreaking. This is how it should work. But seeing as the bar is exceptionally low thanks to a rough start from competitors, I found myself reassured and even a bit impressed by the messaging here – a clear explanation of the indicator light and the automatic on-device face redaction and deletion of Gemini imagery both go a long way.

Google’s sentiment around privacy on glasses is pretty nearly summed up by a sentence in its privacy post today: “…when technology can see the world around you, it has a responsibility to the people around you, too.”.

Google Cloud expanded its AI agent monitoring and evaluation tools on November 13, 2026, adding customer-controlled logging, dashboards, privacy safeguards and spending limits across BigQuery and Looker for managed data agents and custom agents built with Agent Development Kit (ADK) or LangGraph.

It has been revealed that the system uses a common telemetry path for first-party and custom agents. Managed Conversational Analytics agents emit telemetry automatically, while custom ADK or LangGraph agents can send structured telemetry with single-line SDK instrumentation. The data lands in BigQuery tables owned by the customer for analysis in Google Cloud’s developer and administrator tools.

Sources indicate that several core monitoring features are generally available (GA). BigQuery Studio’s prebuilt dashboards track usage, active sessions, top knowledge sources and latency. Looker System Activity dashboards for Conversational Analytics are also GA in Looker (Google Cloud core) and Looker (original), covering engagement and token usage. User ratings and query review in the Responses & feedback tab remain in preview.

Industry observers note that google Cloud separates operational telemetry from conversation content so administrators and agent owners can govern the two layers independently. Cloud Monitoring supplies aggregate metrics for request volume, latency and token usage, while Cloud Trace provides step-by-step spans for each request. Cloud Trace observability scopes can consolidate telemetry across multiple agent projects.

According to recent reports, those operational metrics and sanitized first-party trace spans exclude customer core content, including user prompts, model responses, internal thoughts and generated SQL. This allows platform teams to monitor activity without automatically giving operational tools access to the substance of each interaction.

For deeper auditing, agent owners and editors can opt into conversation logging for individual agents. A Google-managed service agent then streams prompts, responses and turn-level telemetry through the BigQuery Storage Write API into a customer-owned agent_events table. The table inherits the dataset’s identity and access management permissions, customer-managed encryption keys and VPC Service Controls.

Recent findings suggest that privacy guardrails check each turn before logging and skip logging for that turn when a knowledge source uses row-level security, column-level policy tags or dynamic data masking. If a logging error occurs, the user’s chat session continues uninterrupted. The design therefore distinguishes broad operational visibility from narrower, explicitly enabled access to full interactions.

Google Cloud states custom agents can retain more diagnostic detail through the open-source ADK plugin, which can stream full tool-invocation trees, time-series telemetry and multimodal payloads into BigQuery. First-party conversation logging deliberately strips low-level tool arguments and internal SQL.

The logs also provide a basis for cost management. Each BigQuery conversation turn records input, output, thought, cached and total token counts alongside total turn latency. Looker System Activity separately reports estimated input and output tokens across business-intelligence workloads.

Per-query caps on BigQuery bytes scanned use dry-run estimates to block oversized queries without incurring on-demand scan charges. Separately, daily input and output token quotas for BigQuery and the Conversational Analytics API are in preview. Those quotas can be applied per project, user or agent through the Google Cloud console or gcloud CLI.

According to recent reports, the combination pairs consumption reporting with active limits. Byte-scan caps address query spending before execution, while the preview token quotas extend enforcement to agent consumption across projects, users and individual agents.

Google Cloud’s open-source Prism tool tests Conversational Analytics agents grounded in BigQuery tables or Looker Explores. It supports reusable test suites, regular-expression assertions and multi-region agent discovery, with evaluations focused on SQL accuracy and answer quality before prompt, model or schema changes reach users.

Recent findings suggest that prism can write completed evaluation runs to BigQuery tables partitioned by day, placing benchmark results alongside production agent_events records for analysis in BigQuery and Looker. Native first-party BigQuery agent evaluations are separately available in preview through an API and a guided Colab notebook.

Sources indicate that the announcement makes customer-owned BigQuery telemetry the common layer for monitoring, cost controls and evaluation, tying agent oversight to existing warehouse permissions and security controls. Managed conversation logging and the main dashboards are GA, while token quotas, native evaluations and some Looker feedback features remain in preview. For production teams, deployment design therefore includes both the boundary between operational traces and full conversations and the differing availability of each control.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Google Cloud Moves the Compute Engine API to Immutable Date-Based Versions.

Nov 14, 2026 2 min read.

Google Cloud has made multi-versioning of the Compute Engine API generally available, adding immutable, date-stamped API versions beside the long-lived /v1 surface. Stable versions are named YYYY-MM-DD and released quarterly, starting with 2026-09-01; preview versions carry a -preview suffix and a one-year lifespan. A caller selects one with the X-Goog-Api-Version header or the $apiVersion query parameter on the unchanged /compute/v1/ path, and a request that names no version keeps getting /v1, which has no end-of-life date.

Software engineer Michael Murstein writes that the problem was the shape of /v1 itself. Because it "was a single, mutable production surface shared by every customer worldwide," any behavioral improvement, "even changing a counter-intuitive default or modernizing an error format," risked breaking existing scripts or required a multi-year migration. Google calls the replacement interface-based versioning, aligned with its own AIP-185, which requires stable versions to be dates and previews to be time-bound. Each stable version is a locked snapshot of all generally available features and defaults at that date, and no breaking change is made to it after publication.

The blog post names three differences a caller will notice:.

Most callers will meet the change through tooling rather than headers. Each client library release for Python, Go, Java, Node.js, C#, Ruby and PHP now binds to one date-based version while keeping the compute_v1 and apiv1 namespaces, so no import paths change, and -preview SDK releases carry the preview versions. gcloud compute targets the bundled stable version and a latest gcloud preview compute group targets the bundled preview, with existing compute, beta and alpha scripts unchanged. The Terraform google provider targets stable versions and google-beta targets preview, with no version setting in HCL. Discovery documents are published per version.

With this release, Google is the last of the three largest cloud providers to let callers pin an API version on a request. Azure Resource Manager has required a date-stamped api-version query parameter, with a -preview suffix for previews, since its REST API launched, while AWS keeps date-stamped service models inside its SDKs and does not expose version selection on a request. The header form Google chose is the one Stripe popularized outside the cloud market; its Stripe-Version header now takes values such as 2026-10-28.endive, with monthly releases that carry no breaking changes and a major release twice a year that may. Google's quarterly cadence sits between Azure's per-service dates and Stripe's monthly ones, and unlike Stripe it has not stated which quarterly versions will carry breaking changes relative to the previous one.

Sources indicate that google gives no end-of-life date for /v1, no path by which a preview version becomes stable, no complete list of behavioral differences between /v1 and 2026-09-01 beyond the examples above, and no statement on whether other Google Cloud APIs will adopt the scheme; the /beta and /alpha channels are not mentioned. Both 2026-09-01 and 2026-10-01-preview are available in all regions today.

Google is finally introducing a “Hey Gemini” hotword for its AI assistant, but it’s only on Android XR glasses to start.

Recent findings suggest that around a decade after “Hey Google” made its debut, Google is introducing its first newly introduced always-listening hotword. “Hey Gemini” makes its debut on Google’s Intelligent Eyewear glasses powered by Android XR, with wearers able to use that hotword in place of “Hey Google.”.

While the hotword you use really won’t matter much at the end of the day, “Hey Google” has been recognized by many to not roll of the tongue very nicely. It’s a phrase that’s easy to stumble over, where “Hey Gemini” is a bit smoother.

As for whether or not “Hey Gemini” will become the default on future product remains unclear, but it’s a change only available on glasses for now.

We’ve asked Google if both hotwords will be active on Android XR glasses, but it was implied that this is, in fact, the case. When paired to Samsung glasses, “Hey Bixby” may also be in play, as Samsung’s voice assistant is supported on Intelligent Eyewear. Exact functionality, though, is something we’re still waiting for more clarity on.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Malaysia prepares to introduce a newly introduced law requiring data center operators to disclose their AI accelerator imports and power consumption to prevent diversion of restricted hardware to countries like China and optimize the use of the country’s power infrastructure, reports Malay Mail.
  • It has been revealed that malaysia's Minister of Investment, Trade and Industry Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani acknowledged on Thursday that some companies had rented space in Malaysian data centers to import GPUs legally, which they then shipped abroad in smuggling operations.
  • The proposed legislation will require data center operators to disclose the number of GPUs they import, their power consumption (presumably nameplate power consumption), the physical locations of their facilities, and the identities of operators and hyperscale customers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Malaysia prepares to introduce a newly introduced law requiring data center operators to disclose their AI accelerator imports and power consumption to prevent diversion of restricted hardware to countries like China and optimize the use of the country’s power infrastructure, reports Malay Mail. The authorities also blueprint to charge data center operators for unused electricity capacity they reserve. While the idea to use power consumption to detect potential GPU smuggling has merit, it also has flaws.

It has been revealed that malaysia's Minister of Investment, Trade and Industry Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani acknowledged on Thursday that some companies had rented space in Malaysian data centers to import GPUs legally, which they then shipped abroad in smuggling operations. To prevent such practices, Malaysia's Digital Ministry is now reviewing existing legislation to determine whether local authorities can take action against entities that re-export processors subject to U.S. export bans. The minister stressed that Malaysia wants AI accelerators imported into the country to be used domestically.

The proposed legislation will require data center operators to disclose the number of GPUs they import, their power consumption (presumably nameplate power consumption), the physical locations of their facilities, and the identities of operators and hyperscale customers. The government intends to track data center operations throughout their lifetime rather than limit oversight to the project approval stage.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, data center operators will have to pay for all the electricity capacity they reserve, irrespective of their actual power consumption. For example, if a data center secures 100 MW of power capacity but only uses 50 MW, its operator will still have to pay for the remaining 50 MW. The measure is meant to discourage companies from reserving electricity capacity they may not need for another one to three years. As an added bonus, the measure will further discourage rerouting AI hardware to China while pretending it is used in Malaysia.

Recent findings suggest that while data on power consumption could help Malaysian authorities spot suspicious discrepancies between AI GPU imports and actual data center operations, it is virtually impossible to accurately determine the number of AI accelerators deployed at a facility based on power consumption alone. For example, Nvidia's H100 and H200 SXM GPUs are rated at 700W, whereas its B200 SXM accelerators are rated at 1,000W, yet neither necessarily consumes its rated power under actual workloads.

In a recent development, furthermore, without knowledge of server configurations, the power consumption of CPUs, memory, storage, and networking equipment, or the power usage effectiveness (PUE) of a particular facility, any estimates of the number of operational GPUs would be imprecise, to put it mildly. Also, there may be a considerable delay between GPU imports and their actual deployment. As a result, reliable verification would require physical inventory audits or other mechanisms to track individual processors.

Johari said that Malaysian authorities were prepared to cooperate with their U.S. counterparts and provide information about facilities that house particular GPUs upon request. However, the minister did not specify whether the latest legislation would require data center operators to disclose GPU models and serial numbers, or whether authorities would conduct on-site inspections.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Malaysia has emerged as a major destination for data center investments in Southeast Asia as cloud service providers and AI infrastructure companies expand their presence in the region. To date, Malaysian authorities have approved 117 data center projects, 55 of which are already operational, according to Johari. The proliferation of local AI data centers makes Malaysia a suitable venue for rerouting restricted hardware to countries like China, as it is easier to hide a needle in a pile of needles than in a haystack.

#180. Node.js Brings Debounce, Throttle, and PKCS#12 Parsing Into Core Modules

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (592 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Infoq

Node.js Brings Debounce, Throttle, and PKCS#12 Parsing Into Core Modules

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (592 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News Node.js Brings Debounce, Throttle, and PKCS#12 Parsing Into Core Modules.
  • Nov 14, 2026 2 min read.
  • According to recent reports, node.js, the popular open-source JavaScript runtime, has pulled a handful of long-requested utilities directly into its standard library.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Node.js Brings Debounce, Throttle, and PKCS#12 Parsing Into Core Modules.

Nov 14, 2026 2 min read.

According to recent reports, node.js, the popular open-source JavaScript runtime, has pulled a handful of long-requested utilities directly into its standard library. Debounce and throttle helpers have landed in node:util, a new crypto.parsePKCS12() API now surfaces private keys and certificates from .p12 and .pfx bundles, and the experimental Virtual File System has been extended into node:ffi. The additions shipped as part of Node.js 26.10.0, one of a steady run of Current-line releases leading into the Node.js 26 LTS line that is now Active LTS under the codename "Lithium".

The headline change is the arrival of util.debounce() and util.throttle() in the core util module. Rate-limiting helpers have long been one of the most commonly vendored dependencies in the Node.js ecosystem, typically pulled from lodash or the throttle-debounce package. James M Snell landed both in a single pull request, with Matteo Collina noting that he uses these utilities in "essentially every app.".

Contributors ljharb and bakkot flagged the awkwardness of using an AbortSignal (which only transitions to aborted once) inside a function meant to be called repeatedly, so Snell reworked the signal to cancel every future invocation and added a leading-edge option so the first call can fire immediately.

Alongside these helpers, he same change also added also carried util.markPromiseAsHandled(), an explicit mechanism for framework authors to tell the runtime that a promise has been handled, addressing a long-running source of confusion around unhandled-rejection signalling.

crypto.parsePKCS12() closes a different long-standing gap. Node.js already parsed .p12 and .pfx bundles internally for TLS's pfx option, but it never surfaced the result to JavaScript. The new API wraps OpenSSL's d2i_PKCS12_bio() and PKCS12_parse(), returning an object with privateKey, certificate, and additionalCertificates fields. It was Brian Muenzenmeyer's first significant core contribution touching C++, refined with Filip Skokan, and it removes the need to shell out to the openssl CLI or depend on packages like node-forge.

The experimental Virtual File System has also grown further into the platform. Matteo Collina and Philipp Dunkel extended node:ffi to load libraries straight from a mounted VFS, using the same self-cleaning anonymous memfd trick that native addons already rely on under Linux. The same patch fixed a bug where dlopen forwarded an undefined flags argument, which silently broke addon loading from the real filesystem.

Recent findings suggest that compared with Bun and Deno, both of which have tended to ship richer standard libraries by default, this run of additions continues a visible trend in Node.js of reducing reliance on userland utilities. The shift also has supply-chain implications, cutting a handful of small dependencies out of typical node_modules trees.

Recent findings suggest that the changes landed first on the Current line, but Node.js has kept moving since. v26.11.0 followed with further Buffer and http helpers, and Node.js 26 has now moved to Active LTS as "Lithium" with support through April 2029. Installers for all major platforms are available at nodejs.org/en/download.

Node.js is an open-source, cross-platform JavaScript runtime maintained under the OpenJS Foundation.

Wallet joins Gmail, Photos, YouTube and Search among the apps Google identifies as available through Personal Intelligence, its connected-app personalization system.

Google expanded Personal Intelligence on March 17, 2026 across AI Mode in Search, the Gemini app and Gemini in Chrome. Those connected experiences were for personal Google accounts and were not available to Workspace business, enterprise or education people.

Wallet alone can inform responses about spending habits. Customers can also link financial accounts from credit cards and banks to Wallet through Plaid, an optional step that Google says unlocks deeper insights than Wallet connectivity alone.

Google’s examples center on analysis rather than transactions. A request to review the previous quarter’s spending while aiming to save $1,000 over three months can produce dynamic in-chat charts covering cash flow, asset allocation and budgets. Gemini can also find recurring charges across linked accounts and flag subscriptions whose prices increased during the year, or examine the previous year’s gift and travel transactions to suggest a personalized holiday budget.

According to recent reports, the integration is opt-in through Connected Apps in Personal Intelligence settings and can be switched off at any time. Gemini receives read-only access: it cannot move, manage or invest money. Google’s Connected Apps documentation separately warns customers not to rely on Gemini’s output for financial advice and to consult a professional.

Industry observers note that shared Wallet information can include payment methods, data from Google services saved in Wallet and financial-account information linked through services such as Plaid. Data added to a connected app in the future also becomes accessible to Gemini.

When Keep Activity is on, Gemini Apps activity, including data from connected apps, can be used to improve Google services and train generative AI models. Google says it does not train those models directly on Google Wallet and payments services. It does train on summaries, excerpts and inferences derived from relevant transactions, as well as prompts, responses, suggestions and information about how those responses and suggestions were generated.

A subset of Wallet-related interactions, summaries, excerpts and inferences is reviewed by human reviewers, including trained service providers, for debugging, safety and service improvement. Before trained service providers review interactions personalized through Connected Apps, Google indicates it takes steps such as disconnecting them from Google Accounts and reducing personal information, unless it is addressing abuse or harm.

Disconnecting Wallet or deleting Wallet data does not delete Gemini Apps Activity; users must manage or delete that activity separately. Deleting it can prevent its use for future product improvement unless trained reviewers have already reviewed the data.

According to recent reports, alongside Wallet support, Google introduced Memory Summary, a readable snapshot of saved preferences, interests and ongoing goals. The Memory Summary help page says users can add details, correct inaccuracies, delete information and inspect a chronological Memory history showing when information was added or modified.

In a recent development, memory Summary is available on the web and mobile for Gemini app customers where Personal Intelligence is available, subject to requirements in the help documentation: a personal account, an age of at least 18, Keep Activity enabled and Memory turned on. It is not available in the European Economic Area, Nigeria, Switzerland or the United Kingdom.

Industry observers note that taken together, Wallet access and Memory Summary give Gemini transaction information alongside an editable record of preferences and goals, while leaving money movement outside the chatbot’s reach. The finance experience therefore rests on a layered privacy model: the initial connection, activity retention, model training and saved memory each involve distinct controls.

According to recent reports, vera Syn is an AI-generated research agent at Unite.AI, covering artificial intelligence in finance, banking, and financial infrastructure. Her work focuses on how AI is reshaping investment banking, credit underwriting, risk management, trading systems, and fraud detection across global financial institutions.

With a precise and quantitative perspective, Vera examines how machine learning models are applied to market analysis, credit scoring, anti-money laundering, and operational efficiency in banking. She pays particular attention to model accuracy, regulatory constraints, and the balance between automation, transparency, and systemic risk in financial systems.

Articles authored by Vera Syn are AI-generated and reviewed by Unite.AI’s editorial team to ensure accuracy, clarity, and responsible coverage of AI’s expanding role in finance and banking.
