Usability tests should typically include around five participants according to Jakob Nielsen, who found that that number of people can usually identify most of the problems: “As you add more and more users, you learn less and less because you will keep seeing the same things again and again… After the fifth user, you are wasting your time by observing the same findings repeatedly but not learning much new.”.

According to recent reports, there are parallels with storytelling here too; if you try to tell a story with too many characters, the plot may get lost. Having fewer participants means that each user’s struggles will be more memorable and easier to relay to other stakeholders when talking about the research. This can help convey the issues that need to be addressed while also highlighting the value of doing the research in the first place.

Researchers have run usability tests in person for decades, but you can also conduct usability tests remotely using tools like Microsoft Teams, Zoom, or other teleconferencing software. This approach has become increasingly popular since the beginning of the pandemic, and it works well. You can think of in-person usability tests like going to a play and remote sessions as more like watching a movie. There are advantages and disadvantages to each. In-person usability research is a much richer experience. Stakeholders can experience the sessions with other stakeholders. You also get real-time reactions—including surprise, agreement, disagreement, and discussions about what they’re seeing. Much like going to a play, where audiences get to take in the stage, the costumes, the lighting, and the actors’ interactions, in-person research lets you see users up close, including their body language, how they interact with the moderator, and how the scene is set up.

If in-person usability testing is like watching a play—staged and controlled—then conducting usability testing in the field is like immersive theater where any two sessions might be very different from one another. You can take usability testing into the field by creating a replica of the space where owners interact with the product and then conduct your research there. Or you can go out to meet users at their location to do your research. With either option, you get to see how things work in context, things come up that wouldn’t have in a lab environment—and conversion can shift in entirely different directions. As researchers, you have less control over how these sessions go, but this can sometimes help you understand users even better. Meeting users where they are can provide clues to the external forces that could be affecting how they use your product. In-person usability tests provide another level of detail that’s often missing from remote usability tests.

Recent findings suggest that that’s not to say that the “movies”—remote sessions—aren’t a good option. Remote sessions can reach a wider audience. They allow a lot more stakeholders to be involved in the research and to see what’s going on. And they open the doors to a much wider geographical pool of owners. But with any remote session there is the potential of time wasted if participants can’t log in or get their microphone working.

It has been revealed that the benefit of usability testing, whether remote or in person, is that you get to see real consumers interact with the designs in real time, and you can ask them questions to understand their thought processes and grasp of the solution. This can help you not only identify problems but also glean why they’re problems in the first place. Furthermore, you can test hypotheses and gauge whether your thinking is correct. By the end of the sessions, you’ll have a much clearer picture of how usable the designs are and whether they work for their intended purposes. Act two is the heart of the story—where the excitement is—but there can be surprises too. This is equally true of usability tests. Often, participants will say unexpected things, which change the way that you look at things—and these twists in the story can move things in new directions.

Unfortunately, user research is sometimes seen as expendable. And too often usability testing is the only research process that some stakeholders think that they ever need. In fact, if the designs that you’re evaluating in the usability test aren’t grounded in a solid understanding of your users (foundational research), there’s not much to be gained by doing usability testing in the first place. That’s because you’re narrowing the focus of what you’re getting feedback on, without understanding the users' needs. As a result, there’s no way of knowing whether the designs might solve a problem that users have. It’s only feedback on a particular design in the context of a usability test.

On the other hand, if you only do foundational research, while you might have set out to solve the right problem, you won’t know whether the thing that you’re building will actually solve that. This illustrates the importance of doing both foundational and directional research.

In act two, stakeholders will—hopefully—get to watch the story unfold in the user sessions, which creates the conflict and tension in the current design by surfacing their highs and lows. And in turn, this can help motivate stakeholders to address the problems that come up.

While the first two acts are about understanding the background and the tensions that can propel stakeholders into action, the third part is about resolving the problems from the first two acts. While it’s key to have an audience for the first two acts, it’s crucial that they stick around for the final act. That means the whole product team, including developers, UX practitioners, business analysts, delivery managers, product managers, and any other stakeholders that have a say in the next steps. It allows the whole team to hear customers’ feedback together, ask questions, and discuss what’s possible within the project’s constraints. And it lets the UX research and design teams clarify, suggest alternatives, or give more context behind their decisions. So you can get everyone on the same page and get agreement on the way forward.

Sources indicate that this act is mostly told in voiceover with some audience participation. The researcher is the narrator, who paints a picture of the issues and what the future of the product could look like given the things that the team has learned. They give the stakeholders their recommendations and their guidance on creating this vision.

It has been revealed that nancy Duarte in the Harvard Business Review offers an approach to structuring presentations that follow a persuasive story. “The most effective presenters use the same techniques as great storytellers: By reminding people of the status quo and then revealing the path to a better way, they set up a conflict that needs to be resolved,” writes Duarte. “That tension helps them persuade the audience to adopt a new mindset or behave differently.”.

It has been revealed that this type of structure aligns well with research results, and particularly results from usability tests. It provides evidence for “what is”—the problems that you’ve identified. And “what could be”—your recommendations on how to address them. And so on and so forth.

You can reinforce your recommendations with examples of things that competitors are doing that could address these issues or with examples where competitors are gaining an edge. Or they can be visual, like quick mockups of how a newly introduced design could look that solves a problem. These can help generate conversation and momentum. And this continues until the end of the session when you’ve wrapped everything up in the conclusion by summarizing the main issues and suggesting a way forward. This is the part where you reiterate the main themes or problems and what they mean for the product—the denouement of the story. This stage gives stakeholders the next steps and hopefully the momentum to take those steps!

Recent findings suggest that while we are nearly at the end of this story, let’s reflect on the idea that user research is storytelling. All the elements of a good story are there in the three-act structure of user research:.

According to recent reports, the researcher has multiple roles: they’re the storyteller, the director, and the producer. The participants have a small role, but they are significant characters (in the research). And the stakeholders are the audience. But the most key thing is to get the story right and to use storytelling to tell users’ stories through research. By the end, the stakeholders should walk away with a purpose and an eagerness to resolve the product’s ills.

So the next time that you’re planning research with clients or you’re speaking to stakeholders about research that you’ve done, think about how you can weave in some storytelling. Ultimately, user research is a win-win for everyone, and you just need to get stakeholders interested in how the story ends.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that here’s a question: what titles spring to mind when you think about hard video games?
  • But what if I told you that this seemingly cuddly-by-comparison Nintendo Switch 2 game has challenged me more than anything else I’ve played this year?
  • Industry observers note that yes, I just faced off against a boss in the Island Crown mode of Nintendo Switch Sports Resort that pushed me to my very limit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that here’s a question: what titles spring to mind when you think about hard video games? You might consider 2025’s Hollow Knight: Silksong, perhaps a classic like Battletoads — and Dark Souls would certainly pop up in my head.

But what if I told you that this seemingly cuddly-by-comparison Nintendo Switch 2 game has challenged me more than anything else I’ve played this year?

Industry observers note that yes, I just faced off against a boss in the Island Crown mode of Nintendo Switch Sports Resort that pushed me to my very limit. No, really, this was harder than Dark Souls. “Who is this opponent that you speak of?” I hear you cry. Well, it’s none other than the Wii Sports Resort table tennis aficionado, Lucía.

Sources indicate that here’s the deal. In Island Crown (a predominantly single-player mode), you have to climb a ranking table for each respective sport, in a bid to topple the Island Champion and reign supreme. But after you finally rank #1, it turns out that your journey is far from over.

See, reaching the top rank unlocks a unique showdown against a Legend — a highly skilled Mii from Wii Sports Resort and related titles. These Legend matches range from fair yet challenging to absolutely rage-inducing. And for me, the table tennis game against Lucía was the worst of the worst.

Everything about her — whether that be her movement speed, her pinpoint precision, her unshakeable resolve in the face of power shots — made her an extremely formidable opponent. I may have played through titles like Bloodborne and Shin Megami Tensei III: Nocturne before, but their challenge levels pale in comparison to this.

Across my (extremely) numerous attempts, Lucía seemed to return even the most challenging shots and place the ball in spots that my character could only dream of reaching. After a few 6-0 drubbings, I managed to start picking up some points, playing out long rallies until she made the smallest of errors. But it still wasn’t happening.

In a recent development, an hour or so in, though, and I felt like I was getting somewhere. I’d managed to scrape my way to a few deuces here and there, and with the power of slice shots, I was able to recover to the center of the table and avoid leaving myself exposed.

It has been revealed that but it still wasn’t enough. Until one fateful match.

Sources indicate that picture this. The clock strikes midnight. I sit there, Joy-Cons in hand, with dozens of failed attempts to my name. After landing a killer shot, I draw the game level at 4-4. Sweat begins to form on my brow, as my hands tremble — I can feel the arm ache taking over. But I know I have to see this through.

According to recent reports, what ensues is a rally of epic proportions. Returned power-shots, jaw-droppingly accurate placements, last-gasp saves…you name it. But as the rally reaches its climax, I spot a gap on Lucía’s left side; I swiftly strike, and I manage to make it 5-4. I just need one more point.

Industry observers note that lucía releases a barrage of cross-table shots, looping curved balls, and seemingly impossible saves, but then suddenly, she scuffs the ball, leaving her open to a devastating smash. I swing the Joy-Con with bated breath as I watch the ball fling across my screen and…she misses. My hellish ordeal against the table tennis queen was finally over.

With a ridiculous smile on my face, about 50 Ls to my name, and the spoils of war (a golden nameplate item) in hand, I put the controllers down, reflected on my life choice to stay up until 1am playing table tennis with a Mii, and hit the hay.

Industry observers note that so, there you have it. Have you had the chance to play Nintendo Switch Sports Resort yet? Have you managed to defeat any of the Legends? Maybe you beat Lucía on the first try, and I’m simply awful at this game — whatever the case, I’d love to hear from you, so make sure to get chatting in the comments.

It has been revealed that P.S. It turns out that the table tennis Gauntlet, unlocked after beating Lucía, has an even harder Mii to face off against. But for the sake of my own well-being, I’m going to leave that for a later date….

#131. From Beta to Bedrock: Build Products that Stick.

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1796 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Alistapart

From Beta to Bedrock: Build Products that Stick.

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1796 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Alistapart

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that as a product builder over too many years to mention, I've lost count of the number of times I've seen promising ideas go from zero to hero in a few weeks, only to fizzle out within months.
  • As a product builder over too many years to mention, I've lost count of the number of times I've seen promising ideas go from zero to hero in a few weeks, only to fizzle out within months.
  • Industry observers note that financial products, which is the field I work in, are no exception.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that as a product builder over too many years to mention, I've lost count of the number of times I've seen promising ideas go from zero to hero in a few weeks, only to fizzle out within months. Financial products, which is the field I work in, are no exception. With people’s real hard-earned money on the line, user expectations running high, and a crowded market, it's tempting to throw as many features at the wall as possible and hope something sticks. But this approach is a recipe for disaster. Here's why: The pitfalls of feature-first development When you start building a financial product from the ground up, or are migrating existing customer journeys from paper or telephony channels onto online banking or mobile apps, it's easy to get caught up in the excitement of creating newly introduced features. You might think, "If I can just add one more thing that solves this particular user problem, they'll love me!" But what happens when you inevitably hit a roadblock because the narcs (your security team!) don’t like it? When a hard-fought feature isn't as popular as you thought, or it breaks due to unforeseen complexity? This is where the concept of Minimum Viable Product (MVP) comes in. Jason Fried's book Getting Real and his podcast Rework often touch on this idea, even if he doesn’t always call it that. An MVP is a product that provides just enough value to your owners to keep them engaged, but not so much that it becomes overwhelming or difficult to maintain. It sounds like an easy concept but it requires a razor sharp eye, a ruthless edge and having the courage to stick by your opinion because it is easy to be seduced by “the Columbo Effect”… when there’s always “just one more thing…” that someone wants to add. The problem with most finance apps, however, is that they often become a reflection of the internal politics of the business rather than an experience solely designed around the customer. This means that the focus is on delivering as many features and functionalities as possible to satisfy the needs and desires of competing internal departments, rather than providing a clear value proposition that is focused on what the people out there in the real world want. As a result, these products can very easily bloat to become a mixed bag of confusing, unrelated and ultimately unlovable customer experiences—a feature salad, you might say. The importance of bedrock So what's a better approach? How can we build products that are stable, user-friendly, and—most importantly—stick? That's where the concept of "bedrock" comes in. Bedrock is the core element of your product that truly matters to users. It's the fundamental building block that provides value and stays relevant over time. In the world of retail banking, which is where I work, the bedrock has got to be in and around the regular servicing journeys. People open their current account once in a blue moon but they look at it every day. They sign up for a credit card every year or two, but they check their balance and pay their bill at least once a month. Identifying the core tasks that people want to do and then relentlessly striving to make them easy to do, dependable, and trustworthy is where the gravy’s at. But how do you get to bedrock? By focusing on the "MVP" approach, prioritizing simplicity, and iterating towards a clear value proposition. This means cutting out unnecessary features and focusing on delivering real value to your users. It also means having some guts, because your colleagues might not always instantly share your vision to start with. And controversially, sometimes it can even mean making it clear to customers that you’re not going to come to their house and make their dinner. The occasional “opinionated user interface design” (i.e. clunky workaround for edge cases) might sometimes be what you need to use to test a concept or buy you space to work on something more important. Practical strategies for building financial products that stick So what are the key strategies I've learned from my own experience and research? Start with a clear "why": What problem are you trying to solve? For whom? Make sure your mission is crystal clear before building anything. Make sure it aligns with your company’s objectives, too. Focus on a single, core feature and obsess on getting that right before moving on to something else: Resist the temptation to add too many features at once. Instead, choose one that delivers real value and iterate from there. Prioritize simplicity over complexity: Less is often more when it comes to financial products. Cut out unnecessary bells and whistles and keep the focus on what matters most. Embrace continuous iteration: Bedrock isn't a fixed destination—it's a dynamic process. Continuously gather user feedback, refine your product, and iterate towards that bedrock state. Stop, look and listen: Don't just test your product as part of your delivery process—test it repeatedly in the field. Use it yourself. Run A/B tests. Gather user feedback. Talk to people who use it, and refine accordingly. The bedrock paradox There's an interesting paradox at play here: building towards bedrock means sacrificing some short-term growth potential in favour of long-term stability. But the payoff is worth it—products built with a focus on bedrock will outlast and outperform their competitors, and deliver sustained value to users over time. So, how do you start your journey towards bedrock? Take it one step at a time. Start by identifying those core elements that truly matter to your users. Focus on building and refining a single, powerful feature that delivers real value. And above all, test obsessively—for, in the words of Abraham Lincoln, Alan Kay, or Peter Drucker (whomever you believe!!), “The best way to predict the future is to create it.”.

Recent findings suggest that seismic appears to set the tone for this week's events in the hardware industry, and we've covered the biggest beats, including deeper dives on hardware and AI topics over on Tom's Hardware Premium. Stories this week are colored by the fact that Nvidia founder Jensen Huang has stepped away from his post as CEO. The ramifications are wide and far-reaching, as the company transformed from a gaming GPU manufacturer to an AI business over the past five years.

Recent findings suggest that first up, it's not only hyperscalers and neoclouds that have their eyes on AI. An increasingly popular segment among enthusiasts is PCs dedicated to running local AI models. With so many choices on the market at the moment, from the recently released RTX Spark to AMD's Strix Halo platform, we take a look at two unlikely contenders that are now going head-to-head: Nvidia's DGX Spark and Apple's Mac Studio. We ran a suite of real-world and synthetic benchmarks across both devices and tested large models on both machines. With prices at eye-watering levels, it's more crucial than ever that you make the correct choice for your intended workloads.

Recent findings suggest that DRAM capacity constraints have been an industry-wide sticking point as the AI buildout accelerates demand for dies. With costs spiraling across both client and enterprise hardware, AMD has shared further detail about MEXT, a predictive memory engine which aims to offer 99% of a server's performance while running on half the DRAM. Powered by a transformer model and clever use of flash storage, AMD is already running 145 servers with the system in place, with a view to expand that figure to 2,000 next year.

Next, we sat down with Cognichip's Chief Product Officer in an extensive interview to explore how the company is rolling out AI-powered chip design tools. Back in September, the company revealed a suite of proprietary AI models, named Artificial Chip Intelligence (ACI), which are specifically developed for semiconductor engineering. While the tools have yet to be used in a shipping product, it could substantially improve chip development productivity by automating labor-intensive tasks.

The Jensen Huang scandal deepens, as the now-former Nvidia CEO has become embroiled in a series of alleged extramarital affairs and has since resigned from Nvidia. While much of the past week's stories have centered on his relationship with alleged Chinese Spy Alice Huang, we explored the former CEO's unlikely relationship with Kang Wei, Ms. Huang's husband, who recently landed in hot water with China's Securities Regulatory Commission.

Nvidia-based compute remains difficult to find in China, especially as AI labs line up to order racks and newer cards like the RTX 5500 Pro, with over 6 million units reportedly ordered for the export-compliant GB202-based AI accelerator. But the Chinese AI labs that are chasing after Nvidia's tech may still have to pay a premium and ensure that they're running enough homegrown silicon to not fall afoul of Beijing's rules. We explore how some companies have now moved to renting compute in Southeast Asian countries like Malaysia and Singapore in an attempt to get around export controls.

According to recent reports, google's one of the biggest competitors to Nvidia, especially in the AI domain. The company's 8th-gen TPU lineup has now expanded even further, with two fresh chips designed for long-context agentic AI and security. These two new chips, TPU 8i Max and TPU 8tx, signal a further diversification across Google's eighth-generation TPU stack. While TPU 8i Max doubles the specs of the original TPU 8i, TPU 8tx makes a more interesting change to AMD's EPYC to serve its use in specialized security workloads.

The Frontier Model Foundation has proposed a Jailbreak Rating Framework which aims to classify the type and severity of a possible LLM jailbreak. With four scoring components in hand, the foundation aims to identify possible jailbreak vectors and inform labs of them before they happen in the real world, with potentially disastrous consequences.

Pixel Weather Gets a Fresh Option to Report Inaccurate Forecasts

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google Pixel Weather now lets users report incorrect temperatures and conditions through a new in-app option.
  • Google is reportedly adding a fresh option for Pixel owners to report inaccurate weather information through the stock Weather app.
  • As spotted by Android Authority, a fresh option to report inaccurate weather appears in version 1.1.20261012 of the Pixel Weather app.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google Pixel Weather now lets users report incorrect temperatures and conditions through a new in-app option. The feature collects feedback, location, and diagnostic data to help improve local forecasts without linking reports to Google accounts.

Google is reportedly adding a fresh option for Pixel owners to report inaccurate weather information through the stock Weather app. The feature was recently spotted in the latest app version. Users can report to Google whenever they feel the reported temperature or weather conditions do not match what they are experiencing.

As spotted by Android Authority, a fresh option to report inaccurate weather appears in version 1.1.20261012 of the Pixel Weather app. It is available through a card labelled Report current weather. Users can access the card at the bottom of the weather details page. Moreover, the card includes a short message asking users to share current conditions to help improve local forecasts.

Once the user opens it, they will see a panel with two sections covering temperature and weather conditions. For temperature, users can choose between Warmer, Colder, and Seems accurate. The conditions section offers several options, including Cloudy, Clear, Rain showers, Sleet or hail, Snow showers, Strong thunderstorms, and Low visibility. It also displays the current weather conditions and temperature so that the user can get a reference before submitting the report.

Google indicates it will collect these reports along with device location and some diagnostic information. However, to protect privacy, the firm says it won’t link this information to the user’s Google account.

Until now, many Pixel people have reported that the Weather app indicates inaccurate readings. Thankfully, Google has finally done something to address the concern. The tech giant has begun releasing the updated Pixel Weather app with the fresh report weather option. Select Google Pixel phones have already received it. It should reach all eligible users in the coming days, though we do not have an official word on the same. Users who want to try it before the final release can sideload the latest Pixel Weather bundle from APKMirror.

#126. An Holistic Framework for Shared Design Leadership

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 17m • 📚 Deep Dive (3365 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Alistapart

An Holistic Framework for Shared Design Leadership

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3365 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Alistapart

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, picture this: You’re in a meeting room at your tech manufacturer, and two people are having what looks like the same conversation about the same design problem.
  • According to recent reports, picture this: You’re in a meeting room at your tech company, and two people are having what looks like the same conversation about the same design problem.
  • This is the beautiful, sometimes messy reality of having both a Design Manager and a Lead Designer on the same team.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, picture this: You’re in a meeting room at your tech manufacturer, and two people are having what looks like the same conversation about the same design problem. One is talking about whether the team has the right skills to tackle it. The other is diving deep into whether the solution actually solves the user’s problem. Same room, same problem, completely different lenses. This is the beautiful, sometimes messy reality of having both a Design Manager and a Lead Designer on the same team. And if you’re wondering how to make this work without creating confusion, overlap, or the dreaded “too many cooks” scenario, you’re asking the right question. The traditional answer has been to draw clean lines on an org chart. The Design Manager handles people, the Lead Designer handles craft. Problem solved, right? Except clean org charts are fantasy. In reality, both roles care deeply about team health, design quality, and shipping great work. The magic happens when you embrace the overlap instead of fighting it—when you start thinking of your design org as a design organism. The Anatomy of a Healthy Design Team Here's what I’ve learned from years of being on both sides of this equation: think of your design team as a living organism. The Design Manager tends to the mind (the psychological safety, the career growth, the team dynamics). The Lead Designer tends to the body (the craft skills, the design standards, the hands-on work that ships to users). But just like mind and body aren’t completely separate systems, so, too, do these roles overlap in important ways. You can’t have a healthy person without both working in harmony. The trick is knowing where those overlaps are and how to navigate them gracefully. When we look at how healthy teams actually function, three critical systems emerge. Each requires both roles to work together, but with one taking primary responsibility for keeping that system strong. The Nervous System: People & Psychology Primary caretaker: Design ManagerSupporting role: Lead Designer The nervous system is all about signals, feedback, and psychological safety. When this system is healthy, information flows freely, people feel safe to take risks, and the team can adapt promptly to fresh challenges. The Design Manager is the primary caretaker here. They’re monitoring the team’s psychological pulse, ensuring feedback loops are healthy, and creating the conditions for people to grow. They’re hosting career conversations, managing workload, and making sure no one burns out. But the Lead Designer plays a crucial supporting role. They’re providing sensory input about craft development needs, spotting when someone’s design skills are stagnating, and helping identify growth opportunities that the Design Manager might miss. Design Manager tends to: Career conversations and growth planning Team psychological safety and dynamics Workload management and resource allocation Performance reviews and feedback systems Creating learning opportunities Lead Designer supports by: Providing craft-specific feedback on team member development Identifying design skill gaps and growth opportunities Offering design mentorship and guidance Signaling when team members are ready for more complex challenges The Muscular System: Craft & Execution Primary caretaker: Lead DesignerSupporting role: Design Manager The muscular system is about strength, coordination, and skill development. When this system is healthy, the team can execute complex design work with precision, maintain consistent quality, and adapt their craft to new challenges. The Lead Designer is the primary caretaker here. They’re setting design standards, providing craft coaching, and ensuring that shipping work meets the quality bar. They’re the ones who can tell you if a design decision is sound or if we’re solving the right problem. But the Design Manager plays a crucial supporting role. They’re ensuring the team has the resources and support to do their best craft work, like proper nutrition and recovery time for an athlete. Lead Designer tends to: Definition of design standards and system usage Feedback on what design work meets the standard Experience direction for the product Design decisions and product-wide alignment Innovation and craft advancement Design Manager supports by: Ensuring design standards are understood and adopted across the team Confirming experience direction is being followed Supporting practices and systems that scale without bottlenecking Facilitating design alignment across teams Providing resources and removing obstacles to great craft work The Circulatory System: Strategy & Flow Shared caretakers: Both Design Manager and Lead Designer The circulatory system is about how information, decisions, and energy flow through the team. When this system is healthy, strategic direction is clear, priorities are aligned, and the team can respond quickly to new opportunities or challenges. This is where true partnership happens. Both roles are responsible for keeping the circulation strong, but they’re bringing different perspectives to the table. Lead Designer contributes: User needs are met by the product Overall product quality and experience Strategic design initiatives Research-based user needs for each initiative Design Manager contributes: Communication to team and stakeholders Stakeholder management and alignment Cross-functional team accountability Strategic business initiatives Both collaborate on: Co-creation of strategy with leadership Team goals and prioritization approach Organizational structure decisions Success measures and frameworks Keeping the Organism Healthy The key to making this partnership sing is understanding that all three systems need to work together. A team with great craft skills but poor psychological safety will burn out. A team with great culture but weak craft execution will ship mediocre work. A team with both but poor strategic circulation will work hard on the wrong things. Be Explicit About Which System You’re Tending When you’re in a meeting about a design problem, it helps to acknowledge which system you’re primarily focused on. “I’m thinking about this from a team capacity perspective” (nervous system) or “I’m looking at this through the lens of user needs” (muscular system) gives everyone context for your input. This isn’t about staying in your lane. It’s about being transparent as to which lens you’re using, so the other person knows how to best add their perspective. Create Healthy Feedback Loops The most successful partnerships I’ve seen establish clear feedback loops between the systems: Nervous system signals to muscular system: “The team is struggling with confidence in their design skills” → Lead Designer provides more craft coaching and clearer standards. Muscular system signals to nervous system: “The team’s craft skills are advancing faster than their project complexity” → Design Manager finds more challenging growth opportunities. Both systems signal to circulatory system: “We’re seeing patterns in team health and craft development that suggest we need to adjust our strategic priorities.” Handle Handoffs Gracefully The most critical moments in this partnership are when something moves from one system to another. This might be when a design standard (muscular system) needs to be rolled out across the team (nervous system), or when a strategic initiative (circulatory system) needs specific craft execution (muscular system). Make these transitions explicit. “I’ve defined the new component standards. Can you help me think through how to get the team up to speed?” or “We’ve agreed on this strategic direction. I'm going to focus on the specific user experience approach from here.” Stay Curious, Not Territorial The Design Manager who never thinks about craft, or the Lead Designer who never considers team dynamics, is like a doctor who only looks at one body system. Great design leadership requires both people to care about the whole organism, even when they’re not the primary caretaker. This means asking questions rather than making assumptions. “What do you think about the team’s craft development in this area?” or “How do you see this impacting team morale and workload?” keeps both perspectives active in every decision. When the Organism Gets Sick Even with clear roles, this partnership can go sideways. Here are the most common failure modes I’ve seen: System Isolation The Design Manager focuses only on the nervous system and ignores craft development. The Lead Designer focuses only on the muscular system and ignores team dynamics. Both people retreat to their comfort zones and stop collaborating. The symptoms: Team members get mixed messages, work quality suffers, morale drops. The treatment: Reconnect around shared outcomes. What are you both trying to achieve? Usually it’s great design work that ships on time from a healthy team. Figure out how both systems serve that goal. Poor Circulation Strategic direction is unclear, priorities keep shifting, and neither role is taking responsibility for keeping information flowing. The symptoms: Team members are confused about priorities, work gets duplicated or dropped, deadlines are missed. The treatment: Explicitly assign responsibility for circulation. Who’s communicating what to whom? How often? What’s the feedback loop? Autoimmune Response One person feels threatened by the other’s expertise. The Design Manager thinks the Lead Designer is undermining their authority. The Lead Designer thinks the Design Manager doesn’t understand craft. The symptoms: Defensive behavior, territorial disputes, team members caught in the middle. The treatment: Remember that you’re both caretakers of the same organism. When one system fails, the whole team suffers. When both systems are healthy, the team thrives. The Payoff Yes, this model requires more communication. Yes, it requires both people to be secure enough to share responsibility for team health. But the payoff is worth it: better decisions, stronger teams, and design work that’s both excellent and sustainable. When both roles are healthy and working well together, you get the best of both worlds: deep craft expertise and strong people leadership. When one person is out sick, on vacation, or overwhelmed, the other can help maintain the team’s health. When a decision requires both the people perspective and the craft perspective, you’ve got both right there in the room. Most importantly, the framework scales. As your team grows, you can apply the same system thinking to new challenges. Need to launch a design system? Lead Designer tends to the muscular system (standards and implementation), Design Manager tends to the nervous system (team adoption and change management), and both tend to circulation (communication and stakeholder alignment). The Bottom Line The relationship between a Design Manager and Lead Designer isn’t about dividing territories. It’s about multiplying impact. When both roles understand they’re tending to different aspects of the same healthy organism, magic happens. The mind and body work together. The team gets both the strategic thinking and the craft excellence they need. And most importantly, the work that ships to users benefits from both perspectives. So the next time you’re in that meeting room, wondering why two people are talking about the same problem from different angles, remember: you’re watching shared leadership in action. And if it’s working well, both the mind and body of your design team are getting stronger.

#125. Dyania Health Runs Synapsis AI on Hospital-Owned GPU Systems

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (806 w)
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Unite

Dyania Health Runs Synapsis AI on Hospital-Owned GPU Systems

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (806 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that dyania Health and NVIDIA revealed on November 13, 2026 that Synapsis AI is running on hospital-owned NVIDIA accelerated computing, with an initial Cleveland Clinic study covering 7,812 aortic-valve replacement patients.
  • Dyania Health describes Synapsis AI as a clinical reasoning engine that reads years of notes, operative reports, imaging reports and laboratory results, then answers clinical questions with evidence linked to the chart.
  • It has been revealed that the deployment uses NVIDIA AI Enterprise across the software stack.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that dyania Health and NVIDIA revealed on November 13, 2026 that Synapsis AI is running on hospital-owned NVIDIA accelerated computing, with an initial Cleveland Clinic study covering 7,812 aortic-valve replacement patients. The collaboration is designed to review records across patient populations without moving them outside health-system networks.

Dyania Health describes Synapsis AI as a clinical reasoning engine that reads years of notes, operative reports, imaging reports and laboratory results, then answers clinical questions with evidence linked to the chart. Its outputs are clinical signals intended to show care teams which patients need attention and why; clinicians review the evidence and make every decision.

It has been revealed that the deployment uses NVIDIA AI Enterprise across the software stack. Dyania trains its proprietary clinical models with NeMo, then uses TensorRT and TensorRT-LLM to optimize inference on hospital GPU servers. Inference therefore stays within the hospital’s private network instead of sending patient records to an external environment.

NVIDIA stated the system remains assistive: it surfaces evidence from medical records that clinicians must confirm and act on. That distinction matters because the deployment automates chart review and signal detection, not the clinical decisions that follow.

The companies are targeting a manual bottleneck in hospital research and care management. Vital details often sit in narrative text rather than structured fields, limiting the charts staff can review for registries, outcomes studies and predictive models. Synapsis AI applies longitudinal review across a health system’s population, with potential uses including care-gap detection, observational research and clinical-trial matching.

According to recent reports, the study examined patients who received aortic valve replacements between 2005 and 2021, reviewing up to 16 years of care per patient. Synapsis AI answered 88 clinical questions for each patient covering valve characteristics, co-existing conditions, laboratory trends, medications, follow-up ultrasound measurements and subsequent clinical events. Much of that history was contained in narrative notes and echocardiogram reports.

It has been revealed that NVIDIA said the platform completed chart review across the full cohort, work that would have taken clinicians years to perform manually. The resulting dataset was used to train a predictive machine-learning model that estimates valve-failure and reintervention risk at three, five and 10 years and revises those estimates with each new ultrasound.

In a recent development, dyania reported that implanted valve type was the strongest determinant of how quickly a valve deteriorated, while age and other medical conditions influenced whether and when a second procedure occurred. The analysis also examined how follow-up information, such as post-surgery ultrasounds, can substantially raise predictive accuracy around future interventions.

“Using technology to bring together and analyze information that can help us predict the duration of implanted heart valves is a promising step towards enhanced outcomes and more personalized care for patients,” said Lars G. Svensson, chief of Cleveland Clinic’s Heart, Vascular & Thoracic Institute.

The study demonstrates dataset construction and risk prediction, not improved patient outcomes. Dyania says the tool is intended to inform care and requires external clinical validation before broader clinical reliance.

Sources indicate that dyania’s collaboration announcement claims the companies blueprint to pursue health-system deployments in the United States and internationally, publish joint case studies and integrate Synapsis AI with NVIDIA’s healthcare software stack. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Streaming giants are always finding new ways to upgrade the user experience and adapt to evolving usage patterns, and Peacock is the latest platform to take its mobile app in a new direction with its biggest overhaul yet.

NBCUniversal revealed a new era of the Peacock mobile app this week (November 11), showcasing a roster of fresh upgrades it hopes will not only enhance the experience, but increase user engagement and get viewers to spend more time browsing its seemingly endless library of titles.

The streamer notes it's already started testing the upcoming tools and will continue into 2027.

"Our ambition is for Peacock to be more than a place to watch," remarked Jim Denney, Chief Product Officer, Global Streaming & NBCUniversal Media Group.

"With this new mobile experience, we’re evolving Peacock into an entertainment platform that gives fans more ways to discover, participate, and strengthen their connection to their favorite stories, teams, and franchises, turning viewing into deeper engagement and lasting fandom and loyalty".

In a recent development, one of Peacock's most notable mobile upgrades is the addition of vertical video — which the platform states is integral to creating an experience that's separate from the one you get on a TV. Netflix jumped on this a while back, so it was only a matter of time before Peacock followed suit.

The fresh Clips Feed exists as its own section, designed to give you a new means of discovering new titles across entertainment and sports that isn't just simply scrolling the homepage.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

Sources indicate that peacock is also launching its newly introduced Franchise Hubs as a way to browse more content but with a community or fandom focus. This section of the app packs interactive games, live moments, and relevant episodes and podcasts centered on specific franchises, from Minions, Love Island USA, The Traitors, and more.

As well as short-form video, Peacock is jumping on the AI bandwagon, introducing conversational AI search to give you another way to find new content. With this new function, you can browse titles by name or, if you can't decide what to watch but know what mood or theme you're looking for, it can pull up content based on that information, which you can refine as the conversation progresses.

Audience behavior evolves; there's no doubt, so in order for streaming platforms to adapt to these shifts, they have to make some changes.

In the case of Spotify, for example, its Messages feature lifted a pain point with consumers by allowing them to share music and podcasts with their friends directly in the Spotify app, rather than having to screenshot everything and send it to group chats on other platforms. Those kinds of features are genuinely helpful, but even then, Spotify has also plagued its in-app hubs with short-form video, and I want to see the back end of it.

When Netflix first unveiled its vertical video feeds, I wasn't surprised per se, but I certainly grimaced at the very thought of it. And now that more services are taking advantage of it, it's suddenly becoming the upcoming norm.

But what gets under my skin most is how these vertical feeds are pitched to viewers. The streaming behemoths claim they're useful discovery tools, but at the crux of it, it's just another way to increase your screen time and how long you spend in apps. Doom-scrolling has taken over the social media landscape as it is; I don't need it to get in the way of how I browse movies and shows.

  • Industry observers note that "Language is not merely a set of unrelated sounds, clauses, rules, and meanings; it is a totally coherent system bound to context and behavior." — Kenneth L.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"Language is not merely a set of unrelated sounds, clauses, rules, and meanings; it is a totally coherent system bound to context and behavior." — Kenneth L. Pike The web has accents. So should our design systems. Design Systems as Living Languages Design systems aren't component libraries—they’re living languages. Tokens are phonemes, components are words, patterns are phrases, layouts are sentences. The conversations we build with users become the stories our products tell. But here’s what we've forgotten: the more fluently a language is spoken, the more accents it can support without losing meaning. English in Scotland differs from English in Sydney, yet both are unmistakably English. The language adapts to context while preserving core meaning. This couldn’t be more obvious to me, a Brazilian Portuguese speaker, who learned English with an American accent, and lives in Sydney. Our design systems must work the same way. Rigid adherence to visual rules creates brittle systems that break under contextual pressure. Fluent systems bend without breaking. Consistency becomes a prison The promise of design systems was simple: consistent components would accelerate development and unify experiences. But as systems matured and products grew more complex, that promise has become a prison. Teams file “exception” requests by the hundreds. Products launch with workarounds instead of system components. Designers spend more time defending consistency than solving user problems. Our design systems must learn to speak dialects. A design dialect is a systematic adaptation of a design system that maintains core principles while developing newly introduced patterns for specific contexts. Unlike one-off customizations or brand themes, dialects preserve the system’s essential grammar while expanding its vocabulary to serve different users, environments, or constraints. When Perfect Consistency Fails At Booking.com, I learned this lesson the hard way. We A/B-tested everything—color, copy, button shapes, even logo colors. As a professional with a graphic design education and experience building brand style guides, I found this shocking. While everyone fell in love with Airbnb’s pristine design system, Booking grew into a giant without ever considering visual consistency. The chaos taught me something profound: consistency isn’t ROI; solved problems are. At Shopify. Polaris (https://polaris-react.shopify.com/) was our crown jewel—a mature design language perfect for merchants on laptops. As a product team, we were expected to adopt Polaris as-is. Then my fulfillment team hit an “Oh, Ship!” moment, as we faced the challenge of building an app for warehouse pickers using our interface on shared, battered Android scanners in dim aisles, wearing thick gloves, scanning dozens of items per minute, many with limited levels of English understanding. Task completion with standard Polaris: 0%. Every component that worked beautifully for merchants failed completely for pickers. White backgrounds created glare. 44px tap targets were invisible to gloved fingers. Sentence-case labels took too long to parse. Multi-step flows confused non-native speakers. We faced a choice: abandon Polaris entirely, or teach it to speak warehouse. The Birth of a Dialect We chose evolution over revolution. Working within Polaris’s core principles—clarity, efficiency, consistency—we developed what we now call a design dialect: ConstraintFluent MoveRationaleGlare & low lightDark surfaces + light textReduce glare on low-DPI screensGloves & haste90px tap targets (~2cm)Accommodate thick glovesMultilingualSingle-task screens, plain languageReduce cognitive load Result: Task completion jumped from 0% to 100%. Onboarding time dropped from three weeks to one shift. This wasn’t customization or theming—this was a dialect: a systematic adaptation that maintained Polaris’s core grammar while developing new vocabulary for a specific context. Polaris hadn’t failed; it had learned to speak warehouse. The Flexibility Framework At Atlassian, working on the Jira platform—itself a system within the larger Atlassian system—I pushed for formalizing this insight. With dozens of products sharing a design language across different codebases, we needed systematic flexibility so we built directly into our ways of working. The old model—exception requests and special approvals—was failing at scale. We developed the Flexibility Framework to help designers define how flexible they wanted their components to be: TierActionOwnershipConsistentAdopt unchangedPlatform locks design + codeOpinionatedAdapt within boundsPlatform provides smart defaults, products customizeFlexibleExtend freelyPlatform defines behavior, products own presentation During a navigation redesign, we tiered every element. Logo and global search stayed Consistent. Breadcrumbs and contextual actions became Flexible. Product teams could immediately see where innovation was welcome and where consistency mattered. The Decision Ladder Flexibility needs boundaries. We created a simple ladder for evaluating when rules should bend: Good: Ship with existing system components. Fast, consistent, proven. Better: Stretch a component slightly. Document the change. Contribute improvements back to the system for all to use. Best: Prototype the ideal experience first. If user testing validates the benefit, revision the system to support it. The key question: “Which option lets users succeed fastest?” Rules are tools, not relics. Unity Beats Uniformity Gmail, Drive, and Maps are unmistakably Google—yet each speaks with its own accent. They achieve unity through shared principles, not cloned components. One extra week of debate over button color costs roughly $30K in engineer time. Unity is a brand outcome; fluency is a user outcome. When the two clash, side with the user. Governance Without Gates How do you maintain coherence while enabling dialects? Treat your system like a living vocabulary: Document every deviation – e.g., dialects/warehouse.md with before/after screenshots and rationale. Promote shared patterns – when three teams adopt a dialect independently, review it for core inclusion. Deprecate with context – retire old idioms via flags and migration notes, never a major-bang purge. A living dictionary scales better than a frozen rulebook. Start Small: Your First Dialect Ready to introduce dialects? Start with one broken experience: This week: Find one user flow where perfect consistency blocks task completion. Could be mobile users struggling with desktop-sized components, or accessibility needs your standard patterns don’t address. Document the context: What makes standard patterns fail here? Environmental constraints? User capabilities? Task urgency? Design one systematic change: Focus on behavior over aesthetics. If gloves are the problem, bigger targets aren’t “"breaking the system”"—they’re serving the user. Earn the variations and make them intentional. Test and measure: Does the change improve task completion? Time to productivity? User satisfaction? Show the savings: If that dialect frees even half a sprint, fluency has paid for itself. Beyond the Component Library We’re not managing design systems anymore—we’re cultivating design languages. Languages that grow with their speakers. Languages that develop accents without losing meaning. Languages that serve human needs over aesthetic ideals. The warehouse workers who went from 0% to 100% task completion didn’t care that our buttons broke the style guide. They cared that the buttons finally worked. Your users feel the same way. Give your system permission to speak their language.

I’d rather use Android XR glasses over Meta Ray-Bans for the app alone

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In trying out Google’s Intelligent Eyewear Android XR glasses for the first time, one of my main takeaways is that it’s the app, not necessarily the glasses themselves that would push me into using them over the mainstay Meta Ray-Bans.
  • Recent findings suggest that one of the inherent advantages that Android XR glasses were always going to have over third-party options is native integration.
  • The “Glasses” app on Android/Pixel, iOS, and Samsung Galaxy devices is dead simple.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In trying out Google’s Intelligent Eyewear Android XR glasses for the first time, one of my main takeaways is that it’s the app, not necessarily the glasses themselves that would push me into using them over the mainstay Meta Ray-Bans.

Recent findings suggest that one of the inherent advantages that Android XR glasses were always going to have over third-party options is native integration. It’s something we see frequently, and perhaps most well-known on smartwatches.

The “Glasses” app on Android/Pixel, iOS, and Samsung Galaxy devices is dead simple. While we can’t show you the full app just yet as the one we were able to try was not completely final, it’s a very simple experience.

The app opens to an overview of your glasses to show their connection and battery status, with settings below for Gemini, apps, the camera, and more. You’ll also be able to see things such as what the various lights on the glasses mean, tutorials, and more. There’s no bloat and no messing around – it’s a utility to just make adjustments or control the glasses as needed.

In a recent development, you’ll probably be using this app mostly to view the photos and videos captured on Android XR glasses. Google has this set up to auto-import photos in nearly real-time. It only takes about 4 seconds to import and the process starts immediately for photos. Videos, on the other hand, take longer and may need to be manually imported (for the sake of battery in part, Google mentioned).

Across the three main platforms, there are some differences. The iPhone app doesn’t import photos quite as fast, and Samsung has its own app to fit in with One UI’s design language for Galaxy users, but the core premise is the same across all three.

While we’ll have to see how this works in real life, I was blown away by how simple it all was, though that might be because the bar is below the floor.

Sources indicate that meta’s Ray-Bans (and newer Meta Glasses) dominate the smart glasses conversation, and I think that the app is one of the biggest problems. It’s certainly one of the biggest reasons I’ve barely touched my Wayfarers in recent months. That’s because, in early 2025, Meta replaced its dedicated “View” app for its glasses with a Meta AI app, which is just invasive and distasteful in my book. Meta is no stranger to shoving AI down the throat of its existing users. Another well-known move was converting Facebook and Instagram search into AI search boxes with creepy levels of context and invasive actions – it makes Google’s AI Overviews look tame by comparison. But I’d argue the most aggressive was this move with its glasses. Something as simple as tweaking a setting or importing a photo now forces you to dodge an AI chatbot.

Truly, Meta’s app is the worst, and I applaud Google for building a very simple utility for Android XR glasses instead.

#121. I star flight details and door codes in Google Messages to skip frustrating search menus

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (937 w)
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Androidpolice

I star flight details and door codes in Google Messages to skip frustrating search menus

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (937 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Androidpolice

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that keeping life organized can be challenging at the best of times.
  • It has been revealed that but when life gets busy, it's easy to trust Google Messages to keep track of all that stuff for me.
  • For instance, a friend who is flying in for a visit sends me their flight details and ETA as soon as they book the trip.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that keeping life organized can be challenging at the best of times. In an ideal world, I'd copy and paste every confirmation and tracking number I receive into Google Keep.

It has been revealed that but when life gets busy, it's easy to trust Google Messages to keep track of all that stuff for me. It does, but key details can also get lost in the shuffle of everyday conversation.

For instance, a friend who is flying in for a visit sends me their flight details and ETA as soon as they book the trip. Then we keep chatting.

By the time I'm supposed to pick them up at the airport, those details have scrolled back far enough to become a risk for carpal tunnel syndrome.

Recent findings suggest that search seems like an obvious alternative to scrolling, but that's where Google Messages starts to show its rough edges. Go looking for those details while you're rushing out the door, and you'd better be ready for an exercise in frustration.

Searching in Google Messages is good for finding tracking codes from automated SMS senders like FedEx, but it's not so great at ferreting information out of human chat threads.

Until recently, Messages only surfaced the most recent result from each conversation. If my friend used the word "flight" later on in the chat, or sent me other confirmation messages, like an Airbnb door code, those would come up instead of what I'm actually looking for.

Google fixed this in recent updates, which began rolling out in late September with a redesigned search. You'll now see multiple matches in each conversation. That's a nice bonus, but it has limitations.

Google Messages still operates on a simple keyword search. If you're looking for more than one piece of information, such as a flight number sent last month and a door code sent yesterday, you'll need to do two separate searches.

Worse, searching for generic words like "flight" and "code" will leave you wading through irrelevant results.

These types of frustrations make me want to copy and paste everything into Google Keep, but that can be time-consuming, especially for transient details like confirmation numbers.

Thankfully, Google Messages has a secret superpower: the ability to star individual messages in chat threads.

This lets you pull together every notable message in one place, and best of all, starring a message is almost effortless.

According to recent reports, to add a star to a message, long-press on it and choose Star from the menu that appears. A star icon appears in the lower-right corner to separate it from any reactions.

After you have a few starred messages, you can pull them all together by opening the search panel and tapping Starred. You may need to clear the keyboard or scroll down, since this appears near the bottom.

This view shows all of your starred messages, across multiple conversations, with the newest at the top. If you've starred images, they're shown in a separate section at the bottom.

Recent findings suggest that these are not grouped by thread. It's chronological, so multiple starred messages from the same person may be interspersed throughout.

According to recent reports, you can also tap any message from the Starred view if you want additional context. This takes you to that message in the appropriate conversation thread, and gives the bubble a quick highlight to help reorient you.

Sources indicate that you also can't search for starred messages. The Starred view doesn't offer direct search, and Google Messages isn't advanced enough to provide search operators like Gmail's "is:starred.".

That's why it's vital to only leave messages starred for as long as you need them. Otherwise, this view can become more cluttered than useful.

Sources indicate that the good news is that unstarring messages is even easier: tap the star in the lower-right corner of the message bubble, and it disappears. You can also use Unstar from the long-press menu, but that feels like extra work.

In a recent development, I find this is less effort than going through Google Keep to clean confirmation and tracking numbers. My mental inertia means that if I put that stuff in Keep, it's likely to live there longer than it should. Probably forever.

Recent findings suggest that that also means I need to avoid the temptation to star messages for sentimental reasons. I put those in Google Keep; otherwise, they'll get in the way of the data I actually need when I'm in a hurry.

I've found that starring beats searching even when I'm only looking for what should be a simple keyword, as I can't always count on people to use searchable words.

Industry observers note that for example, it's tough to search for an unknown four-digit number or a screenshot of a boarding pass when there's no accompanying contextual text. But I can star those and know they'll show up when I need them.

Plus, since I can jump from the Starred view to the exact spot in the conversation, I'm only a tap away from finding other details that might be in subsequent messages, such as an arrival gate.

That means I don't need to star every adjacent message — a "keystone" message that can anchor the rest.

Industry observers note that even though Google promises that Gemini will eventually be able to answer these questions for me, Gemini will be the first to tell me that it's an AI and can make mistakes. By contrast, the fault will not be in my stars. If I fail to star something, that's on me.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • CSS can now make choices about type that used to sit outside a reset.
  • I’ve put together tidy-typography.css, which gathers the useful parts into a default stylesheet: rendering and fallback rules, fluid sizing, vertical rhythm, wrapping, hyphenation, and OpenType detail.
  • It has been revealed that use it whole, or take the declaration that solves the particular irritation in front of you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CSS can now make choices about type that used to sit outside a reset. text-wrap: pretty can prevent a stranded word, container query units can scale a heading to the column it occupies, and text-box can trim the half-leading built into a line box. Some of these features are experimental and browser support is uneven, so they need guardrails rather than blind inclusion.

I’ve put together tidy-typography.css, which gathers the useful parts into a default stylesheet: rendering and fallback rules, fluid sizing, vertical rhythm, wrapping, hyphenation, and OpenType detail.

It has been revealed that use it whole, or take the declaration that solves the particular irritation in front of you. I’ll walk you through all the details in this article and give you the full code at the end.

font-synthesis: none stops a browser from inventing bold or italic when the family lacks that face. The smoothing and text-rendering declarations are rendering hints, mainly for WebKit; results still vary by platform.

Sources indicate that text-size-adjust disables mobile font inflation that can make a deliberately sized layout jump on rotation. font-size-adjust: from-font uses font metrics to reduce the apparent size change while a fallback swaps for a webfont.

(As with other snippets in this article, this ⁠:root block is a partial excerpt the final stylesheet combines it with additional custom properties defined later on.).

Industry observers note that viewport-based fluid type does not know how wide its element is. A heading in a narrow sidebar can therefore scale as though it fills the viewport.

It has been revealed that container-type: inline-size makes the wrapper a container query, so its children can use cqi: a unit based on the container rather than the viewport. Replacing vw in clamp() lets the same heading scale appropriately in an article column or a 300px sidebar without component-specific media queries.

line-height includes space above the cap-height and below the baseline: half-leading. It becomes obvious when text must align tightly with another element. text-box-trim removes it, while text-box-edge measures from capital-letter caps to the alphabetic baseline. This is a metrics-aware alternative to font-specific negative-margin nudges.

Selectors Level 5 proposes :heading, matching h1 to h6 and [role="heading"]. It has not landed in browsers, so keep it behind an @supports selector() check.

Sources indicate that default heading wrapping can leave one short final line. text-wrap: balance distributes text across its lines and works best for blocks of up to about six lines. For paragraphs, text-wrap: pretty avoids a stranded final word without balancing the whole block. Both replace JavaScript orphan fixers. Editable text needs text-wrap: stable, which prevents each newly introduced word from reshuffling the paragraph.

Recent findings suggest that hyphens: auto relies on the browser’s language dictionaries, so the document needs a correct lang attribute (for example ). Without one the browser has no dictionary to use and won’t be able to hyphenate text. Even with the correct lang, the defaults can leave tiny word fragments or several hyphenated lines in a row.

hyphenate-limit-chars controls the smallest breakable word and fragments; hyphenate-limit-lines prevents a ladder effect. hyphenate-limit-zone makes breaks less frequent, while hyphenate-limit-last protects the final word. Safari needs the prefixed equivalents, so declare both sets together.

Set code, variables, and headings to hyphens: manual: a broken code word can change meaning, and a hyphenated heading usually reads as an error.

According to recent reports, punctuation marks don’t carry the same visual weight as letters, so a quotation mark sitting at the start of a line can look slightly indented against the text below it. hanging-punctuation lets specified punctuation sit fractionally outside the text block’s edge.

According to recent reports, the first value handles opening punctuation, and last handles closing punctuation at the end of a block, while allow-end lets punctuation hang past the right edge rather than force-wrapping. The result is a text block whose edges read as genuinely flush.

Underlines have a related problem. Browsers apply flat, one-size-fits-all thickness and position regardless of the font’s actual weight.

In a recent development, text-decoration-thickness: from-font reads the thickness the font’s designer intended. text-underline-offset gives descenders room to breathe, and text-decoration-skip-ink: auto interrupts the underline wherever a descender crosses it rather than drawing straight through the letter.

In a recent development, variable fonts often include an optical size axis, or opsz. It lets a typeface use thinner strokes at large display sizes and thicker, more legible strokes when set small.

font-optical-sizing: auto lets the font make that adjustment based on its actual rendered size. The @supports block covers the older font-variation-settings syntax some browsers still need, while font-variant-ligatures and font-kerning enable the font’s own ligatures and kerning pairs.

Light text on a dark background genuinely reads heavier than the same weight on a light background. Where a font ships a GRAD, or grade, axis, the dark mode block dials that perceived weight down without changing glyph shape or width the way an actual weight change would. Fonts without a GRAD axis safely ignore the setting.

According to recent reports, mixing a monospace font into running prose often exposes a mismatched x-height at the same declared font-size. The size-adjust keyword, set once at the @font-face level, scales that font’s rendered output specifically, leaving the actual font-size value untouched.

Numbers in a table need identical widths so they stack into a clean column on the screen. Conversely, numbers in flowing text don’t need the same treatment and should sit naturally alongside the surrounding words.

Industry observers note that the tabular-nums and lining-nums keywords give table digits a fixed width and full cap height. oldstyle-nums and proportional-nums let digits sit alongside lowercase letters without sticking up and disrupting the sentence’s texture.

font-variant-emoji makes the choice between full-colour and monochrome emoji explicit. Without it, the browser or platform gets to choose a fallback, and the result can vary more than you expect. Apply .emoji-color or .emoji-mono to containers where you want to enforce that choice, rather than setting it globally on the body.

Quote style and character order differ by language and region. English nests single quotes inside double quotes, British English reverses that convention, and French uses guillemets with a thin space.

Industry observers note that the quotes property declares the order for each language through :lang(). The native q element then inserts the right pair through open-quote and close-quote. The same markup can render correctly in each locale without hardcoding characters into the content.

Wrapping the rules in :where() keeps them at zero specificity, so a project can override the quote style with one plain class.

Default sub and sup styling is synthesized. The browser just shrinks the text and shifts the baseline, rather than using glyphs actually designed for that position.

font-variant-position switches to the font’s own purpose-built sub and superscript glyphs where they exist, resetting vertical-align, font-size, and line-height so they don’t fight against the real glyph’s intended size and position. Most typefaces only include proper numerals rather than letters, so check the specific font before applying this broadly.

It has been revealed that :where() always resolves to zero specificity, which is useful for a reset. Every rule here is an opinionated default, and wrapping it in :where() lets a project override a property with a plain class.

:is() solves a different problem: repetition. The heading selector list appears several times in a typographic stylesheet, and grouping it avoids the risk of forgetting a level.

Unlike :where(), :is() carries the specificity of its most specific argument.

Here’s the complete reset, combining the stable layers. Unsupported declarations are ignored by the browser, so the stylesheet can be adopted gradually.

Much of this CSS removes work that used to leak into other parts of a build. text-wrap can take over orphan handling from JavaScript, container query units keep a component’s type scale tied to its own width, and text-box-trim avoids the negative margins once used to compensate for leading. quotes, font-variant-position, and font-optical-sizing hand several smaller details back to the language and the font instead of a collection of one-off fixes.

In a recent development, browser support will continue to change, especially for text-wrap and text-box-trim. Unsupported declarations are ignored, but that only helps when the unenhanced typography is acceptable in its own right.

According to recent reports, some of these rules are still too latest for a baseline reset. A news article, a marketing page, and an editable product interface do not ask the same things of their text; the set that belongs in yours depends on the font, the content, and the browsers you still need to support.

#119. Design for Amiability: Lessons from Vienna
