Design for Amiability: Lessons from Vienna

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (3987 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Alistapart

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today’s web is not always an amiable place.
  • According to recent reports, today’s web is not always an amiable place.
  • In a recent development, these tensions are often at odds with a site’s goals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today’s web is not always an amiable place. Sites greet you with a popover that demands assent to their cookie policy, and leave you with Taboola ads promising “One Weird Trick!” to cure your ailments. Social media sites are tuned for engagement, and few things are more engaging than a fight. Today it seems that people want to quarrel; I have seen flame wars among birders. These tensions are often at odds with a site’s goals. If we are providing support and advice to customers, we don’t want those customers to wrangle with each other. If we offer news about the latest research, we want readers to feel at ease; if we promote upcoming marches, we want our core supporters to feel comfortable and we want curious newcomers to feel welcome. In a study for a conference on the History of the Web, I looked to the origins of Computer Science in Vienna (1928-1934)  for a case study of the importance of amiability in a research community and the disastrous consequences of its loss. That story has interesting implications for web environments that promote amiable interaction among disparate, difficult (and sometimes disagreeable) people. The Vienna Circle Though people had been thinking about calculating engines and thinking machines from antiquity, Computing really got going in Depression-era Vienna. The people who worked out the theory had no interest in building machines; they wanted to puzzle out the limits of reason in the absence of divine authority. If we could not rely on God or Aristotle to tell us how to think, could we instead build arguments that were self-contained and demonstrably correct? Can we be sure that mathematics is consistent? Are there things that are true but that cannot be expressed in language? The core ideas were worked out in the weekly meetings (Thursdays at 6) of a group remembered as the Vienna Circle. They got together in the office of Professor Moritz Schlick at the University of Vienna to discuss problems in philosophy, math, and language. The intersection of physics and philosophy had long been a specialty of this Vienna department, and this work had placed them among the world leaders. Schlick’s colleague Hans Hahn was a central participant, and by 1928 Hahn brought along his graduate students Karl Menger and Kurt Gödel. Other frequent participants included philosopher Rudolf Carnap, psychologist Karl Popper, economist Ludwig von Mises (brought by his brother Frederick, a physicist),  graphic designer Otto Neurath (inventor of infographics), and architect Josef Frank (brought by his physicist brother, Phillip). Out-of-town visitors often joined, including the young Johnny von Neumann, Alfred Tarski, and the irascible Ludwig Wittgenstein. When Schlick’s office grew too dim, participants adjourned to a nearby café for additional discussion with an even larger circle of participants. This convivial circle was far from unique. An intersecting circle–Neurath, von Mises, Oskar Morgenstern–established the Austrian School of free-market economics. There were theatrical circles (Peter Lorre, Hedy Lamarr, Max Reinhardt), and literary circles. The café was where things happened. The interdisciplinarity of the group posed real challenges of temperament and understanding. Personalities were often a challenge. Gödel was convinced people were trying to poison him. Architect Josef Frank depended on contracts for public housing, which Mises opposed as wasteful. Wittgenstein’s temper had lost him his job as a secondary school teacher, and for some of these years he maintained a detailed list of whom he was willing to meet. Neurath was eager to detect muddled thinking and would interrupt a speaker with a shouted “Metaphysics!” The continuing amity of these meetings was facilitated by the personality of their leader, Moritz Schlick, who would be remembered as notably adept in keeping disagreements from becoming quarrels. In the Café The Viennese café of this era was long remembered as a particularly good place to argue with your friends, to read, and to write. Built to serve an imperial capital, the cafés found themselves with too much space and too few customers now that the Empire was gone. There was no need to turn tables: a café could only survive by coaxing customers to linger. Perhaps they would order another coffee, or one of their friends might drop by. One could play chess, or billiards, or read newspapers from abroad. Coffee was invariably served with a glass of purified spring water, still a novelty in an era in which most water was still unsafe to drink. That water glass would be refilled indefinitely. In the basement of one café, the poet Jura Soyfer staged “The End Of The World,” a musical comedy in which Professor Peep has discovered a comet heading for earth. Prof. Peep: The comet is going to destroy everybody! Hitler:  Destroying everybody is my business. Of course, coffee can be prepared in many ways, and the Viennese café developed a broad vocabulary to represent precisely how one preferred to drink it: melange, Einspänner, Brauner, Schwarzer, Kapuziner. This extensive customization, with correspondingly esoteric conventions of service, established the café as a comfortable and personal third space, a neutral ground in which anyone who could afford a coffee would be welcome. Viennese of this era were fastidious in their use of personal titles, of which an abundance were in common use. Café waiters greeted regular customers with titles too, but were careful to address their patrons with titles a notch or two greater than they deserved. A graduate student would be Doktor, an unpaid postdoc Professor. This assurance mattered all the more because so many members of the Circle (and so many other Viennese) came from elsewhere: Carnap from Wuppertal, Gödel from Brno, von Neumann from Budapest. No one was going to make fun of your clothes, mannerisms, or accent. Your friends wouldn’t be bothered by the pram in the hall. Everyone shared a Germanic Austrian literary and philosophical culture, not least those whose ancestors had been Eastern European Jews who knew that culture well, having read all about it in books. The amiability of the café circle was enhanced by its openness. Because the circle sometimes extended to architects and actors, people could feel less constrained to admit shortfalls in their understanding. It was soon discovered that marble tabletops made a useful surface for pencil sketches, serving all as an improvised and accessible blackboard. Comedies like “The End Of The World” and fictional newspaper sketches or feuilletons of writers like Joseph Roth and Stefan Zweig served as a second defense against disagreeable or churlish behavior. The knowledge that, if one got carried away, a parody of one’s remarks might shortly appear in Neue Freie Presse surely helped Professor Schlick keep matters in hand. The End Of Red Vienna Though Austria’s government drifted to the right after the War, Vienna’s city council had been Socialist, dedicated to public housing based on user-centered design, and embracing  ambitious programs of public outreach and adult education. In 1934 the Socialists lost a local election, and this era soon came to its end as the new administration focused on the imagined threat of the International Jewish Conspiracy. Most members of the Circle fled within months: von Neumann to Princeton, Neurath to Holland and Oxford, Popper to New Zealand, Carnap to Chicago. Prof. Schlick was murdered on the steps of the University by a student outraged by his former association with Jews. Jura Soyfer, who wrote “The End Of The World,” died in Buchenwald. In 1939, von Neumann finally convinced Gödel to accept a job in Princeton. Gödel was required to pay large fines to emigrate. The officer in charge of these fees would look back on this as the best posting of his career; his name was Eichmann. Design for Amiability An impressive literature recounts those discussions and the environment that facilitated the development of computing. How can we design for amiability? This is not just a matter of choosing rounded typefaces and a cheerful pastel palette. I believe we may identify eight distinct issues that exert design forces in usefully amiable directions. Seriousness: The Vienna Circle was wrestling with a notoriously difficult book—Wittgenstein’s Tractus Logico-Philosophicus—and a catalog of outstanding open questions in mathematics. They were concerned with consequential problems, not merely scoring points for debating. Constant reminders that the questions you are considering matter—not only that they are consequential or that those opposing you are scoundrels—help promote amity. Empiricism: The characteristic approach of the Vienna Circle demanded that knowledge be grounded either in direct observation or in rigorous reasoning. Disagreement, when it arose, could be settled by observation or by proof. If neither seemed ready to hand, the matter could not be settled. On these terms, one can seldom if ever demolish an opposing argument, and trolling is pointless. Abstraction: Disputes grow worse when losing the argument entails lost face or lost jobs. The Vienna Circle’s focus on theory—the limits of mathematics, the capability of language—promoted amity. Without seriousness, abstraction could have been merely academic, but the limits of reason and the consistency of mathematics were clearly serious. Formality: The punctilious demeanor of waiters and the elaborated rituals of coffee service helped to establish orderly attitudes amongst the argumentative participants. This stands in contrast to the contemptuous sneer that now dominates social media. Schlamperei: Members of the Vienna Circle maintained a global correspondence, and they knew their work was at the frontier of research. Still, this was Vienna, at the margins of Europe: old-fashioned, frumpy, and dingy. Many participants came from even more obscure backwaters. Most or all harbored the suspicion that they were really schleppers, and a tinge of the ridiculous helped to moderate tempers. The director of “The End Of The World” had to pass the hat for money to purchase a moon for the set, and thought it was funny enough to write up for publication. Openness: All sorts of people were involved in discussion, anyone might join in. Each week would bring different participants. Fluid borders reduce tension, and provide opportunities to broaden the range of discussion and the terms of engagement. Low entrance friction was characteristic of the café: anyone could come, and if you came twice you were virtually a regular. Permeable boundaries and café culture made it easier for moderating influences to draw in raconteurs and storytellers to defuse awkward moments, and Vienna’s cafés had no shortage of humorists. Openness counteracts the suspicion that promoters of amiability are exerting censorship. Parody: The environs of the Circle—the university office and the café—were unmistakably public. There were writers about, some of them renowned humorists. The prospect that one’s bad taste or bad behavior might be ridiculed in print kept discussion within bounds. The sanction of public humiliation, however, was itself made mild by the veneer of fiction; even if you got a little carried away and a character based on you made a splash in some newspaper fiction, it wasn’t the end of the world. Engagement: The subject matter was important to the participants, but it was esoteric: it did not matter very much to their mothers or their siblings. A small stumble or a minor humiliation could be shrugged off in ways that major media confrontations cannot. I believe it is notable that this environment was designed to promote amiability through several different voices. The café waiter flattered each newcomer and served everyone, and also kept out local pickpockets and drunks who would be mere disruptions. Schlick and other regulars kept discussion moving and on track. The fiction writers and raconteurs—perhaps the most peripheral of the participants—kept people in a good mood and reminded them that bad behavior could make anyone ridiculous. Crucially, each of these voices were human: you could reason with them. Algorithmic or AI moderators, however clever, are seldom perceived as reasonable. The café circles had no central authority or Moderator against whom everyone’s resentments might be focused. Even after the disaster of 1934, what people remembered were those cheerful arguments.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that CAPTCHAs are something most of us have come across while browsing the internet. Sometimes we're asked to identify traffic lights in pictures, solve a small puzzle, or simply tick a box to confirm we're human. Websites use these challenges to help distinguish real users from automated bots.

Recent findings suggest that but there's an interesting problem with this approach. What happens when a bot doesn't need to solve the CAPTCHA itself because a real person can solve it for them?

This is how CAPTCHA farms work. Attackers use services where real people solve CAPTCHA challenges on behalf of automated programs. The person completing the challenge is human, but the activity happening behind it may still be controlled by a bot. This makes it harder for websites to identify suspicious requests, even when their CAPTCHA system appears to be working correctly.

It has been revealed that here, we'll look at how CAPTCHA farm attacks work, why attackers use human solvers, and what makes these attacks difficult to detect. We'll also go through some of the security measures developers can use to identify suspicious activity and better protect their websites.

To understand how these attacks work, it helps to distinguish between the two primary ways attackers deal with verification gates: machine-driven recognition and human-driven outsourcing.

In an automated CAPTCHA-solving attack, an attacker uses computer vision models, optical character recognition (OCR), or neural networks to parse the challenge image and guess the answer without human intervention.

This approach is fast and computationally cheap, but it frequently fails when security vendors revision their visual distortions, introduce interactive logic puzzles, or assess human-like mouse kinematics.

Industry observers note that A CAPTCHA farm attack takes the opposite route. Instead of attempting to outsmart the defensive algorithm with software, the attacker routes the challenge to a human solving service. These commercial operations maintain large networks of manual workers who solve puzzles continuously around the clock. By inserting a human into the loop, the attacker converts what should be a technical roadblock into an outsourced labor pipeline.

Industry observers note that the attack doesn't break the cryptography or reverse-engineer the underlying challenge code. Instead, it relies on a CAPTCHA relay attack: software manages the speed and scale of the attack, while real human eyes provide the cognitive validation the website expects.

According to recent reports, A functional CAPTCHA farm is neither an ad-hoc group of rogue hackers nor an obscure black-box script. It's a commercial, multi-tiered infrastructure built around standard web development protocols.

Four distinct components work together to make the relay happen in a matter of seconds.

In a recent development, first is the attacker’s automated script. This client bot typically runs headlessly via browser automation tools like Puppeteer, Playwright, or custom HTTP client libraries. The script navigates to a target platform, such as a user registration portal, and fills in usernames, passwords, and demographic fields at machine speed until it hits a defensive challenge.

Second is the CAPTCHA-solving platform's API. Commercial solver platforms act as brokers between abuse operators and manual laborers. When the attacker's script encounters a challenge, it intercepts the site's public key, the challenge URL, and the visual assets, packaging them into an HTTP POST request directed at the solving service’s application programming interface (API).

Third is the distributed human workforce. Workers access these services through dedicated web dashboards, mobile apps, or browser plug-ins. When the API receives a task from an attacker, it pushes the image directly onto a worker’s screen. The worker identifies the bicycles or fire hydrants, types the distorted characters, or drags the puzzle slider into place, earning a microscopic payout, often ranging from $0.50 to $2.00 per thousand puzzles solved.

Fourth is the payload delivery back to the target. Once the worker submits the correct solution, the broker API returns the generated verification token back to the attacker’s script. The script injects this validation token into the target website's hidden form field and fires the final submission request. To the receiving server, the request bears an authentic verification signature generated by a real human session.

To see how these parts interact in practice, consider a credential-stuffing or mass-account registration campaign against an online service.

The entire loop completes well before typical session timeouts kick in, leaving the target server with no obvious visual anomaly to flag.

Building and maintaining custom neural networks to break modern visual challenges requires constant development effort. Defensive providers frequently alter noise patterns, camera angles, distortion algorithms and semantic puzzles specifically to break automated image classifiers.

It has been revealed that human solvers bypass this arms race entirely because the human visual cortex processes semantic context effortlessly. A person instantly understands what constitutes a "motorcycle," even if the image is cropped awkwardly, partially obscured by street foliage, or rendered under strange lighting.

This human adaptability is supported by extensive security research. In a foundational study, Towards Understanding the Security of Modern Image Captchas and Underground Captcha-Solving Services, researchers analyzed the commercial ecosystem across 152 solving platforms. They found that human-solving services achieved near-flawless accuracy rates across complex, diverse image challenges where purely automated computer vision solvers repeatedly struggled or degraded over time.

Industry observers note that outsourcing the problem is also remarkably inexpensive. Because labor pools are drawn from regions with low living costs, attackers can bypass thousands of protective checkpoints for less than the price of a cup of coffee. The workflow is highly scalable: software handles millions of connections, while human labor is summoned on-demand only for the few seconds required to clear a barrier.

Sources indicate that CAPTCHA farms rarely serve as self-contained attacks. Instead, they act as an operational enabler for wider abusive campaigns across the web.

First, they enable mass fake account creation. Malicious actors generate millions of disposable profiles on social media, dating networks, and developer platforms to distribute phishing links, spam search engines, or run coordinated disinformation campaigns.

They also facilitate credential stuffing. When attackers test databases of leaked usernames and passwords against banking or retail portals, defensive systems usually throw a CAPTCHA after a handful of failed attempts. Solver APIs allow the credential-testing bots to continue cycling through login credentials uninterrupted.

Industry observers note that inventory hoarding and scalping is another common use case. High-demand retail drops, concert tickets, and travel bookings are frequent targets. Security researchers tracking real-world bot traffic at DataDome documented an operation where an attacker combined bot automation with a CAPTCHA farm to orchestrate 18 million automated ticket-scalping attempts, successfully bypassing front-line interactive verification.

And they enable data scraping at scale. Web crawlers harvesting competitive pricing, directory databases, or intellectual property frequently utilize solver APIs whenever protected search and discovery pages present challenge gates.

In every case, the CAPTCHA farm doesn't execute the underlying abuse: it merely removes the specific verification tripwire meant to halt it.

Stopping CAPTCHA farms is inherently difficult because they exploit the core assumption behind standard challenge-response security: that the entity answering the challenge is the entity making the request.

It has been revealed that this systemic blind spot is analyzed in the research paper On the Security and Usability of Dynamic Cognitive Game CAPTCHAs, which evaluated how puzzle formats hold up against relay systems. The study demonstrated that regardless of how cognitively engaging, gamified, or technically dynamic a test is, relay architectures successfully decouple cognitive processing from the requesting client. The server receives a mathematically legitimate, human-generated solution token, making the puzzle itself effectively irrelevant.

Also, attackers route their client requests through residential proxy networks. The initial HTTP request comes from one residential IP address, the CAPTCHA is rendered by an automated browser mimicking common hardware profiles, and the solution is completed remotely. The defender’s server can't verify the physical proximity between the solver and the requesting client, creating an asymmetric advantage for the attacker.

Because human solvers can easily clear visual and cognitive challenges, treating a solved puzzle as a blanket guarantee of trustworthiness is no longer a viable defensive strategy. Web applications require a defense-in-depth model that monitors behaviors before, during, and long after a verification challenge appears.

Automated scripts can easily spoof screen resolutions and user-agent strings, but reproducing organic human cursor movement across an entire page requires far more work. Real people demonstrate micro-deviations, variable acceleration curves, pauses, and continuous mouse tremors.

When a CAPTCHA farm attack takes place, there's often a distinct behavioral mismatch: the form fields are filled out instantaneously or via scripted keyboard events, followed by an abrupt pause while the remote worker solves the puzzle, followed by an instantaneous token injection. Monitoring telemetry across the whole lifecycle of the page exposes this artificial stitching.

Sources indicate that defenders must assess context beyond the single page interaction. Inspecting TCP/IP packet behavior, TLS fingerprints (JA3/JA4 fingerprints), HTTP/2 frame parameters, and device APIs reveals whether the underlying runtime environment is a standard consumer browser or an orchestrated automation tool running inside a data center.

Relying entirely on puzzle solving often introduces accessibility barriers for real owners while doing little to stop funded attackers. As explored in research published by the Association for Computing Machinery regarding mCaptcha and Proof-of-Work Rate Limiting, defensive architectures can enforce cryptographic proof of work puzzles at the transport layer.

By forcing the connecting client's CPU to compute complex mathematical problems proportional to the platform's current traffic load, defense systems raise the economic and computational cost of running automated campaigns, neutralizing attacks without demanding manual human puzzle-solving.

Passing an authentication challenge should never grant unconditional trust. Web architectures should monitor post-login activity for anomalous actions:.

Identifying these signals allows security teams to invalidate sessions even if the initial challenge was solved cleanly.

Industry observers note that CAPTCHA farms show why websites can't rely on a single security check to keep automated attacks away. Even when someone successfully completes a CAPTCHA, the request may still be part of an automated operation.

CAPTCHAs are designed to check whether a person can solve a particular challenge. But they can't tell whether that person is the actual user trying to access the website or someone solving the challenge on behalf of a bot. This is one of the reasons CAPTCHA farms can bypass a security measure that would normally stop automated traffic.

According to recent reports, for developers, this means a completed CAPTCHA should be treated as just one part of the verification process. Websites also need to monitor user behavior, network activity, and suspicious requests to identify possible attacks. Combining these checks makes it easier to spot activity that a CAPTCHA alone might miss.

Industry observers note that CAPTCHA farms make it difficult for websites to tell whether a completed verification challenge actually came from a legitimate user. Even when a real person solves the puzzle, the request may still be part of an automated attack.

For developers, this means it's worth paying attention to what happens before and after a CAPTCHA is completed. Things like unusual login attempts, repeated requests, unexpected changes in user behavior, and suspicious account activity can provide useful clues.

It has been revealed that using CAPTCHA alongside rate limiting, behavioral monitoring, and other security checks can help websites identify these attacks more effectively. It's also important to review these protections regularly as attackers change how they operate.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Decagon announced on November 13, 2026 that Hertz is joining its Personal Agent Gateway in a pilot that will let renters ask Meta’s Muse to change or extend existing reservations and receive a confirmed outcome in the same conversation.

It has been revealed that the connection will use Poppy, Meta’s implementation of the open Personal Agent Protocol, to link Muse with Hertz’s AI-powered reservation and customer-support platform. Decagon describes Hertz as one of the first enterprises to give personal agents a direct channel, with Muse set to be the first personal agent on Hertz’s channel.

Recent findings suggest that for a renter who wants to keep a car for two extra days, Muse will send the request to a dedicated agent-to-agent channel alongside Hertz’s chat and voice channels, rather than requiring a phone call or a visit to Hertz’s website. Hertz’s Decagon agent will process the change and send the updated booking back to Muse for confirmation with the renter.

The request will use the same Agent Operating Procedures, or AOPs, that handle reservation requests in Hertz’s existing agent. Those procedures cover customer verification, rental policies and handoffs to live agents. The setup lets Hertz reuse reservation logic built for its other service channels while gaining visibility into requests arriving through the fresh one.

According to recent reports, hertz decides which requests are available through the channel, which actions occur, their order and the policies that apply. Muse will carry the renter’s request and the outcome, while Hertz’s own agent will fulfill it under that workflow. Hertz can expand the available request types as it learns from the pilot.

Yatin Patel, senior director of product management, customer experience and mobile app at Hertz, mentioned: “As more travelers begin using personal agents like Muse to proposal and manage their trips, our collaboration with Decagon allows us to explore new ways to serve customers while delivering the consistent, reliable experience they expect from Hertz.”.

In a recent development, decagon introduced Personal Agent Gateway on October 1, 2026 to identify personal agents, route their requests and control what they can do. Its detection function flags likely personal agents in live chat and voice, while the business decides what happens next and what those agents can access. The dedicated channel handles routing, trust and resolution for agents that identify themselves.

Permissions sit inside AOPs. A business defines the scopes an agent may request and marks the workflow sections requiring each scope; sections without the required scope are not exposed to the agent. Decagon claims that once those policies are set, additional personal agents can connect to the same channel and AOPs regardless of their authorization protocol, without rebuilding the workflow logic.

The pilot therefore tests whether Hertz can extend an existing reservation workflow to a customer’s personal agent without giving up control over scope or escalation. A confirmed booking returned through Muse would complete the agent-to-agent handoff, while visibility into pilot traffic gives Hertz a basis for deciding whether to add more request types.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google is reportedly in active development on new features for the Transit Mode on Pixel devices, specifically automatic triggers for features like Motion Assist and Take A Message.

According to recent reports, google is said to be working on automatic triggers for two Pixel features, one of which is Motion Assist and the other being Take A Message, with these triggers activating when Transit Mode is enabled. Transit Mode, for those unaware, is a mode that works similar in nature to Do Not Disturb Mode but with one key difference; it doesn’t block off notifications from everyone, like Do Not Disturb Mode does. Instead, it allows for preferred contacts and apps to communicate with you while everyone and everything else is blocked off.

It’s intended to curb distractions and minimize interruptions while driving. To coincide with these automatic triggers, Google developed Transit Mode 2.0, which detects when you’re in motion and now automatically turns itself on. This was pushed out as part of the most recent revision. There’s also reportedly a toggle for that so you can disable the automatic activation of Transit Mode 2.0.

In a recent development, much like the toggle for Transit Mode itself, there’s a toggle for Motion Assist that when enabled, allows the automatic trigger to push through. A screenshot from Android Authority shows this toggle just a couple of settings below the toggle for Transit Mode, with a toggle for Bluetooth as well.

With regard to Take A Message, there is code that Android Authority found within the app that shows Google is at the moment working on it receiving an automatic trigger as well. When enabled, this would automatically send voice calls directly to the voicemail, but only if you’re recognized as being in motion. There is currently no mention of a time frame for when this feature is going to arrive. Nor is there any indication of when Google will roll out the automatic trigger toggles for Motion Assist.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that I want to discuss accessibility because it is the most important thing for making websites. Other A List Apart articles give you innovation and insight. This article will give you homework. These are just my personal views, but they’re pretty good. I want to start off with a couple of statements, and you will agree: Designers are good people. I have never heard a designer say, “I don’t care if somebody can’t read this text”, “Not my fault if somebody can’t use this device”, or “Who cares if this is confusing?” Some designs exclude people. You have seen people unable to read the text on a website or app that somebody designed. You’ve seen people unable to use a physical device that somebody has designed. You’ve seen people utterly bamboozled while trying to use a service that somebody designed. So what? The first question is, “Is this life-or-death stuff?” The answer is, “Yes.” In my favorite essay, This Is All There Is, Aral Balkan makes the point that pretty much everything that we design can affect life events and death events. Aral gives the example of how even a straightforward bus timetable app can affect life and death events, if we design it badly: somebody might miss a life event, such as their daughter’s fifth birthday party; or somebody might miss a death event, such as the chance to say goodbye to a dying grandmother. The next—and frustrating—question is, “Why do some designs still exclude people?” After all, we know that: not everybody can see perfectly; not everybody can hear perfectly; not everybody thinks the same way; and not everybody moves the same way. I think the answer is that there’s too much to recall. Consider, if you will, the wide variety of topics that A List Apart articles cover. Designers are expected to remember all of that guidance, plus all of the accessibility guidance, plus so much more. It is too much. Recognizing accessibility concerns while designing I’d like to point toward one possible solution, starting from Jakob Nielsen’s 10 Usability Heuristics for User Interface Design. These are from the mid-1990s, and—although there’s a good chance that you, gentle reader, are a lot younger than that—please bear with me. Seeing as the problem is that there’s too much to recall, I want to look at heuristic № 6, “Recognition rather than Recall.” Jakob Nielsen said that for owners, information required to use the design should be visible or easily retrievable when needed. I suggest we tweak that to make life easier for designers. Let’s say that the information required to produce the design should be visible or easily retrievable when needed. In other words, let’s make it easier to recognise accessibility issues while we’re designing. How are we going to do that? I really like the book A Web for Everyone—Designing Accessible User Experiences by Sarah Horton and Whitney Quesenbery. I really like this book not only because it includes a quote from me—actually two quotes, but I don’t like to boast—but because it includes personas that are perfect for helping us to recognise accessibility issues. That’s the good news. The even better news is that these personas are available now for free on the companion website to the book What Every Engineer Should Know About Digital Accessibility, again by Sarah Horton, with David Sloan this time. Meet your users I’m going to introduce you to these personas now: Vishnu, an engineer and global citizen with low vision claims, “I want to be on the same level as everyone else”, “If I can adjust my screen, I can read comfortably”, and, “Translating in my head is easier with simpler sentences.” Trevor, a high school student with autism, says, “I like consistent, familiar places on the web”, “When I can learn the pattern, I can find my way”, and, “Reading is hard for me”. Steven, a deaf graphic artist and American Sign Language speaker, says, “My only disability is that everyone doesn’t sign”, and, “Without captions, it’s meaningless to me”. Maria, a bilingual community health worker, says, “I love this. It’s all here … when I can find it”, “When a site is confusing, I just leave”—fair enough, Maria!—and, “When I hear and see it, health information makes more sense”. Lea, an editor living with fatigue and pain, says, “No one gets that this really is a disability”, “Don’t make me work so hard”—please do not bombard this lady with drop-down lists—and, “Links at the top of the page make navigation easier for me”. Jacob, a blind paralegal and a bit of a geek, says, “The right technology lets me do anything”, and “This makes it possible to do my job”. Emily, who has cerebral palsy and is living independently, says, “I want to do everything for myself”, “Simpler screens are easier screens”—hell yeah, Emily!—and, “Tell me what I need in advance”. Carol, a grandmother with macular degeneration which affects her sight, says, “My grandkids are dragging me into the world of technology”, “I don’t understand what the screen is saying”, and, “Why can’t the text be just a little bit larger?” I want to throw one more persona at you now, because, well, A List Apart readers are overachievers. One of my favorite authors, Cennydd Bowles—who literally wrote the book on Future Ethics—says to create Personas Non Grata. In other words, every time we design something, we have to think about what a bad guy could do with that thing, and whom that might affect. To actually use these personas while designing, I like what Eric Meyer and Sara Wachter-Boettcher in Design for Real Life call the Designated Dissenter: for each project that you work on, one of your teams should be responsible for asking, “Will this work for Vishnu?”, “How’s Trevor going to get on with this?”, and so on. Then, once you’ve used the personas to recognise the accessibility issues, you can look up the guidelines for whichever platforms you’re designing for:  Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2 Accessibility designing — Material Design 3 Accessibility — Windows apps Accessibility | Apple Developer Documentation Check your interface for accessibility (Ubuntu) Your mission, should you choose to accept it I told you in the introduction of this article that I would give you homework. You thought I was joking. So, here’s your homework: I want you to grab the personas from the Know About Accessibility website, and use them throughout every design project to help you recognise accessibility issues while you work—and reclaim design for everyone. Even a club with a magnet inside that makes a convincing “thwack!” sound every time you swing it. But the AMVR GA2’s inclusion of a proper club head at the bottom does something fascinating for its physics, and I immediately noticed the difference at the end of the first course I played with this Quest 3 golf club.

Industry observers note that most VR golf club accessories, including the first-gen AMVR GA1, stick the controller at the bottom of the shaft where the head usually goes. This makes sense since you don’t hit a real ball with a VR golf club accessory; it’s all virtual. But, ironically, putting a proper golf club head on the end (and the controller in the middle of the shaft) apparently does make a difference. This one works with both the Meta Quest 3 and Quest 3S, but not the older Meta Quest 2 or Quest Pro.

In a recent development, I’m not going to delve into the physics of why this works, but it’s likely that shifting the fulcrum point improves it. I didn’t expect this at all. When AMVR told me about their new club, I accepted because the firm typically makes top-notch accessories. I really didn’t need another club in my extensive Quest 3 golf club collection. But I’m glad I did, because I’ve done much better than usual in my weekly Walkabout Mini Golf rounds with friends since I got it.

The mechanism for securing the controller onto the club is identical to previous AMVR controllers; only the location of the mount is different. Slide the controller (with wrist strap attached) into the holster. Click the rubber stopper in so the controller doesn’t move, then loop the wrist strap around the controller as a backup in case you didn’t secure the rubber stopper properly. It’s quite simple.

All major VR golf games allow custom spacing for Quest 3 golf clubs, so it doesn’t take more than 30 seconds to get comfortable with the club in your game of choice.

The only problem I’ve found with this club is its price. Most Quest 3 golf club accessories cost between $30 and $50, depending on the capabilities. This one is normally double that, but AMVR was kind enough to pass along a 25% off coupon for 9to5Google readers, making it more palatable if you’re looking to improve your VR golf scores. Just apply the coupon code 1FD4JYT5 at checkout on Amazon for an extra 25% off the AMVR GA2 golf club.

If you’re serious about your scores in Golf+, Walkabout Mini Golf, or another favorite of yours, this might just be the ultimate enthusiast Quest 3 golf club accessory.

Sources indicate that this is one reason I like shadcn/ui's approach. You don't install a traditional component package and treat its components as fixed. The CLI copies the source code into your project, where you can change it whenever you need to. For React Native, there's a project built around the same idea called React Native Reusables.

Recent findings suggest that to make this practical, I'll use React Native Reusables, Expo, and Uniwind to build a cart and checkout screen for a coffee shop's pickup orders. Sources indicate that before creating the app, let's look at the tools in this project. Each one has a specific job, and knowing that will make the setup easier to follow.

It has been revealed that shadcn/ui is a collection of UI components for the web. It's not installed as a package. Instead, a command-line tool (CLI) copies the source code of each component into your project, and from then on the code is yours to edit.

React Native Reusables is the React Native version of shadcn/ui. It gives you components such as Button, Card, Select, and Dialog that are written for React Native and styled with Tailwind-style class names. It uses the same CLI idea as shadcn/ui.

Sources indicate that RN Primitives is a React Native port of Radix UI, which is the library that shadcn/ui uses for behavior on the web. A "primitive" is a component that handles the behavior but has no styling. For example, the select primitive knows how a dropdown opens and closes and how it's declared to screen readers, but it has no colors or borders. React Native Reusables adds the looks on top.

Sources indicate that uniwind is a tool that lets you style React Native components with Tailwind CSS class names, such as className="bg-primary p-4". It converts those classes into regular React Native styles while the app is being bundled, so there's no extra work at runtime. Nativewind does a similar job, and React Native Reusables supports both. This tutorial uses Uniwind.

Expo and Expo Router provide the project setup, the development server, and file-based navigation. If you have used Next.js, Expo Router works in a similar way.

Sources indicate that this is not a component library. It is how you build your component library.

Sources indicate that you won't add shadcn/ui as a regular dependency in package.json. It uses a registry instead. A registry is a collection of JSON files hosted on a server. Each file describes a component and includes the information the CLI needs to add it to your project. When you run the CLI, it reads the relevant file and copies the component's source code into your project.

To see what this looks like, here's the registry entry for the Badge component. A Badge is a small label, such as the "Medium" tag next to a coffee in the cart you will build later. This is a shortened version of the real file:.

That's how a component gets from the registry into your app. The registry stores the component information, and the CLI uses it to create the files in your repository. React Native Reusables uses the shadcn CLI behind the scenes, so you can follow the same workflow when adding React Native components.

There are a few reasons this approach is useful when you're building an app:.

In a recent development, there's one trade-off to keep in mind. Since the component code is copied into your project, updates from the registry aren't applied automatically. If a bug is fixed upstream, you'll need to run the CLI again with --overwrite. If you have customized that component, you may also need to reapply your changes. This is worth considering before you make large changes to several components.

hitSlop={8} makes small buttons easier to tap. Apple recommends touch targets of at least 44 points and Android recommends 48dp, but a size-7 button is only 28 points wide. The hitSlop prop makes the touchable area larger without changing how the button looks. There's no CSS equivalent.

If you need more control, react-native-keyboard-controller is already a dependency of the template, and it provides KeyboardAwareScrollView and KeyboardProvider.

When you open the dropdown, it should appear right under the trigger at the same width, with a check mark next to the current value:.

Try picking a time and check that the trigger updates. Tap the words "Bringing my own cup" and confirm the switch flips. Type in the name field and confirm the keyboard doesn't cover it. If the dropdown opens and indicates nothing, check your PortalHost.

The bill component is pretty small, but there are two details you should pay particular attention to here, especially when the values change while someone is editing their order.

Create components/cart/bill.tsx:.

First, use tabular-nums on every number. Right-aligned prices in a proportional font don't line up at the decimal point, and using tabular-nums fixes that, as in the order rows.

Second, only show the discount row when it applies. The code uses {discount > 0 ? : null} instead of {discount && }. In JSX, if the left side of && is the number 0, React renders the 0. In React Native, a bare number outside a Text component throws the error Text strings must be rendered within a component. Using a boolean check and returning null avoids this whole category of bugs.

Recent findings suggest that to test it, turn on the own cup switch and scroll down. An Own cup line should appear with -$0.25, and the tax should change from $1.54 to $1.52, because tax is calculated on the discounted subtotal:.

It has been revealed that the total changes from $20.19 to $19.92, which is 27 cents lower instead of 25. The extra two cents come from the lower tax.

I want the total and checkout button to remain visible while the user scrolls through the cart. On the web, you might reach for position: sticky and bottom: 0. React Native doesn't work that way, but we can get the same result with a simple flex layout.

You can get the same result with Flexbox. This is the layout from Step 5 again:.

The outer View is a column. The ScrollView has flex-1, so it takes all the leftover height. The checkout bar is a sibling placed after it, so it sits at the bottom and doesn't scroll. You don't need any positioning or z-index.

According to recent reports, on phones without a home button, the bottom 34 points or so belong to the system. A button drawn there is hard or impossible to press. To avoid this, add the bottom safe area inset as padding.

According to recent reports, the bottom padding is an inline style instead of a class because its value depends on the device and is only known when the app runs. Using className and style on the same element is fine, and this is the case it's meant for.

On devices with no gesture bar, and in a browser tab, insets.bottom is 0, so the extra 12 keeps the bar from looking cramped.

Industry observers note that create the full component in components/cart/checkout-bar.tsx. It includes the confirmation dialog, which Step 10 explains.

border-t draws a line that's one logical point thick, which is two or three physical pixels on most modern screens. Next to a true one-pixel line, it looks heavy. React Native's StyleSheet.hairlineWidth gives you the thinnest line the screen can draw, and the template connects it to Tailwind with this line in global.css:.

This adds hairline to Tailwind's spacing scale, so h-hairline gives you a divider that's one physical pixel tall. The Common Mistakes section later explains one catch when you try to use it as an override.

That's the checkout bar in place. Scroll to the bottom of the screen and check that it stays below the bill:.

Scroll back to the top and the bar stays in the same place:.

On a phone with a notch, the button should be above the gesture bar. If you remove all items with the trash buttons, the button should be disabled and the label should say "Nothing in the cart".

The checkout bar already contains the confirmation dialog. Before putting the full screen together, there are two differences between the React Native implementation and the web version that are worth looking at.

Industry observers note that on iOS, it also wraps itself in FullWindowOverlay from react-native-screens, so it draws above the native navigation header instead of under it. This is handled inside alert-dialog.tsx, which is why that file imports something that looks unrelated.

AlertDialogFooter uses flex-col-reverse and only becomes a row at the sm: breakpoint. On a phone, the button you write last is shown on top. Writing Cancel first and Action second puts the confirm button where the thumb is and the cancel button below it.

According to recent reports, when the customer confirms the order, the confirm function calls Haptics.notificationAsync(Haptics.NotificationFeedbackType.Success). This gives a short success vibration on supported devices.

It has been revealed that you might expect to wrap this call in a platform check because browsers don't have the same haptics support as native apps. In this case, expo-haptics already includes a web implementation that uses navigator.vibrate, with a fallback for iOS Safari. If the browser can't provide haptics, the call simply does nothing, so we don't need an extra platform check.

In a recent development, notificationAsync is meant for outcomes such as success or failure. impactAsync is for physical collisions, and selectionAsync is for moving through a list of options. Using the wrong one won't cause an error, but it feels slightly off.

Now we can bring everything together in the main screen. This is where we'll keep the state, calculate the bill using billFor, and pass the required values and callbacks to each component.

Sources indicate that when an order is placed, it sets orderNumber, and the screen shows a confirmation instead. Inside that confirmation, changes the header title to "Order sent" without navigating anywhere, so the whole flow stays in one file and one route.

Sources indicate that notice that pickupLabel is the fix from Step 7 in use. The screen looks up the label from PICKUP_TIMES and passes a plain string to CheckoutBar, so CheckoutBar never touches an Option object or the incorrect web label.

Sources indicate that to test it, place an order. The dialog should show your name and the pickup time you chose (such as "in 30 minutes"), not the raw value 30. Confirm the order, and you should see the confirmation screen:.

Tap "Start another order" and the cart returns to its original state.

According to recent reports, the checkout screen is now working, and each part is kept in its own component. You can use the same approach when you build other screens: keep the component focused, pass the data it needs through props, and let the shared theme handle the styling.

In a recent development, we already added the theme toggle in Step 10. Here's the component again so we can look at how it switches between light and dark mode:.

In a recent development, this code also uses the ios: and web: prefixes. Uniwind supports platform variants, so web:mx-4 only adds margin in the browser, and ios:size-9 only applies on iOS. It's similar to Platform.select, but it stays inside the class string.

Three things aren't handled by setTheme, and if you forget them, you end up with a screen that's only partly dark. The template already sets up the first two.

React Navigation takes its colors from a plain object, so the root layout needs to pass it the right one:.

The clock and battery icons are drawn by the operating system, so you need to tell it which style to use. Without this, you can get dark text on a dark bar.

Uniwind.setTheme only applies to the current session. The next time the app starts, it follows the system setting again. To keep the user's choice, save it with expo-secure-store or AsyncStorage and call setTheme when the app starts. You can call setTheme('system') to go back to following the operating system.

When you tap the header icon, the cards, borders, inputs, switch, header, and status bar should all change together. You can explore more ready-made shadcn blocks if you want examples of how these components are used in larger interfaces:.

Look for anything that stays light while the rest goes dark. A light header usually means the ThemeProvider is not receiving the new NAV_THEME.

Industry observers note that the screen is right now using the default gray theme. Let's change it to a coffee-inspired palette with warm cream backgrounds and brown accents. This will also help us see why the palette needs to be updated in both global.css and lib/theme.ts.

Replace the @layer theme block in global.css with this coffee palette:.

Recent findings suggest that if you don't want to choose thirty colors by hand, you can generate a theme with the shadcn theme generator or tweakcn. Both export CSS variables, but you need to make two changes before the output works in this project:.

It has been revealed that also remove --radius from what you paste, because the template already defines it along with the derived sizes. Remove any --shadow-* variables too, since nothing in the registry reads them.

After you save and reload, the result looks like this:.

The page is cream, the button is brown, and the badges have the right color, but the header is still white with a visible line under it. The reason is that React Navigation draws the header using lib/theme.ts, and that file still has the old palette. Nothing is broken and nothing warns you, so this mistake is easy to miss. If you're designing the same interface in Figma, the shadcn Figma resources can also help you keep the design and implementation aligned.

This isn't a direct copy of global.css, so three points need explanation:.

After this change, the header and page match in both light and dark mode, and you didn't edit any component files:.

Sources indicate that switch between light and dark a few times and watch the header. If it's a shade lighter or darker than the page, one of the values in lib/theme.ts is still from the old palette.

If you're coming from web development, some of these differences may catch you off guard. I've collected the complications covered in the tutorial in the table below, along with the fix for each one. You can refer back to it when something doesn't behave as expected.

The last row needs more explanation, because it looks like a bug in cn(), but it's not.

cn() uses tailwind-merge, which resolves conflicts between classes. It knows the default Tailwind scale, but it doesn't know about custom values you declare in global.css. The value hairline comes from --spacing-hairline: hairlineWidth(), so tailwind-merge can't tell that h-hairline and h-[1px] set the same property, and it keeps both:.

In a recent development, the second result is correct. In the first, which height wins depends on the order of the CSS. The other overrides in this tutorial, such as size-14 over size-8, work correctly because those are names tailwind-merge recognizes. If you want it to understand your custom scale, you can teach it with extendTailwindMerge in lib/utils.ts. Otherwise, use an arbitrary value, or edit the component file directly, since you own it.

There's a related case in the stepper buttons. They pass size-7 to a Button whose icon size is h-10 w-10 sm:h-9 sm:w-9:.

Recent findings suggest that size-7 replaces the base h-10 w-10, but the two sm: classes stay, because tailwind-merge treats a responsive variant as a different class. On a phone this makes no difference, since sm: starts at 640px and phones are narrower than that. In a desktop browser, though, those buttons grow to 36 points.

In this tutorial, we built a coffee shop cart and checkout screen with React Native Reusables, Expo, and Uniwind. We added the order rows, pickup options, bill summary, fixed checkout bar, and confirmation dialog. We also looked at how the registry and CLI add component source code to the project and how the theme tokens control the app's colors.

Recent findings suggest that one thing worth getting into the habit of is checking the component source when something doesn't behave the way you expect. Since the components live in your project, you can open them and see how they work. That's how we understood the difference in the Select label between web and native. It also makes customization easier because you can see which part of the component needs to change instead of adding more workarounds around it.

You can find the complete project in the GitHub repository. If you run into an glitch or want to compare your code with the finished screen, clone the repository and check the implementation. If you're looking for more complete starting points for your next project, take a look at shadcn templates.

I captured the screenshots using the React Native Web build at a phone-sized viewport. The same project also runs on iOS and Android. I've called out the platform differences in the relevant sections, including the Select label and portal host in Step 7, safe area handling in Step 9, and haptics in Step 10.

#110. Designed for a Dead Language

Designed for a Dead Language

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3006 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Alistapart

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every language app in your pocket inherited a teaching method built for Latin.
  • Every language app in your pocket inherited a teaching method built for Latin.
  • In 1788, Prussia introduced the Abitur, a standardized national examination required for entry into universities and the civil service.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every language app in your pocket inherited a teaching method built for Latin. Understanding why that happened is a more useful design lesson than anything the apps themselves will teach you. In 1788, Prussia introduced the Abitur, a standardized national examination required for entry into universities and the civil service. To pass it, students needed to demonstrate measurable, gradable knowledge. The system needed to teach language to large classrooms, produce consistent outcomes, and do it with one teacher and thirty students. The educators responsible for designing this system reached for the only teaching template they had, one that had been used in European schools for two centuries: the method developed to teach Latin. Latin, by 1788, was a dead language. Nobody needed to speak it. The scholars who studied it were reading Cicero and Virgil, not conducting conversations. The method built around it, memorizing grammar rules, constructing translations, analyzing written texts, reflected that reality exactly. Oral skills were irrelevant. Comprehension of written form was everything. The method was not designed to produce speakers. It was designed to produce readers of texts in a language nobody spoke. When Prussia applied this template to French and German, living languages spoken by living people, the premise did not change. Johann Valentin Meidinger's textbook Praktische Französische Grammatik, published in 1804, ran to 37 editions across Europe by 1857. Karl Plotz formalized the approach into what became the dominant model for teaching modern languages across Europe and eventually the United States, where it became known simply as the Prussian Method [1]. Each institution that adopted it trained teachers in it, who trained students who became teachers. The constraint that created the method, how do you grade language at scale with limited resources, became invisible inside the method itself. What remained was the assumption: language is a body of rules to be learned consciously and measured. It was a design decision dressed up, over time, as a pedagogical truth. The observation that should have ended it There are people in the world who cannot read or write a language and speak it fluently. There are children who hold full conversations years before they can read a single word. There are immigrants who arrive in a country knowing nothing of its language and come out, years later, speaking it naturally, not because they studied it, but because they lived inside it. Literacy and fluency are separate things produced by entirely separate mechanisms. The Grammar-Translation method, as it became known, assumed they were the same thing. That assumption was inherited from a method designed for a language nobody needed to speak, and it was wrong the moment it was applied to a language people actually used. The evidence against it accumulated slowly. In the mid to late nineteenth century, reformers including François Gouin in France and Maximilian Berlitz in the United States argued independently that language should be taught the way it is actually acquired, through immersive exposure to real communication in the target language, not through analysis of its rules. Berlitz built an entire school network around this principle. The reformers were correct. They were also largely ignored by mainstream education systems, because the Grammar-Translation method had one decisive advantage that direct immersion did not: it could be graded. In 1982, the linguist Stephen Krashen gave the argument its most formal articulation in what he called the Monitor Model of second language acquisition. His distinction was precise: language acquisition, the unconscious process through which children absorb their native language and through which adults succeed in immersive environments, is categorically different from language learning, the conscious study of grammar rules and vocabulary that classrooms deliver [2]. Acquisition produces fluency. Learning, at best, produces the ability to pass a test. The evidence supporting this distinction, and the observation that immersive exposure to real native-speaker communication is the mechanism that produces genuine fluency, has only grown since. I went to Brazil without a word of Portuguese and came out speaking it. I studied French in a classroom for years and cannot hold a conversation in French today. This is not an unusual experience. It is the expected outcome, and it has been the expected outcome for as long as we have had formal language education. The same decision, made again in a different medium Prussian educators faced the question: How do you deliver language learning at scale, measure progress, and retain consumers over time? The answer it arrived at was structurally identical to the one arrived at in 1788. Duolingo gamified the grammar drill into a streak. Anki formalized the translation exercise into a spaced-repetition flashcard. Babbel organized grammar lessons into structured modules. The interfaces were latest. The underlying assumption, that language is a thing you study rather than an environment you inhabit, was not. This was not a failure of design skill. The products that emerged from these decisions are, in many respects, genuinely well-crafted. Duolingo's retention mechanics are sophisticated. Anki's spaced repetition is grounded in real cognitive science. They are excellent at what they actually do. The problem is what they actually do: produce measurable engagement with a proxy for language rather than the conditions that produce language itself. A streak is measurable. A vocabulary score is measurable. The moment a user walks out of an app and holds a real conversation in another language, that happens in the world, outside the product, and cannot be instrumented. When the outcome a user needs is difficult to measure directly, the design process tends to reach for something that can be measured. The proxy becomes the goal. The interface optimizes for it. The gap between what the product delivers and what the user actually needed grows. This is not a pattern unique to language learning. It is a pattern that repeats across product categories whenever a design constraint—the need to measure, the need to scale, the need to produce a grade—gets built into a system so deeply that it stops being visible as a constraint and starts being mistaken for a truth about the problem itself. What happens when the constraint changes The constraint that made the Grammar-Translation method necessary in 1788 was real and rational. One teacher. Thirty students. A standardized exam. You cannot grade a conversation at scale. You can grade a translation exercise. The method was not chosen because it produced fluency. It was chosen because it produced a score. That constraint no longer exists in the same form. Technology has made it possible to deliver immersive, real-time conversation practice to anyone with a smartphone, at a cost that continues to fall. The design problem is no longer how to make language learning gradable at scale. It is how to make the conditions of genuine language acquisition accessible to people who cannot move to another country or afford a native-speaker tutor. The products that are now closest to solving the actual problem are not the ones that invented a new pedagogy. They are the ones that removed the access barrier to an old one. Praktika builds AI conversation partners with distinct personalities, regional dialects, and cultural context, replicating the specificity of a real native speaker rather than a generic language-learning voice. Langua clones native speaker voices so that the interaction feels like a real conversation rather than a lesson. Rosetta Stone's foundational methodology, image association in the target language with no translation, was built on the same insight Berlitz arrived at in the nineteenth century: language is acquired through immersive exposure, not through analysis of its rules [3]. A 2025 meta-analysis of 31 studies found that AI conversation tools produced a statistically significant improvement in language learning outcomes, a result that no amount of flashcard optimization has consistently matched [4]. None of these products invented a new theory of language acquisition. They translated an existing one into something more people could reach. The design question this leaves The Grammar-Translation method persisted not because educators were wrong about design, but because a design decision made under a specific constraint became, over two centuries, indistinguishable from the thing itself. The constraint, how do you grade language at scale, was forgotten. The method it produced was inherited as if it were a description of how language works, passed from Prussia to Europe to America to the App Store, from the grammar drill to the streak. Every time a design team optimizes for a metric because the actual outcome is hard to measure, they are making a version of the same decision. It is often the right decision given real constraints. The question worth asking is whether the constraint that made it necessary still exists, or whether it has simply become invisible inside the system it originally produced. Before reaching for what can be measured, it is worth asking what the user actually needs to do, and what stopped them from doing it before. Sometimes the answer is a new solution. More often it is an old one that was always out of reach.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Getting your hands on fast NVMe storage for your PC or laptop has become extremely challenging. That said, the Samsung 990 SSD is currently available at a discounted price of $189.99, against its original list price of $229.99 on Amazon. Although the $40 saving might not seem that impressive, deals on high-performance internal SSDs are becoming harder to come by amid the ongoing NAND and DRAM crisis. If you've been holding off on a storage upgrade, this could be a good opportunity to pick up a reliable, high-speed SSD.

Recent findings suggest that the Samsung 990 is a PCIe 4.0 NVMe SSD that uses Samsung's latest V9 QLC NAND flash memory and a DRAM-less controller. It was introduced earlier this year with MSRPs of $269.99 for the 1TB model and $529.99 for the 2TB model. The 1TB model offers sequential read and write speeds of up to 7,150 MB/s and 6,450 MB/s, making it an excellent option for everyday computing, gaming, and handling large files. Samsung rates the drive for up to 400TB of written data, although it offers just three years of warranty. It features a single-sided M.2 2280 design, which should make it compatible with a wide range of desktop motherboards, laptops, and even mini-PCs.

Samsung's 990 is rated for read speeds of up to 7,150 MB/s and write speeds of up to 6,450 MB/s, offering plenty of bandwidth for modern games, large files, and everyday applications.

In our testing of the 2TB variant, we found that the Samsung 990 delivers reasonably good all-around performance, particularly for gaming and everyday applications. It offered similar performance to the Samsung 990 EVO Plus in some tests. However, it fell behind competing drives such as the Crucial P310 and WD Blue SN5100 in others, particularly during file transfers. One of its biggest advantages is its large write cache, which allows it to maintain speeds of nearly 6,100 MB/s for more than 57 seconds before performance drops once the cache is exhausted. Its power efficiency may not be the best, but overall it is a competent budget PCIe 4.0 SSD.

For anyone upgrading from an older SATA SSD or a traditional hard drive, the Samsung 990 should offer a noticeable improvement in boot times, application loading, and overall system responsiveness. At its current price of $189.99, it is also a suitable option for expanding game storage without spending a fortune.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From payment cards to transport passes to ID cards, Google Wallet can store a lot. It's a remarkable place to store key documents, but until recently it hasn't been able to store the item that nobody wants to store in their wallets but ends up with anyway.

I'm talking about receipts. Crumpled, dirty, and illegible, they plague our wallets with their unnecessary relevance.

Fortunately, Google has saved us from these scrunched-up annoyances by letting us not only store receipts, but also track them in Google Wallet.

Recent findings suggest that the app doesn't have a dedicated "Add receipt to Google Wallet" button. Instead, it identifies the receipt and draws the relevant information.

According to recent reports, the process is automatic, so you can't edit the information after scanning. Complicated receipts with lots of codes and numbers can confuse it, but in my testing, it got the vendor and payment amounts correct every time.

Industry observers note that in one case, I tried scanning a Post Office receipt twice. While it correctly identified the vendor and the transaction value, it identified a different code as the order number after each scan.

Industry observers note that I don't blame the app for getting it wrong; I don't have a clue what these codes mean. However, it's worth double-checking that the app pulls the correct data if you need to record information like this.

Google Wallet saves a photo of the receipt with each scan, so you can reference the full receipt there.

When added, you can find the receipt by heading to the Transactions tab, found by tapping the View More button.

Google Wallet tracks digital receipts sent to a Gmail address. All email receipts are scanned and sorted into Wallet for later reference, along with a link to the original email.

The only way to separate these from in-person transactions is to search for "receipts" in the app. It groups digital and physical receipts, so you have a total record of all your transactions.

The one thing that Google does wrong with Google Wallet is not informing customers of its best features.

If I relied on Google's apps to tell me about newly introduced features, I never would have noticed I could scan receipts into Google Wallet.

Google has taken a significant step to solve this problem by adding an in-app message center to Google Wallet, but in my app it only shows me a tip for paying contactless, something I've been doing for years.

Google Wallet can store boarding passes, event tickets, transit passes, loyalty cards, gift cards, hotel keys, corporate badges, student IDs, driver's licenses, passports, health insurance cards, vaccination records, and more.

It can replace transit apps, gym apps, shopping apps, and, in a limited way, banking apps.

It's a remarkable app that can store huge amounts of useful information, so if you're only using it for bank cards, give it another look.

As soon as I scan a receipt in Google Wallet, I can safely throw the receipt away. All the information is stored on my phone, so why do I need it cluttering up my wallet?

It has been revealed that I carry plenty of other miscellaneous documents that I would love to store in Google Wallet. Yes, I can scan them to my phone, but I want them in the same place I keep them in reality, in my wallet.

In a recent development, if I try to scan any other document, Google Wallet tries to force it into one of the existing categories. This means relevant information doesn't get copied over, and I can't search for it easily.

It has been revealed that google Wallet needs custom categories where I can save documents that don't fit into the existing categories. As it stands, if I try to store them, they get lost in the noise.

While I think Google Wallet could improve its organization features (why do I have to search for "receipts"?), it's an excellent repository for my various documents.

Adding support for miscellaneous physical documents like receipts helps reduce physical clutter while keeping things on hand.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that cloudflare revealed on November 13, 2026 that Kitesurf, its experimental browser engine for AI agents, is now available as open source under the Apache 2.0 license.
  • Recent findings suggest that the public repository gives developers the option to operate and alter the engine in their own Cloudflare accounts instead of relying solely on its managed Browser Run APIs.
  • Kitesurf turns HTML and CSS into rendered pages, executes page JavaScript and produces screenshots without Chrome or a browser container.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that cloudflare revealed on November 13, 2026 that Kitesurf, its experimental browser engine for AI agents, is now available as open source under the Apache 2.0 license. Developers can inspect and modify the code, run it locally, or deploy their own instance on Cloudflare Workers.

Recent findings suggest that the public repository gives developers the option to operate and alter the engine in their own Cloudflare accounts instead of relying solely on its managed Browser Run APIs. Cloudflare had promised this step when it introduced Kitesurf on August 6, 2026, and again in a September 28, 2026 upgrade that added WebMCP support, expanded browser API and Browser Run coverage, and introduced terminal rendering.

Kitesurf turns HTML and CSS into rendered pages, executes page JavaScript and produces screenshots without Chrome or a browser container. It exposes a Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) endpoint, the control interface used by Chrome DevTools and compatible automation software, allowing Puppeteer clients and AI agent harnesses to connect.

Internally, the Engine coordinates browser sessions and client connections, PageScript runs the page and its JavaScript, and PageRenderer produces the visual result. Cloudflare’s Developer Platform is combined with Rust components compiled to WebAssembly: Blitz supplies HTML parsing, DOM, layout and painting; Stylo handles CSS; Linebender libraries cover text and 2D graphics; and Krilla creates PDF output. Boa provides a fallback JavaScript runtime inside WebAssembly when the page’s code cannot run in Dynamic Workers.

Statelessness is another part of that design. The Engine retains session state, while other components are disposable where possible, allowing capacity to track bursts of agent activity. PageRenderer holds no persistent page state, so the Engine can replace it after a failed or stalled rendering request.

Local development requires Bazelisk, Node.js 22 or newer and pnpm 9.15.4. The development command builds the WebAssembly modules and page and renderer bundles, then starts a local engine at 127.0.0.1:8787. The initial build compiles the Rust core and vendored dependencies, while later builds reuse Bazel’s cache. Developers can then inspect pages through Chrome DevTools or attach Puppeteer and other CDP clients.

It has been revealed that deployment on Cloudflare requires a Workers Paid strategy because Dynamic Workers create the isolated workers used for pages and renderers. After testing locally, operators can deploy the engine to their own account as an alternative to Browser Run’s managed APIs.

Self-hosting also transfers an notable security responsibility. The engine has no authentication of its own, and its workers.dev address is public by default. Without Cloudflare Access or another authentication layer, anyone with the URL could browse through the engine, connect CDP clients, problem requests originating from the operator’s Cloudflare account and consume paid CPU time and Dynamic Workers. The repository instructs operators to protect the URL immediately and explains how to enable Access across the account before deployment to avoid a public interval.

Kitesurf remains experimental and under heavy development. The repository describes it as a CDP endpoint rather than a complete Chrome implementation, with some Chrome DevTools features still unsupported. Cloudflare is prioritizing compatibility, reliability and efficiency.

Sources indicate that at the August launch, Cloudflare noted Kitesurf was not yet suitable for video, WebGL, bot-challenge handshakes requiring real TLS fingerprints, or long authenticated sessions that depend on persistent state. Those limitations illustrate the compatibility checks that still matter for agent workloads, even where a lighter browser’s resource use is attractive.

Industry observers note that the contribution process is structured around that ongoing work. Cloudflare asks prospective contributors to open an problem with a minimal reproduction or proposed approach and obtain maintainer vouching before submitting a pull request. Focused changes with tests and a defined scope are preferred, although reproducible rendering bugs, failing automation workflows and documentation corrections are also welcome.

For developers, the trade-off is direct control of the browser stack in exchange for securing the deployment themselves and accommodating an engine whose Chrome and web-platform compatibility remains incomplete.

I’ve been bashing on updating this site’s design for the last couple of weeks. It’s high time things get a fresh coat of paint, right? The last version of CSS-Tricks was pushed five years ago. That’s ancient in web (and dog) years.
