Industry observers note that now, before there’s a chorus of “things don’t look thaaaat different” I want to say I’m rarely a fan of complete re-builds and tend to lean into iterative releases. And the new v20 theme is what I’d call an iterative rollup that’s worthy of a version bump.

Let’s go over the most notable updates to see why.

First and foremost, some of the biggest changes are what you don’t see. As you might imagine, this site has carried over plenty of pieces across 19 years. I decided to excavate the theme and definitely found some ghosts to bust.

Things like handling embedded versions of the newsletter from before we began self-hosting the posts. There were relics that catered specifically to the Flexbox Guide for handling toggles back before we had proper HTML . There was a jQuery lazy-loader thing that is well-covered by WordPress core now. I also decided to formally retire the CSS-Tricks Forum. We put it in “archive mode” back in, like, 2018. None of those discussions are particularly valuable for today as they were over 10 years ago, so I deactivated the bbPress plugin that powered it and cleared out the database… and wow, that carved a whopping 400 MB from the ol’ database, not to mention it allowed me to drop several custom templates from the theme.

It has been revealed that there were more ghosts busted along the way and, to be sure, there are still some lurking around. But it’s way less scary poking around the theme directory now, and further cleanup should be a lot easier from here on out.

Yeah, yeah, raise your hand if you’re still running Gulp. We are 🙋‍♂️. That’s not a bad thing in and of itself, but keeping it in a fixed state for all this time is not the greatest. Industry observers note that for years, I endured the same errors every time I fired up a new terminal. Those are gone and things run super cleanly, not to mention quickly. Very happy here.

Oof, this is everyone’s favorite job, right?! Aside from being able to spot and fix a few unescaped custom field calls here and there, I decided to ask Claude to help me with a holistic audit. I prompted it to review recent WordPress security release notes and identify areas where the theme could be hardened to comply with what WordPress is doing.

Recent findings suggest that whoa, you used AI? Yeah, I sure did. But for things like this where it could be my little gopher and allow me more time to do what I do best: front-end. I’m still able to make most of the patches myself based on the output recommendations, but it’s nice to have a gut-check for things where I’m clearly no expert, like security.

I still use and like Sass very much. I mean, yes, I would like to be straight-up vanilla CSS everywhere, but I can’t tear myself away from partials in particular.

I’m happy here. There are some things I just don’t have the control to fix when it comes to performance, so seeing v20 come in consistent with v19 is just fine by me. Members of your household with the Google Home app can add the digital home key to their own personal Google Wallets, too.

The update is currently available as part of Public Preview for the Google Home app, but will roll out to more people in the coming weeks.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Learning on my phone used to feel unnecessarily complicated. I'd jump between YouTube videos, articles, notes, and course apps when I wanted to understand something upcoming.

According to recent reports, still, I felt like I wasn't making progress. The material lived across apps on my phone, and keeping track of where I left off took more effort than the learning itself.

I wanted an easier way to stay on track without juggling multiple tools.

That's when I stumbled into Guided Learning, a Gemini feature I'd mostly been ignoring, and slowly realized I was opening my learning apps less and less.

I kept downloading learning apps, thinking they'd make me more productive or help me pick up upcoming skills faster.

In a recent development, at first, everything seemed fine. The courses were well-designed, and the progress bars made me feel like I was moving forward.

It has been revealed that but after a few days, the shine wore off. Each app demanded its own attention. Where did I leave off? Was I ready for the next lesson, or should I revisit the last one?

It has been revealed that sometimes a topic would spread across multiple sources. I would hop between tabs, copy and paste notes, and try to remember what I'd learned.

By the end of the week, I'd often give up.

Everything changed when I started using Gemini's Guided Learning feature.

Unlike traditional learning apps, it didn't need me to follow a rigid path or track progress across multiple tools.

Industry observers note that instead, it guided me step by step, building on what I already knew and adjusting as I went. I didn't have to blueprint my learning sessions or decide which topic to tackle next.

Recent findings suggest that guided Learning remembered where I left off and suggested the next logical step. If I paused for a few days, I could pick up where I left off without needing to figure out the context.

It also made mistakes and gaps useful. When I misunderstood a concept, Guided Learning explained why I made the mistake and how to approach similar problems in the future.

The best part was flexibility. I could proceed at my pace, skip sections I understood, or explore topics I found interesting, without switching between multiple apps or tutorials.

I don't open Gemini with a syllabus in mind. Most of the time, I start with a vague goal and a rough sense of what I want to understand next.

Guided Learning works best when I treat it like a conversation, rather than a lesson I have to finish in one sitting.

One example of this was learning the basics of self-hosting.

I wasn't trying to become a sysadmin overnight; I just wanted to understand what it would take to run a few services on my hardware.

Instead of searching for a self-hosting beginner course, I asked Gemini to start a guided learning path focused on the fundamentals.

Sources indicate that to get started, open a new chat in the Gemini mobile app or on the web and tap the Add Files. Select Guided Learning and input the topic you wish to explore.

From there, the topic was divided into manageable sections, beginning with concepts such as the meaning of self-hosting, the trade-offs when compared to cloud services, and the types of hardware that are suitable for beginners.

As I asked follow-up questions, Guided Learning automatically adjusted the depth.

Industry observers note that I liked how easy it was to pause and resume. I'd read through a step, close the app, and come back later without feeling lost.

Guided Learning remembered the context and continued from there, rather than resetting the conversation or forcing me to repeat myself.

One of the simplest ways to better understand the topic is to ask for quick check-ins along the way.

If I'm not sure whether something has sunk in, I prompt Gemini to quiz me on the last concept or to give me a couple of short questions before moving on.

It's an easy way to catch gaps early, instead of realizing later that I only half understood what I read.

According to recent reports, follow-up questions matter just as much. When something feels unclear, I ask about it immediately.

Guided Learning adjusts based on those interruptions, often rephrasing the explanation or adding context that makes the rest of the path easier to follow.

I also try to end sessions with a lightweight recap. Asking for a summary of what I've covered helps reinforce the key ideas and makes it easier to resume learning.

On days when I don't have time to continue, that recap becomes a natural stopping point.

Guided Learning isn't perfect, and its biggest weakness reveals up when you spend enough time with it.

Gemini relies heavily on examples and analogies, especially when it explains unfamiliar concepts. That can be helpful at first, but over time it starts to feel repetitive.

Different ideas are compared to the same kinds of real-world scenarios, which can slow things down when you're past the beginner stage.

It also tends to over-explain. Even when I'm comfortable with a topic, Guided Learning sometimes insists on walking through familiar ground, framing it with another analogy instead of moving on.

According to recent reports, another limitation is depth. Guided Learning is good at building understanding, but it's not always the fastest way to get highly specific or technical answers.

When I want exact commands, edge cases, or detailed troubleshooting, I sometimes have to switch out of guided mode and ask more direct questions instead.

While context awareness is a substantial part of the appeal, it can occasionally feel too cautious.

Gemini often tries to make sure you're "ready" before advancing, which is helpful early on but can feel restrictive when you're comfortable moving faster.

Guided Learning works for me because it removes the setup that usually gets in the way of learning something new.

I didn't have to pick the right app, commit to a course, or remember where I left off.

However, it isn't flawless. Gemini can over-explain, and it sometimes needs a push to get past familiar ground.

But those are trade-offs I'm willing to make for something that adapts to my pace.

Breaking: 6 Fighter Jets That Can Pull The Most Gs

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that when it comes to measuring the Gs a fighter jet can pull, the concern isn't the pilot's safety, but rather a measurement of the structural capability of the aircraft.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that modern fighter jets are among the most complex and impressive pieces of military machinery ever put into service. They're capable of reaching incredible speeds, and thanks to advancements like thrust vectoring, they're far more maneuverable than ever before. Flying one takes a great deal of training and skill to not only pull off high-speed maneuvers, but also to stay conscious due to the high G-forces a pilot experiences while flying a fighter jet.

G-force is the measure of gravity endured by a pilot during flight. 1G is what everyone experiences on Earth — it's the baseline gravity we're all accustomed to. Fighter jets changing direction quickly increase the number of Gs felt by the pilot, and the higher they get, the more dangerous it becomes. Modern G-suits are pressurized to limit this danger, so while most people could remain conscious at around 5Gs, something you might experience on a roller coaster, fighter pilots typically endure up to 9Gs.

Recent findings suggest that when it comes to measuring the Gs a fighter jet can pull, the concern isn't the pilot's safety, but rather a measurement of the structural capability of the aircraft. Most can pull up to 9Gs, but some are rated higher, despite the risk to the pilot. In rare cases, fighter jets have pushed to around 12Gs in emergency situations, and some pilots have proven that they can endure this for short periods. These aircraft can pull more Gs than other modern fighter jets.

It has been revealed that the United States military's second fifth-generation fighter began operating in 2015, and the F-35 Lightning II comes in three variants. The F-35A belongs to the U.S. Air Force (USAF), the F-35B is capable of vertical take-off and landing and is flown by the U.S. Marine Corps, and the F-35C is a carrier-based version used by the U.S. Navy. While the B and C variants are rated at 7G and 7.5G, respectively, the F-35A has a maximum G-limit of +9Gs, making it the strongest F-35 model.

The F-35A runs on an exceptionally powerful engine, the Pratt & Whitney F135-PW-100, which produces 40,000 pounds of thrust. This gives the F-35A the power it needs to reach speeds of Mach 1.6 (1,228 mph), and it's also highly maneuverable, thanks to its impressive flight control software. This helps control the aircraft during different types of flight operations, including high alpha maneuvers, which is when an aircraft like the F-35A uses an incredibly high angle of attack.

While pilots can fly up to 9Gs, which is the limit of the F-35A, there have been instances of pilots experiencing oxygen deprivation (hypoxia) during flights. In 2017, Luke Air Force Base, Arizona, grounded 55 F-35s for 11 days following pilot reports of hypoxia. Steps were taken to limit the problem while the USAF investigated the cause. Eventually, flight operations returned to normal after the USAF addressed the oxygen generation system and other elements, enabling a return to normal flight operations.

It has been revealed that the F-22 Raptor is the world's first fifth-generation fighter jet, and it remains one of the most advanced aircraft operating today. It was so expensive to develop that fewer than 200 aircraft were initially produced. As of this writing, it's unlikely that any additional F-22s will be made and put into service. That makes flying it a rare opportunity for any USAF fighter pilot.

In terms of speed, the F-22 Raptor is fast. Its supercruise ability enables supersonic cruising speeds up to Mach 1.5 (1,151 mph) without the need for its afterburner, and because the F-22 features 2D thrust vectoring, it's exceptionally maneuverable. The F-22 is rated with a +9/-3 G-limit, where +9 refers to upward G-forces, and -3 is for its downward G-force limit. Those figures are the extremes of what a human can endure while operating a fighter jet, even with G-suits and extensive training in centrifuges. Interestingly, several pilots have nearly blacked out while flying the F-22, but not because of the intense G-forces sustained during operation.

It has been revealed that in July 2012, the Pentagon reported at least 11 incidents of pilots becoming woozy and nearly blacking out. The subsequent investigation determined the G-forces weren't the cause, but rather the G-suits were. Due to a faulty valve, the suits would inflate their air-filled bladders prematurely. This made it difficult to breathe, resulting in hypoxia, but fortunately the problem was addressed.

It's not just American aircraft that endure high Gs; the Russian Federation's Sukhoi Su-57 "Felon" is also rated up to 9Gs. Introduced in 2020 as the first Russian-designed fighter jet with stealth capabilities, this multirole fighter boasts plenty of impressive stats and equipment. It's not only stealth capable, it also features supercruise, supermaneuvrability, and more, aligning closely with the F-22 Raptor and F-35 Lightning II's flight capabilities.

Since its introduction, Russia has continuously produced Su-57s to meet its goal of 76 aircraft by 2027. Apparently, it's well on its way to reaching that goal, though the Su-57 has seen only limited combat, as Russia prefers to keep it safe from Ukrainian air defenses during the Russia-Ukraine war. While the Su-57 is undeniably fast, its high G-limit threshold comes into play via its supermaneuvrability, which is achieved via its 3D thrust-vectoring engine nozzles, digital fly-by-wire system, and its aerodynamic design. The Su-57's 3D thrust vectoring exceeds the F-22's capabilities, as it affects not just the pitch, but also the yaw and roll.

While there aren't any public records of pilots blacking out while flying the Su-57, there have been accidents. An Su-57 used for training crashed in July 2026, though Russia claimed this was due to a technical malfunction. Regardless, Russia, like the U.S. and other nations, employs high-tech G-suits to ensure their pilots maintain consciousness while flying advanced fighter jets. Russia began testing a new G-suit specifically designed for the Su-57 in 2019, showing an increased interest in pilot safety.

France developed the Dassault Rafale as its primary fourth-generation multirole fighter, which entered service in 2001. The Rafale is one of the most innovative fighters of its generation, thanks to its use of a digital fly-by-wire system. Along with the aircraft's canards, this gives the Rafale improved aerodynamics and maneuverability. It's powered by two Snecma M88 turbofan engines and is capable of reaching Mach 1.8 (1,381 mph), so the Rafale is undoubtedly fast.

Sources indicate that in fact, a Rafale successfully "downed" an F-22 Raptor in an exercise in 2009, showing that it had what it takes to go up against a higher-generation fighter. The Rafale is rated up to +9Gs and -3.2Gs, making it one of the strongest European fighter jets in active service. However, in emergency situations, the Rafale has demonstrated a capability of +11Gs. While that wouldn't be survivable for long, pilots have remained conscious at and above 11Gs for short durations.

While the aircraft can handle that many Gs, normal operations are limited to the standard scale, and higher than 9Gs are only reached during emergencies. There aren't any known instances of pilots passing out while flying a Rafale, but there have been accidents. In December 2007, a Rafale crashed in southwestern France. The investigation found that the pilot became disoriented, though it wasn't made public whether that disorientation was the result of hypoxia. This caching approach avoids unnecessary PDF rendering while keeping memory usage under control, especially when users work with longer documents.

#94. Tech Report: Beyond 12 Columns: Designing Layouts With Personality

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1641 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Css-tricks

Tech Report: Beyond 12 Columns: Designing Layouts With Personality

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1641 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Css-tricks

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When I started designing websites thirty years ago, David Siegel had just published Creating Killer Web Sites, the book that popularised HTML tables and spacer GIFs for laying out web pages.
  • When CSS frameworks began providing ready-made grid systems, things got a little easier.
  • Recent findings suggest that twelve-column grids weren’t invented in the 2000s.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When I started designing websites thirty years ago, David Siegel had just published Creating Killer Web Sites, the book that popularised HTML tables and spacer GIFs for laying out web pages. CSS eventually gave us more control over layouts through floats and positioning. Neither was intended for page layout, and inconsistent browser behaviour could make using them frustrating. Still, that didn’t stop me and a generation of other designers from using floats and positioning.

When CSS frameworks began providing ready-made grid systems, things got a little easier. Blueprint CSS) offered a 24-column grid, while Nathan Smith’s 960 Grid System offered 12- and 16-column options. These frameworks gave designers and developers a shared structure, making layout planning and implementation considerably easier.

Recent findings suggest that twelve-column grids weren’t invented in the 2000s. Graphic designers had used column-based and modular grids for decades, and twelve is a convenient number because you don’t need to be a maths genius to divide it into halves, thirds, and quarters to create the 2-up, 3-up, and 4-up components we see everywhere online.

Sources indicate that frameworks like Bootstrap and Foundation followed, helping establish twelve-column grids as the de facto standard for page layouts. I get why that happened. But somewhere along the way, one layout option became the default starting point for almost everything.

CSS Grid changed what’s possible for page layouts, but I still see designers start by dividing a page into twelve equal columns, then deciding how to fit their content into them. The designs they end up with might be perfectly fine, but they can also look remarkably similar.

Industry observers note that still, I don’t think twelve-column grids themselves are the problem. It’s reaching for a familiar solution before considering what makes the organization I’m designing for distinctive and what its website needs to communicate. So what happens when I start with those questions instead?

Before I decide how many columns a layout needs, I want to understand the organization I’m designing for. What makes it different from its competitors? What does it want people to remember? Does it have a personality that could influence how its website looks and feels?

These questions matter because a layout does more than arrange content. The size, position, and relationships between elements influence how people experience a website. A restrained, orderly composition can communicate something very different from one that’s full of energy and movement. So to demonstrate what I mean, I’ll use Wheelman. It’s a fictional organization I invented for my book, Standout Designs for the Web.

Pre-orders for Standout Designs for the Web are now open in the CSS-Tricks store.

Industry observers note that wheelman provides products and services for getaway drivers, including legal advice, robbery insurance, and an online shop selling break-in essentials. It also publishes a magazine with advice, news, and stories about life behind the wheel.

Wheelman isn’t an ordinary company, so why should its website look like an everyday collection of components? It takes its business seriously, but isn’t afraid to have fun with its design. It’s rebellious, but doesn’t want to look off-putting. Its audience is criminals, but they demand professionalism. Wheelman has plenty of personality to work with, and I want its designs to reflect that.

That doesn’t mean making Wheelman different for difference’s sake. Its customers still need to find what they’re looking for, understand what it provides, and buy its products and services. But I can make those experiences more memorable by choosing layouts that fit the company, rather than settling for familiar arrangements.

Recent findings suggest that let’s imagine I’m designing a latest landing page for Wheelman’s online shop. It includes two products, one with a gigantic headline, product images, and the type of functionality and information you’ll find on most stores.

Before I decide how to arrange these elements, I want to look beyond them and consider how they relate. I ask myself questions like:.

It has been revealed that only then do I start thinking about visual design questions: “Would a large photograph set the scene? Should I make the introduction more prominent? Can whitespace lead the eye and create spaces to pause? How can I bring images and text together into a considered composition?”.

These questions help me understand what the layout needs to accomplish before I decide which grid might help me achieve it.

I could arrange everything in a single column for a straightforward reading experience. That would make responsive design considerably easier. But I won’t.

Wheelman has a rebellious personality, and I want its shop to reflect that. A more energetic layout seems appropriate, but I still need to establish a clear hierarchy between the products and their information. Two equal-width columns give both products equal prominence.

Changing their proportions creates a hierarchy, even when most elements stay the same size.

I could base those proportions on a twelve-column grid, but I won’t. Columns only divide space vertically, and I want a layout that adds another dimension.

Recent findings suggest that dividing a layout into columns is a useful starting point, but adding rows creates another dimension and opens up more creative possibilities. Where columns and rows intersect, they form rectangular or square units called modules.

Combining these modules creates larger spatial zones that can establish hierarchy, control whitespace, and add variety to a composition.

Industry observers note that using a modular grid, I can add drama, establish hierarchy by varying scale, and make the composition feel far less predictable. Starting with four columns and four rows gives me sixteen modules to work with, but I don’t need to fill them all.

I can create drama by spreading the large graphic headline and product image across four modules, while the product information and shopping tools occupy one module each.

In a recent development, the modular structure becomes even more apparent in the grid of alternative products. Most occupy just one module, while others fill two, either horizontally or vertically. Varying their sizes gives some products more prominence and makes the overall arrangement feel less predictable.

The result still feels like a product page, with a clear reading order and space for the content to breathe. But it also feels unmistakably like something Wheelman would publish.

I don’t expect this composition to work at every screen size, so I can adjust the size and quantity of modules to improve the reading experience.

And if one grid offers this much flexibility, imagine what combining two or more grids can do.

Recent findings suggest that one thing I want from Wheelman’s website is variety. Its magazine, shop, and services serve different purposes, and I don’t want every page to feel like I’ve poured its content into the same template.

Wheelman needs layouts which feel organised without being predictable. Compound grids give me the structure I need while leaving room for less conventional arrangements.

A compound grid combines two or more grids of any type — column, modular, or hierarchical — on the same page. These grids can overlap, sit side by side, or be stacked one on top of the other. Combining grids creates possibilities which neither grid offers on its own.

I can start by overlaying a two-column grid with one containing three columns. Their combined grid lines create four columns of two different widths, giving me more flexibility without losing the underlying structure.

Industry observers note that those proportions offer more possibilities for arranging content. I might use a wider area for a photograph or headline, then place a pullquote into one of the narrower spaces. Another page could use the same underlying grid but combine its spaces differently to suit another story.

Combining grids with different column counts gets even more interesting as those numbers increase. In Standout Designs for the Web, I explore several combinations, including mixing four- and five-column grids to create different compositions for Wheelman’s pages while maintaining a connected visual structure.

The point isn’t to make every page look different for its own sake. It’s to give each section a layout that suits its content while keeping them all feeling like part of the same tech giant.

Twelve-column grids are useful, and I’m certainly not suggesting you should stop using them entirely. But they’re only one option among many, and starting every design with the same structure limits your possibilities before you’ve even considered the story your design is telling.

There’s also nothing inherently wrong with the 2-up, 3-up, and 4-up patterns a twelve-column grid inspires. They can sometimes be exactly what’s needed. But reaching for them automatically can leave little room for the character and personality that make websites memorable.

Wheelman gives me plenty of reasons to choose different layouts. Its stories, products, and services don’t all need the same arrangements, and its personality gives me opportunities to make those arrangements more distinctive. The grids are simply tools that help me put those ideas into practice.

Sources indicate that and this applies to much more than layout. The same thinking should influence the colours I choose, the typography I use, the images I commission, and the way I bring those elements together.

Recent findings suggest that that’s why I wrote Standout Designs for the Web. I want to encourage designers to look beyond familiar solutions and make more deliberate decisions about colour, typography, imagery, and layout. Not to be different for difference’s sake, but to create websites that look and feel like they belong to the companies behind them. And no one else.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • For this, you'll need a cleaning agent.
  • Alternatively, you can opt for a specialized flushing kit that contains everything you need, which costs as little as $70.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From supplying hot water on demand to the compact and unobtrusive form factor, tankless water heaters are a great addition to any home. Plus, a tankless water heater has a significantly longer lifespan than a traditional unit, meaning the higher upfront investment can be worth it. However, one of the most prominent disadvantages of a tankless water heater is the cost of repairs. Proper routine maintenance, including flushing the system, can help avoid issues and repairs. So, how do you flush a tankless water heater on your own?

For this, you'll need a cleaning agent. Pure white vinegar will do. The type matters, though, and you're best off using 2 to 4 gallons of white vinegar with a 5% concentration of acetic acid. You'll also need a 5 gallon bucket to hold the cleaning agent, two hoses, and a sump pump.

Alternatively, you can opt for a specialized flushing kit that contains everything you need, which costs as little as $70. For deep cleaning, you may also want to ditch white vinegar in favor of a high-grade descaler. This solution may cost at least $20 extra, but it's a specialized concoction that contains stronger acids. Because it is a stronger chemical, be sure to check your water heater's manufacturer guidelines before using a descaler.

The entire flushing process takes about an hour. Here's how to do it:.

After you've completed the process, you'll probably feel confident enough to flush your tankless water heater more often.

In a recent development, this should become routine maintenance. That remarked, you should probably drain your tankless water heater more often than you do. Most areas in the US have varying levels of hard water filled with mineral sediment. Thus, to keep the water heater operating as efficiently as possible, the bare minimum is to flush once a year. In areas with extremely hard water, you should flush your tankless water heater at least twice a year — in the spring and in the fall.

Sources indicate that how can you tell if a tankless water heater needs to be flushed? Chances are, you'll notice it struggling to provide hot water when sediment starts building up. You may even feel the water pressure dropping or see cloudy hot water coming from your faucets. The dead giveaway is popping sounds coming from the unit. By sticking to routine maintenance, you'll keep these symptoms at bay, and your heater will work as intended for years to come.

According to a new report, An “internal suggestion box” has been posted within the company that is urging the board to reconsider Huang’s exit. The post has gained over 1,600 comments from employees calling for his return, with some noting that “NVIDIA is NVIDIA because of Jensen.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, driving simulators have been teaching tools for a very long time, both in professional motorsports and for aspiring young road drivers who have never been behind the wheel. As far back as 2010, for instance, Lexus developed what was then considered the world's most advanced driving simulator in a 15-foot-high, 56-foot-diameter dome. Formula One teams, meanwhile, spend millions on bespoke simulators to give their drivers every possible edge on real-world tracks when race day rolls around.

Recent findings suggest that as that level of investment suggests, it's possible driving simulators can help develop driver proficiency, though the evidence isn't conclusive. According to a 2024 systematic review of 15 studies published in the Journal of Safety Research, training with a simulator can improve performance in virtual driving scenarios ranging from speed regulation to reaction to stimuli, but it wasn't clear from the data how well those abilities transferred to the real world.

Industry observers note that auto manufacturers like Lexus and Volvo (which built the "ultimate driving simulator" based on gaming tech in 2020) use simulators to help improve vehicle safety and develop autonomous driving technology. Racing schools, however, claim that simulations can contribute directly to skill building, like strengthening a driver's hand-to-eye coordination, enhancing spatial awareness, and making quick decisions in high-pressure scenarios.

Industry observers note that that said, simulated driving alone shouldn't be considered a wholesale replacement for real-world road lessons. The aforementioned 2024 study review, for instance, pointed out that various factors, like selection bias or weaknesses in the design of the research, could be skewing the data. They concluded that simulator training should instead supplement existing driver education programs.

While they have come a long way, even the most realistic manual driving simulators have some practical drawbacks, which may prevent certain learners from participating. A number of sims, especially those built for virtual reality headsets, can cause dizziness or intense nausea that makes it impossible for some people to use them in longer sessions.

Recent findings suggest that there are some pretty remarkable success stories, however, of sim racers transitioning to professional motorsports, one of which was captured by Hollywood back in 2023. The film "Gran Turismo" tells the real-life account of a Welsh gamer who sharpened his skills playing the video game of the same name and went on to win actual racing competitions in the real world. While driving sims shouldn't replace real-world training, they can potentially be a helpful supplement.

#89. No water required —the upcoming way to fight fires is with sound waves

No water required —the upcoming way to fight fires is with sound waves

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (972 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Techradar

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Fires are typically tackled using sprinkler systems and fire extinguishers across homes and larger buildings, but Ohio company Sonic Fire Tech is testing a fire-fighting system with a difference: it uses sound waves rather than water or chemicals.
  • According to recent reports, the immediate benefits are obvious, in that people and properties don't get drenched at the same time as the fire is put out.
  • Former NASA engineers form part of the team behind the "acoustic fire suppression technology", and Sonic Fire Tech raised $15 million in funding earlier this year, CNN reports.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fires are typically tackled using sprinkler systems and fire extinguishers across homes and larger buildings, but Ohio company Sonic Fire Tech is testing a fire-fighting system with a difference: it uses sound waves rather than water or chemicals.

According to recent reports, the immediate benefits are obvious, in that people and properties don't get drenched at the same time as the fire is put out. There's another advantage too, because unlike water, sound waves can tackle grease fires — a type of blaze that's increasingly common.

Former NASA engineers form part of the team behind the "acoustic fire suppression technology", and Sonic Fire Tech raised $15 million in funding earlier this year, CNN reports. So is it the next substantial thing in fire defenses? These are the details.

Recent findings suggest that the overall trend for fires in the US is, thankfully, downwards. However, while there are fewer fires than there were 40 years ago, they've become deadlier — if a fire is reported in your home, you're more likely to die. Fires from cooking have actually been on the rise in recent years, which is a worrying trend-within-a-trend.

As pointed out on the Sonic Fire Tech website, the standard dousing you get with a sprinkler system can cause as much damage as the fire itself in some cases: furniture and fittings get drenched, electronics are put out of action, and family heirlooms and keepsakes can be damaged beyond recovery.

With sound waves, those problems aren't there. In basic terms, the Sonic Fire Tech system works by producing high-pressure infrasound waves. These are sent down a dedicated system of pipes, in a similar way to how a sprinkler or air conditioning system would work, and then the sound waves are targeted at the source of the blaze.

According to recent reports, the sound waves vibrate the oxygen molecules in the air, which essentially pushes them away faster than the fire can grab hold of them. That leaves the fire starved of the oxygen supply it needs, and it dies out. It can be put into action as soon as heat is detected, and false alarms don't matter, because there's no damage done.

In a recent development, you can see how the setup might work in one of the official videos on the Sonic Fire Tech YouTube channel. In an apartment building, a network of ducting pipes lead from a central acoustic generator to each individual living space, with the emitters placed right over the cooking areas. Sensors detect the fire, and in response the sound waves are generated at the same time as the fuel supply for the cooking appliance is switched off.

The fire suppression tech has been proved to work at distances of up to 25 feet (7.6 meters), and certification testing is beginning before the end of the year — with the UL 300A protocol, for stovetop fire extinguishing, one of the safety standards that the sound wave system has been designed to comply with.

There's a lot that's promising about the systems Sonic Fire Tech is working on: there's nothing to run out of (only electricity is required), no water supply is needed (making this tech potentially transformative for wildfires), and there's no water damage or chemical residue when the fire's been put out.

It has been revealed that it can tackle types of fires that water alone can't (grease fires), and it can act earlier and more reliably because false alarms are less of an issue. There's even a portable, backpack version of the system in development — one that firefighters could potentially carry with them when tackling blazes.

However, the technology isn't a sure thing yet, and there's work to do before you'll see it installed anywhere (or on board a fire truck). Researchers have actually been working on the idea of sound waves suppressing fires for several years now, and one of the challenges has been scaling the techniques up for larger fires across bigger areas.

There are also questions about everything that comes along with a blaze. "Sound may knock down a small flame, but it does not cool hot surfaces or wet fuel," Los Angeles fire protection engineer Nate Wittasek told Ars Technica. "That raises real questions about re-ignition, smoldering fires, hidden fires, and fires that are partially blocked by contents.".

It has been revealed that michael Gollner, an associate professor of mechanical engineering at the University of California, Berkeley, has some concerns about whether the whole package will end up improving on sprinklers. "Water suppression sprinklers are terribly efficient, and this upcoming technology still needs to prove that it’s more efficient than this," he told CNN.

These are challenges that the Sonic Fire Tech experts think they can overcome, not least because CEO and co-founder Geoff Bruder has a background in NASA, working on acoustic wave systems for spacecraft designed to land on Venus. That's a decent foundation for anyone working on putting out fires in homes and offices.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The biggest problem I've faced lately is paying my credit card bills on time without getting hit with predatory interest rates.

And since my Gmail inbox is always full of work and spam emails, I often miss credit card statements or other payment notifications.

Some months I pay on time if I see the email; other months I pay fees and watch my credit score drop.

That's when I got sick of my own shortcomings and decided to use Gemini as my bill watcher.

Before asking Gemini to scan your bills, turn on a few features that let it communicate with your email.

Since I use Gmail, setup was easy: I just had to turn on Google Workspace in the Connected Apps section.

To connect Gmail with Gemini, open Gemini's settings, tap Connected Apps, and turn on the Google Workspace option. This will also connect other Google apps such as Tasks, Keep, and Calendar.

Now that Gemini and Gmail are connected, I want to create a recurring Scheduled Task in the Gemini app that scans my email for upcoming payments and due dates.

Scheduled tasks have now moved to the main sidebar on both Gemini's web and app platforms.

I use a simple prompt that I instructed Gemini to provide, which I run every morning as a Scheduled Task. Here's the prompt:.

According to recent reports, scan my Gmail for any credit card statements, bills, or payment due notices received in the last few days. List the card name, total due, minimum due, due date, and any payment link or account number if available. Flag anything due within the next 7 days.

You can set up the Scheduled Task based on your time and frequency preferences, but I have it turned on for every morning.

This prompt makes sure I never miss a payment because I get notified the moment bills hit my inbox and when payments need to be cleared in the next seven days.

I also instructed Gemini to add high-priority due dates as advance reminders in Google Tasks, but you can also add them as events to Google Calendar.

After setting up the Scheduled Task, I get a morning notification and a chat summary showing all my credit card due dates.

When a latest statement hits my email, Gemini parses the information and sets up a reminder in Google Tasks. I usually cross-check the details with the text message I received just to make sure the information is accurate.

I don't need to open the Gemini app, as I can use Gemini Voice to ask what my due dates and payment amounts are for a specific credit card.

This meant I didn't miss any payments, and it reduced the late-payment fees and interest I'd been racking up earlier.

Sources indicate that it saved me quite a bit of money, and I never had to dig for statement emails again. To make this process more detailed, I asked Gemini to list all my credit cards and their details in a Google Sheet.

I also added my monthly income and fixed expenses to that sheet, so I know my real cash flow for the month. You don't have to do this, but it lets me check my bank liquidity and control credit card spending accordingly.

This gave a clear picture of all recurring charges and subscriptions that I could weed out later if I no longer needed them.

If you also use Google Wallet, you can set up Autopay, get deeper spending insights via Plaid, and correlate the information as well.

Industry observers note that but this system does come with some caution. Since AI parsing isn't perfect, double-check everything before you fully rely on this system.

Even though this Gemini method can have minor shortcomings, I haven't faced any challenges to this day.

The real benefit might be financial, but I've also noticed I no longer panic or wonder if I've made my payments this month.

I still use my banking apps to make payments since I prefer to do them manually, but Gemini removed most of my anxiety about missed payments.

Industry observers note that while I use this Gemini system solely to track credit card bills, you can apply it to any bill you get by email. You can use it to track utility, phone, and internet bills like I did with credit cards.

Recent findings suggest that I recommend trying it and starting with one or two cards or bills to see if it works for you. If it works as intended, you will never have to stress about managing payments again.

  • In its technical explanation, Fortreum describes a workflow that connects scan findings to assets, produces first-pass vulnerability evaluations, and tracks response activity and evidence.
  • The distinction matters because identifying a software flaw is only the beginning.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that fortreum has introduced its Kovr-powered VDR/VER offering to help cloud providers put FedRAMP’s fresh vulnerability rules into operation ahead of the December 7, 2026 migration deadline. The offering combines security specialists, implementation support, and AI-assisted evaluation rather than treating compliance as a scanner report that gets filed once a month.

In its technical explanation, Fortreum describes a workflow that connects scan findings to assets, produces first-pass vulnerability evaluations, and tracks response activity and evidence. Customer teams review the determinations and direct the response.

The distinction matters because identifying a software flaw is only the beginning. A provider also needs to establish where it exists, whether an attacker can reach it, what exploitation would affect, and why its response is appropriate.

According to recent reports, fedRAMP is the U.S. government’s program for assessing and overseeing the security of cloud services used by federal agencies. Its updated vulnerability rules split the work into two closely related areas.

Vulnerability Detection and Response, or VDR, covers identifying and managing vulnerabilities over time. Vulnerability Evaluation and Reporting, or VER, concerns evaluating their implications and reporting the relevant information.

A severity score alone cannot answer every operational question. The same flaw could appear on an isolated test machine and on a public-facing service holding sensitive information. The software weakness may be identical, while the paths an attacker could take and the consequences of exploitation are very different.

Sources indicate that the rules therefore make context crucial: likely exploitability, internet reachability, potential agency impact, and the effectiveness of mitigation. Providers need to retain the evidence behind those judgments as conditions change.

It has been revealed that fortreum says its implementation approach starts with the provider’s environment and existing vulnerability process, then establishes responsibilities and reporting workflows. Kovr ingests scan and inventory information, associates findings with assets, and prepares initial evaluations of exploitability, reachability, and potential agency impact.

The useful output is more than another list of vulnerabilities. A finding needs an owner, a response deadline, supporting evidence, and a record of what happened next. Keeping those elements connected makes it easier for security engineering and compliance teams to work from the same facts.

For example, an analyst might determine that a vulnerable component is present but not exposed through the service’s external interface. That conclusion needs evidence about the affected asset and its configuration. If a deployment later changes the exposure, the earlier determination may no longer describe the risk.

AI can help organize the records and prepare an evaluation, but the decision remains tied to the provider’s environment. Fortreum explicitly places review and response direction with the customer, rather than presenting automated output as a substitute for the provider’s obligations.

According to recent reports, kovr is Fortreum’s AI-native compliance automation platform for regulated organizations. Its wider capabilities include evidence collection, documentation management, control mapping, remediation tracking, and continuous monitoring support across multiple frameworks.

The platform uses large language models and is built on the Open Security Controls Assessment Language, or OSCAL. OSCAL provides structured formats for exchanging security-control and assessment information between systems. That is different from simply storing a folder of PDFs: structured records can be processed, compared, and reused by software.

Kovr also provides Agent Artemis, a compliance-focused assistant for navigating requirements, locating documentation, and understanding controls. Those capabilities illustrate the surrounding platform; Fortreum’s VDR/VER description focuses specifically on the vulnerability evaluation and response workflow.

In a recent development, unite.AI previously covered Fortreum’s acquisition of Kovr.AI. The upcoming offering applies that combination of assessment expertise and automation to a concrete operational change in federal cloud oversight.

Industry observers note that the deadline needs to be read alongside FedRAMP’s current guidance. In its November 10 migration notice, FedRAMP confirms December 7, 2026 as the migration date and retains a grace period through March 7, 2027 for certified cloud services.

It has been revealed that services that are not fully migrated on December 7 must explain corrective actions and target timelines for each outstanding rule. Those planning to finish after February 3 will be listed as in remediation until completion. FedRAMP also describes case-by-case extensions beyond March 7, requiring an approved corrective action initiative and agreement to a coordinated red-team assessment.

Consequently, December 7 is not an automatic certification revocation date for every provider with unfinished work. It is a milestone that requires an operational response and a defensible account of remaining gaps. The notice also calls for migration progress reporting, including example machine-readable and human-readable vulnerability activity reports.

It has been revealed that the central challenge is coordinating a continuing process. A scan can reveal a flaw, but reducing its risk may involve an engineer applying a patch, an infrastructure team changing access, and a compliance team recording why the chosen response meets the applicable requirements.

Sources indicate that fortreum’s proposition is to connect that work through a shared dataset and repeatable workflow. The practical measure of success will be whether teams can make timely, well-supported decisions and show the evidence behind them, rather than merely produce more compliance documents.

Husqvarna started to make robotic lawn mowers back in 1995, when it first introduced a solar-powered model. Three decades later, the company still ranks among the best robot lawn mower brands, offering machines built for everything from suburban yards to steep hillsides. Its prices reflect that reputation and can be a bit of a shock, especially if you just want something to keep your grass short.

It has been revealed that the half-acre Automower 410 iQ, for example, is listed at $2,599.99 and lets you set a virtual boundary or install a perimeter wire, while the 420 iQ doubles that coverage. The 435 iQ AWD uses all-wheel drive to tackle slopes of up to 70%, and all three options work with the Automower Connect app, allowing you to control mowing schedules and cutting heights with your phone.

If you're interested in saving some money, it's possible to spend considerably less and still get a robotic lawn mower. Although those models might give you fewer options for keeping your grass trimmed, some brands offer cheaper alternatives to Husqvarna. So we've picked some of them for different budgets and looked at what each one provides for the money.

In a recent development, the LawnMaster OcuMow 400 Series lists for $449.99 at Walmart, roughly one-sixth the price of the Husqvarna Automower 410 iQ. On the performance side, it can cut up to 2,600 square feet on a charge, or about 0.06 acres of grass. So if you're interested in one, check the size of your yard before buying a robotic lawn mower, especially if you want the machine to cover all of it.

It has been revealed that A wide-angle camera helps the mower distinguish grass from its surroundings, and ultrasonic sensors enable it to steer around obstacles. It can mow in parallel lines as well, and magnetic strips let you mark spots you want it to avoid, like a flower bed in the middle of the lawn.

While it's way cheaper than a Husqvarna, you'll have to do a bit more work yourself. This model from LawnMaster leaves it to you to take out the battery and put it into a separate charger after it runs out. Its cutting height also tops out at 2.5 inches, compared with 4 inches on the 410 iQ.

Industry observers note that even a small lawn can be awkward to mow if a narrow passage connects two patches of grass. Luckily, the Anthbot M5 Robot Lawn Mower is built for that kind of space. By using satellite positioning and two cameras to find its way around, it can work without a perimeter wire. Through the app, you can give each patch its own mowing schedule and adjust the cutting height from your phone if you'd rather leave the grass a little longer.

You can find the Anthbot M5 for $799, which is less than a third of the price of a Husqvarna Automower 410 iQ. Both models are engineered for slopes of up to 45% within the mowing area, but the M5 covers up to ⅛ acre, only a quarter of what the 410 iQ handles in systematic mowing mode. If you're willing to pay a little more for greater coverage, but want to stay among affordable robotic mowers, it's possible to get the Anthbot M9, which uses the same combination of cameras and satellite positioning but covers about a quarter acre for $899.

Sources indicate that for less than $1,000, some Greenworks mower models can get you to the half-acre mark. The Greenworks AiMowbot Wire-Free RTKVision Robotic Mower C20, for example, is listed for $998 at some stores, which is about $1,600 below what you would pay for the 410 iQ. The C20 also matches Husqvarna's advertised lawn capacity and can handle slopes of up to 45%.

In a recent development, like some other products in this price range, it uses satellite positioning and a camera to navigate within virtual boundaries, so you don't have to worry about a perimeter wire. Another feature is that when the battery is running low, the mower heads back to its charging dock on its own.

According to recent reports, the C20 cuts an 8-inch strip on each pass, compared with 9.4 inches on the Husqvarna. That narrower cut means more runs across the same stretch of grass, which is easier to notice on larger lawns. Greenworks also sells the AiMowbot C40 for $1,448, which is designed for twice the acreage and has the same slope limit.

If the steepest part of your lawn is exactly the one you want to stop mowing yourself, the Sunseeker X5 has a higher slope rating than the Husqvarna Automower 410 iQ. Its all-wheel drive is designed to handle slopes of up to 60%, or about 30 degrees, compared with 45% for the Husqvarna within the mowing area.

It's possible to find the Sunseeker X5 AWD Robot Lawn Mower for $1,499.99, which means that you're paying less than you would for a Husqvarna while getting the same mowing capacity. You can also set virtual boundaries and mark areas like flower beds to keep the mower out, but you'll need to choose a spot with a clear view of the sky for the satellite reference station.

However, the X5 gives you less flexibility in how tall you can leave the grass. Its cutting-height settings span 1.6 to 3.2 inches, while the 410 iQ goes from 1 to 4 inches. If you like to keep your grass a little taller sometimes, that lower ceiling can be a drawback.

Setting up the Mova LiDAX Ultra 2000 Robot Lawn Mower starts with letting it scan the yard. It uses 3D LiDAR and a camera to build a map and detect objects in its path, with no perimeter wire to bury or satellite reference station to position. The app can also save up to two maps, which is handy if you have to carry the mower to different places, like the front lawn and a fenced backyard. You can view live video on your phone from the onboard camera.

In a recent development, amazon has the Ultra 2000 on sale for $1,199, with a regular price of $1,799. Both prices are still below what Husqvarna asks for the 410 iQ. The Mova can map up to half an acre, but even its faster mode is designed for a maximum of 0.4 acres per day. If you're using its full coverage capacity, you may need to schedule mowing across multiple days to cut all of your grass.

#83. What Happens When You Upload a Large File & Generate a Temporary Download Link

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2483 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Freecodecamp

What Happens When You Upload a Large File & Generate a Temporary Download Link

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2483 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Freecodecamp

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sending a 5 GB video file might seem simple.
  • The file has to travel across a network, reach a server, and be stored somewhere before another person can download it.
  • File transfer services use HTTP requests, storage systems, databases, encryption, and background processes to manage these tasks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sending a 5 GB video file might seem simple. You select the file, click Upload, wait for the progress bar to finish, and share a link with someone. But there are several things happening in the background while the file is being uploaded.

The file has to travel across a network, reach a server, and be stored somewhere before another person can download it. The service also needs to make sure that the recipient can access the file without accessing the sender's account. If the internet connection drops halfway through the upload, it needs a way to continue without sending the entire file again.

File transfer services use HTTP requests, storage systems, databases, encryption, and background processes to manage these tasks. But how does a website actually handle a file that's several gigabytes in size? Does it upload everything in one request? Where does the file go after the upload finishes? And what happens when its download link expires?

In this article, we'll look at how file transfer services handle large uploads, store files, generate download links, and manage interrupted connections and expired transfers. Then, once you understand the theory behind how it all works, we'll also build a basic chunked file uploader using Node.js to see some of these processes in action.

Before looking at dedicated file transfer services, it helps to understand why we can't just attach massive files to an email. Sending large files through email is fundamentally flawed because the underlying architecture was built for text, not high-resolution media.

Recent findings suggest that simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) handles the transmission of email messages across the internet. Because servers have limited bandwidth and storage, email providers impose strict attachment size limits, usually capping out around 25 MB. However, these limits apply to the encoded message size, not just the original file sitting on your hard drive.

Recent findings suggest that email attachments are commonly encoded using MIME and Base64 formats. Base64 is necessary because it converts binary data into text-compatible characters that email servers can safely route. While this solves the transmission problem, it creates a massive efficiency issue: this encoding increases the data size by approximately 33%.

You can read the foundational specifications for this in RFC 2045, which defines MIME's Base64 transfer encoding. In practice, this means a 30 MB video file will require roughly 40 MB of space before additional message overhead is even calculated, guaranteeing it will bounce back from most email servers.

In a recent development, to bypass the limitations of email, file transfer services use a specialized, decoupled architecture. Having built a few of these systems myself, I believe establishing a clear mental model of the five major components is crucial for understanding the flow of data.

According to recent reports, the journey begins in the client, which is usually a web browser or a desktop application where the sender selects a file. Modern browsers use JavaScript's File API to access file metadata, read the raw contents and intelligently divide the file into smaller, manageable parts before any data hits the network.

Sources indicate that once the client starts sending data, the upload server steps in. This server receives the upload requests, authenticates the user, validates incoming data and coordinates the entire upload process. It acts as the traffic cop, ensuring that chunks of data are arriving in the correct format.

Traditional application servers are terrible at holding massive files, so the storage layer handles the actual heavy lifting. Uploaded files are typically routed directly to object storage solutions. This allows the system to scale infinitely without crashing the primary upload servers.

According to recent reports, while the physical file goes to object storage, the application needs a way to remember what that file is. The metadata database stores critical information, including the original filename, file size, content type, the specific object storage key, a unique transfer identifier and the exact expiration timestamp.

When someone opens a shared link, the download server takes over. It checks the database to verify permissions and expiration dates, and if everything is valid, it retrieves the stored object from the storage layer for delivery.

According to recent reports, transferring a 5 GB file in one continuous network request is a disaster waiting to happen. If a connection drops at 99%, a single-request architecture forces the user to start all over again.

In a recent development, to solve this, modern clients divide large files into smaller parts, such as 10 MB chunks. Each chunk is uploaded to the server as an independent HTTP request. The server meticulously tracks which chunks have arrived. Some advanced systems even allow multiple chunks to upload simultaneously in parallel, drastically reducing the overall waiting time.

It's vital to note that chunked uploads are an architectural pattern, which is entirely different from HTTP chunked transfer encoding (a mechanism for framing an HTTP message body).

Suppose 80% of a massive file has successfully uploaded when your Wi-Fi randomly disconnects. Without resumable uploads, that progress is lost. With resumable architecture, the client reconnects and asks the server for the upload offset, the exact number of bytes successfully received and stored. The client then seamlessly continues uploading from that exact position.

Network transfers can sometimes flip bits, resulting in corrupted files. To prevent this, clients generate a cryptographic hash (checksum) for an individual chunk before sending it. The server receives the chunk, calculates its own hash, and compares the two. If the checksums don't match, the server rejects the chunk and asks the client to try again.

Sources indicate that if you're looking to implement this, the TUS Resumable Upload Protocol is a fantastic, standardized reference for managing upload offsets and checksum verification. Also, the Amazon S3 Multipart Upload Documentation provides an industry-standard blueprint for handling parallel transfers and retrying failed parts.

Once every chunk is verified and reassembled, the service needs a secure place to keep the file until the recipient is ready to download it.

In my opinion, attempting to store gigabytes of user uploads on a traditional local server directory is architectural malpractice. Instead, services rely on object storage. Files are stored as flat objects and each object is assigned a unique key. Object storage is highly durable and scales quite easily to accommodate millions of massive files simultaneously.

The relationship between the stored file and its shareable link relies on the metadata database. When the upload finishes, the application saves the file's storage key in the database and generates a unique access token. The recipient receives a URL containing that specific token. When they click the link, the server reads the token, locates the relevant file in the database and checks the download permissions.

Recent findings suggest that A secure file transfer link relies heavily on high entropy, which is randomness that makes tokens mathematically near-impossible to predict. Also, secure systems use signed URLs. These are URLs containing cryptographic signatures that authorize access for a limited, strictly-enforced period.

As outlined in the OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet, a random link isn't automatically secure without appropriate access controls, expiration policies, and protection against token leakage.

File transfer services process petabytes of data, meaning they can't store uploaded files forever without going bankrupt. They rely on aggressive lifecycle management.

Every transfer is assigned a Time to Live (TTL) or expiration timestamp. Once that time passes, the database instantly invalidates the transfer identifier, ensuring that the download link no longer authorizes access.

Sources indicate that because link expiration and physical deletion aren't necessarily simultaneous, background workers or scheduled cron jobs handle the actual cleanup. These workers periodically scan the database to find expired transfers, mark them as permanently unavailable, delete the associated multi-gigabyte objects from the storage layer, and finally remove the outdated metadata.

Some services also allow senders to limit how many times a file can be downloaded. Once the download count reaches the threshold, the link behaves exactly as if the TTL had expired, offering an excellent way to control unauthorized distribution.

Security in file transfers is never about a single magic feature. It requires multiple layers of defense to keep data safe from interception or theft.

When data travels between the sender, the transfer service, and the recipient, it's heavily encrypted. Modern platforms use HTTPS backed by strict TLS protocols to ensure no one can snoop on the data packets mid-route.

It has been revealed that for a deep dive into how this is configured at an enterprise level, NIST SP 800-52 Rev. 2 offers exhaustive guidelines for TLS implementations.

In a recent development, once the file arrives at the storage layer, encryption at rest ensures that even if a bad actor physically accessed the server hardware, they would only find scrambled, unreadable data. It's key to note that encryption at rest isn't the same as end to end encryption. The service provider still manages the encryption keys in a standard setup.

Industry observers note that to prevent unauthorized people from accessing a valid URL, senders can add a password. This creates a secondary access-control layer that must be cleared before the server will even attempt to fetch the file from object storage. Additional safeguards, like rate-limiting against automated password guessing, ensure this layer remains effective.

Seeing how established companies implement these concepts helps bridge the gap between theory and practice.

Industry observers note that weTransfer is built entirely around temporary shareable links. Transfers have strict expiration timelines and premium users can enforce password protection. According to their security documentation, they utilize standard TLS encryption during transit and AES-256 encryption at rest to secure files on their servers.

It has been revealed that unlike a standard shared folder, Dropbox Transfer creates standalone downloadable links. Recipients don't need a Dropbox account to download the payload. They utilize configurable expiration dates, passwords, and automated download notifications, with maximum file size limits dictated by the sender's specific subscription plan.

Recent findings suggest that send Anywhere takes a fascinating hybrid approach. Its six-digit key transfer mechanism operates in real-time for one-time use within a 10-minute window, often leveraging peer to peer connections. Conversely, its standard Share Link option falls back to a server-based architecture, uploading files and keeping the link valid for up to 48 hours.

Offering robust email and shareable-link delivery options, Filemail handles massive payloads easily. They provide highly configurable expiration controls and rigorous password protection. Their free service tier currently allows a 5 GB transfer limit, holding the data securely for a maximum seven-day storage period before automated cleanup takes over.

According to recent reports, understanding the theory is great, but building it yourself proves how it actually works. Let's create a simple application that divides a file into smaller chunks in the browser, uploads them to a Node.js server and stitches them back together.

Industry observers note that you'll need Node.js, the Express framework, and multer for handling incoming file chunks. The built-in fs module will handle our file operations. First, create a Node project and install the required dependencies:.

It has been revealed that first, create a public directory inside your project folder if it doesn't already exist. Then, create a file named upload.js inside that directory. We'll use the browser's JavaScript File API and its slice() method to read smaller portions of a file without loading the entire 5 GB payload into your computer's RAM.

Here, crypto.randomUUID() generates a unique ID for the upload. The browser sends each chunk separately and uses the same ID to associate all the chunks with the original file.

Recent findings suggest that on the server side (server.js), we need an endpoint to receive and temporarily store each chunk. The server uses the upload ID and chunk index to determine where each part belongs, while the total number of chunks helps validate the upload. We use multer to parse the incoming multipart form data.

The server stores each chunk using its upload ID and index, making it possible to identify and retrieve the individual parts when the upload is complete.

Industry observers note that once the client confirms all chunks have been transmitted, it triggers a final reassembly route. The server first checks whether every expected chunk exists in the chunks/ directory. It then reads the chunks sequentially using fs.createReadStream() and writes them to the same output file using fs.createWriteStream(). The first chunk creates the file, while subsequent chunks are appended to it. Once the original file has been reassembled, the server deletes the temporary chunks to free up space.

Finally, add the following code at the bottom of server.js to start the Express server:.

Start the server by running node server.js in your terminal. Then, open http://localhost:3000 in your browser and select a medium-sized video file to test the upload. Open your browser's Network tab to observe how the file is divided into chunks and sent sequentially. Finally, check your server's uploads/ directory. The assembled file should have the same byte size as the original and should open correctly.

It has been revealed that note: This implementation demonstrates the basic mechanics of chunked uploads and file reassembly. It doesn't implement resumable uploads, checksum verification, authentication, object storage, or temporary download links.

A production-grade file transfer service would also require persistent upload states, access controls, retry handling, integrity checks, and automated cleanup.

Sources indicate that sending a large file involves several processes working together. From upload handling and chunk management in the browser to object storage, metadata tracking, encryption, and automated cleanup, each component has a specific role in making file transfers work.

These processes also explain how services handle interrupted uploads, control access to shared files, and remove data when a transfer expires. Understanding how these components work together makes it easier to see what happens behind the scenes whenever someone uploads a large file and shares a download link.

#79. Tech Report: What Can Happen If A Lithium Battery Gets Wet?

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (524 w)
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Slashgear

Tech Report: What Can Happen If A Lithium Battery Gets Wet?

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (524 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashgear

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that these days, you can find lithium-ion batteries in many gadgets, from phones to laptops and beyond.
  • What happens in that scenario varies by battery and device, including whether either (or both) has an IP rating.
  • A wet lithium battery can short-circuit, corrode, or otherwise become damaged, making it a fire risk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that these days, you can find lithium-ion batteries in many gadgets, from phones to laptops and beyond. That's no surprise: they're generally reliable, tend to offer long lifespans, and are fairly versatile. But since they power such common devices, most of us will probably have found ourselves in situations where we got a lithium-ion battery wet.

What happens in that scenario varies by battery and device, including whether either (or both) has an IP rating. An IP rating indicates how resistant a product is to water and dirt. If a device has a high IP rating, such as IP66, IP67, or IP68, water exposure shouldn't have any significant effect. However, if a battery (or battery-powered device) doesn't have a high enough IP rating to survive submersion or heavy water exposure, you may encounter all kinds of negative consequences.

A wet lithium battery can short-circuit, corrode, or otherwise become damaged, making it a fire risk. In some cases, battery damage or improper use can trigger something called thermal runaway. Thermal runaway happens when heat is released from cells inside the battery, triggering a chain reaction. That chain reaction can then cause further damage, gases being released, smoke, and fire. If this happens, your battery might look swollen or expanded. In turn, this can render your battery unusable or unsafe — at which point, you need to safely dispose of your battery.

It has been revealed that all isn't necessarily lost the minute you get a lithium battery or a device containing one wet. There are a few steps you can take to help minimize any potential damage or short-circuiting as much as possible — and some of them are remarkably simple. If it's safe to do so, then the first thing you want to do is switch off your device or battery. Doing this as soon as possible helps to make sure that any corrosion is kept to a minimum, which consequently protects your battery.

If your battery is inside of another device and it's possible to do so, then remove it once you've switched it off. In a lot of cases, this might not be possible, as many devices use integrated, non-removable batteries, but check just in case. Pat your battery dry, and set it aside for a while. Despite common advice, don't use any direct heat sources on it, like a hairdryer, as this can actually cause further damage. Instead, you could try placing the battery in a sealed container with desiccants. You might have something like silica gel hanging around in a junk drawer.

Make sure you don't use or charge your battery or device again while it's still wet, and assume it's wet for longer than you think. Just because a device or battery feels dry on the outside doesn't mean it is, as pesky droplets could have worked their way inside. Lastly, make sure you assess the battery for any visual signs of damage before considering using it again. If your battery looks corroded or swollen, then it isn't safe to use. If in doubt, reach out to a professional or replace the battery.
