📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Microsoft’s first games console hit North America 25 years ago today.
  • Recent findings suggest that the Xbox arrived on Nov 15, 2001, during the sixth generation of consoles, facing stiff opposition from the legendary Sony PlayStation 2, Nintendo GameCube, and Sega Dreamcast.
  • It is interesting to weigh up the performance hardware that was a major reason behind the OG Xbox’s success.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Microsoft’s first games console hit North America 25 years ago today. Effectively a PC in a box, the original Xbox was powered by an Intel Pentium III CPU and an Nvidia GPU inside a bulky black and green case. This first-gen device would sell 24 million units and be succeeded by the sleek PowerPC/ATI-powered Xbox 360 in late 2005.

Recent findings suggest that the Xbox arrived on Nov 15, 2001, during the sixth generation of consoles, facing stiff opposition from the legendary Sony PlayStation 2, Nintendo GameCube, and Sega Dreamcast. However, it established a very respectable foothold in the console market thanks to its formidable hardware and a killer app in the shape of Halo: Combat Evolved. It would end up outselling Nintendo and Sega rivals, only living in the shadow of the PS2.

It is interesting to weigh up the performance hardware that was a major reason behind the OG Xbox’s success. Though the contemporary PC parts it used probably made it one of the biggest and ugliest consoles ever, powerful hardware is a great foundation for cutting-edge gaming experiences. The key components behind the Xbox were the Intel Pentium III 733 MHz CPU and an Nvidia NV2A 233 MHz GPU. Systems came with 64MB of DDR SDRAM and accessed games via optical media through its DVD drive. Perhaps most unusual for the time, the system included a built-in HDD (8GB), as well as offering 8MB memory cards for removable storage.

Another hardware advantage of the Xbox and key to connected gaming fun during the early broadband proliferation era was the inclusion of an Ethernet jack as standard. Xbox Live online gaming would launch in 2002. Microsoft used a heavily modified controller-friendly version of Windows 2000 for the system’s OS.

Sources indicate that setting the foundation for the next 25 years of Xbox, the original console was clearly a success. However, as the games industry prepares for a latest generation of hardware, Microsoft’s strategy looks less certain than ever before. Even more so than with Sony, it seems less clear where the Xbox business is headed.

Microsoft couldn’t pass such an vital anniversary without a celebratory promotion, and it looks like a very attractive one. If you are buying a latest pre-built PC for gaming, you should keep an eye out for the 25-year Xbox bundle. This bestows new system purchasers with “25 fan-favorite Xbox games.” You’ll find the following games in your Microsoft Store Library, under the ‘Included with device’ tab on qualifying machines:.

The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim Special Edition.

Halo: Combat Evolved Anniversary.

The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion Game of the Year Edition.

Age of Empires II: Definitive Edition.

Rise of Nations: Extended Edition.

Pillars of Eternity II: Deadfire.

Zoo Tycoon: Ultimate Animal Collection.

Crimson Skies: High Road to Revenge.

Recent findings suggest that those who aren’t getting a new gaming PC can still harvest a few commemorative freebies from Microsoft. On the dedicated page about the 25th anniversary, I spied free wallpapers, free in-game anniversary items for various titles, and an Xbox account badge. Fans are asked to check back at the linked page for “updates, freebies, exclusive experiences and the latest news throughout the year.”.

It can route you to a doctor's appointment sitting in your calendar, or find a place you once snapped a photo of and start directions.

Depending on your life, though, the passenger seat might never be empty. I haven't seen anything suggesting it can tell a solo commute from a packed back seat.

So before your next drive with people in the car, you might want to change these Gemini and Android Auto settings.

It has been revealed that personal Intelligence is only for personal Google accounts belonging to people 18 and older. Workspace business, enterprise, and education accounts can't use it.

It also isn't available in the European Economic Area, Switzerland, the UK, or Nigeria.

In a recent development, android Auto is getting it now. Cars with Google built-in are next in line, with the feature arriving in the coming months.

If you're in one of those regions, on a work or school account, or driving a car with Google built-in, this setting won't apply yet.

Personal Intelligence is off until you turn it on. But chances are, you already switched it on in the Gemini app on your phone, which carries over to Android Auto.

To turn it completely off, open the Gemini app and go to Menu > Settings & help > Personal Intelligence, then turn off the main toggle.

This is less drastic than it sounds. Everything in the car still works without Personal Intelligence. Navigation and music carry on. Calls still go through, and Gemini still answers general questions.

What you lose is personalization, because Gemini stops consulting your account data for context.

If switching everything off is overkill, the Connected Apps menu lets you pick and choose which services Gemini can reach.

In the Gemini app, go to Menu > Settings & help > Personal Intelligence > Connected Apps. The riskiest switch for a full car is also the easiest one to miss.

Google Workspace looks like a single app, but it covers Gmail, Google Drive, Google Calendar, Google Keep, and Google Tasks.

In a recent development, your email and your schedule share a single switch, so you can't keep one without the other. Mine's off.

I would also turn off Google Photos. A vague prompt could surface where my photos were taken. That's not something I want narrated.

I'd leave Google Maps and YouTube on. Google Maps knows your past destinations and saved places. YouTube knows your watch history.

They are useful for route planning and music that fits what you like, which is most of what you want from an assistant in the car.

A cabin is small. Everyone in it is within earshot of the mic.

If the assistant isn't tuned to your voice, a passenger saying "Hey Google" could ask for your personal data without meaning to.

It has been revealed that voice Match is your best defense here, even if it isn't perfect. In my experience, it gets confused now and then, but retraining it means fewer passengers accidentally waking the assistant.

In the Gemini app, tap your profile picture, go to Settings > Talk to Gemini hands-free, and retrain your voice model. On some phones, it's still called Hey Google & Voice Match.

Industry observers note that some of the risk has nothing to do with AI. By default, Android Auto pushes incoming messages onto the car's display and can read them aloud with text-to-speech.

Recent findings suggest that that's convenient when you're solo. But with passengers, it's your texts on a massive screen and over the speakers for the whole car.

Recent findings suggest that open Android Auto settings on your phone and scroll down to Notifications. Turn off Show message notifications to stop the pop-ups on the dashboard.

Then turn off Notifications with Assistant, which lets Android Auto read your messages aloud.

#73. How to Build a Browser-Based Image Storyboard to PDF Tool Using JavaScript

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3237 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Freecodecamp

How to Build a Browser-Based Image Storyboard to PDF Tool Using JavaScript

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3237 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Freecodecamp

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Before anyone films a video, shoots an ad or draws the final pages of a comic, someone usually sketches the strategy as a storyboard: one picture per shot, in order, with a short note about what happens and how long it lasts.
  • Recent findings suggest that most people already have those pictures.
  • In this tutorial, you'll build a browser-based tool that does exactly that.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Before anyone films a video, shoots an ad or draws the final pages of a comic, someone usually sketches the strategy as a storyboard: one picture per shot, in order, with a short note about what happens and how long it lasts.

Recent findings suggest that most people already have those pictures. They are phone photos, screenshots, rough sketches or AI-generated frames sitting in a folder. What they don't have is a quick way to turn that folder into clean, numbered sheets they can print or send to a client.

In this tutorial, you'll build a browser-based tool that does exactly that. You'll add a set of images, give each one a title, a description and a duration, choose a layout, preview the sheets, and download a print-ready PDF.

It has been revealed that everything runs in the browser. The images are never uploaded to a server, which matters when the frames are unreleased product shots or client work.

Along the way, you'll learn how to fix sideways phone photos, sort files the way people expect, lay out a page in PDF points, wrap text on a canvas, save a draft with IndexedDB, and build a PDF that keeps photos sharp without making the file huge.

In a recent development, I built this tool for AllInOneTools, where it runs as the Image Storyboard to PDF tool. This article walks through a simplified version that you can build in three files.

Recent findings suggest that the tool takes a list of images and turns them into storyboard sheets. Each image becomes a frame with:.

The frames are placed on sheets in one of four layouts:.

Each sheet has a title, the total running time and a sheet number at the top.

Here's the flow from start to finish:.

Recent findings suggest that PDF-lib can write real text into a PDF, but only with a font file you embed. The standard PDF fonts only cover basic Latin characters, so a description in Hindi, Gujarati, Arabic or Japanese would fail.

It has been revealed that A canvas, on the other hand, can draw any text the device can show, using the fonts the device already has. So this tool draws all the text on a canvas at 300 dpi and puts that canvas into the PDF as an image.

Sources indicate that the trade-off is that the text in the PDF isn't selectable or searchable. For a storyboard, which is mostly printed and looked at, that's usually fine. If you need searchable text, you'd embed a font with PDF-lib's fontkit support instead.

Open index.html through a local server (for example, the Live Server extension in VS Code) rather than as a file:// page, so that IndexedDB and downloads behave the same way they will on a real site.

This project uses one library and a few built-in browser APIs:.

You don't need PDF.js here, because there's no PDF to read. Everything starts from images.

Add PDF-lib with a pinned version at the end of the body, before your own script:.

Pinning the version means a future release of the library can't break your tool without you knowing.

Here's the upload area and the draft bar:.

The file input only accepts the formats every browser can decode: JPEG, PNG, WebP and GIF.

The workspace holds the three panels:.

Recent findings suggest that the settings panel is a list of select and number inputs. Each one has an id that matches a key in the settings object you'll create in JavaScript:.

The preview panel has the canvas, the sheet navigation and the download controls:.

In style.css, add one rule that's easy to forget:.

The workspace uses display: grid and the draft bar uses display: flex. Those rules are more specific than the browser's default style for the hidden attribute, so without this line, hidden elements would still show.

At the top of script.js, set up the constants, the state and the element references:.

The state object is the single source of truth. The frame list, the preview and the PDF are all built from it, which keeps them in sync.

The paper sizes are in PDF points. One point is 1/72 of an inch, so an A4 page is 595.28 × 841.89 points. You'll do all layout math in points and only convert to pixels when drawing.

The "Select images" button opens the hidden file input, and dropping files anywhere on the page adds them too:.

Resetting fileInput.value after each pick lets the user choose the same file again later. The dataTransfer.types.includes('Files') check makes sure the drop highlight only appears for files, not for frames being dragged inside the list.

Sources indicate that phones don't rotate the pixels when you hold them sideways. They save the image in the sensor's orientation and add an EXIF tag that says "rotate this 90° when you show it.".

If you draw such a photo on a canvas with an img element in some browsers, or read its width and height before the rotation is applied, the frame comes out sideways or with the wrong shape.

createImageBitmap with imageOrientation: 'from-image' asks the browser to apply the EXIF rotation while decoding:.

Recent findings suggest that if createImageBitmap isn't available or fails, the code falls back to a normal img element. Modern browsers apply EXIF rotation to img elements by default too.

canvasToBlob wraps the callback-based canvas.toBlob() in a Promise, so you can use it with await.

Recent findings suggest that A phone photo can be 4000 × 3000 pixels or more. Drawing dozens of those every time the user types a letter would make the preview slow.

So each frame keeps the original file for the PDF, plus a small JPEG copy (at most 1000 pixels on its longest side) for the frame list and the preview:.

According to recent reports, notice that w and h are read after decoding, so they're the size after rotation. A portrait phone photo gets a portrait frame.

Sources indicate that the white fill before drawing matters for PNG images with transparency. JPEG has no transparency, so transparent areas would otherwise turn black.

Industry observers note that people name their files shot-1.jpg, shot-2.jpg … shot-10.jpg. A normal string sort puts shot-10 before shot-2, because it compares the character 1 with 2.

localeCompare with the numeric option compares the numbers inside the names as numbers:.

addFiles filters out unsupported files, sorts the rest, turns each into a frame and reports anything it skipped:.

Recent findings suggest that the images are read one at a time, not all at once with Promise.all. Decoding 50 large photos in parallel can run a phone out of memory, and reading them in order also keeps the status message accurate.

Each frame gets a card with its thumbnail, a title field, a description box, a duration field and three buttons:.

Recent findings suggest that titles and descriptions come from the user, so they're escaped before going into the HTML. Without escapeHtml, a title like Shot "A" would break the value attribute.

Sources indicate that if you rebuilt the whole list on every key press, the text field would lose focus after each letter. Instead, one input listener on the list updates only the state:.

In a recent development, this uses event delegation: one listener on the list handles every field in every card, including cards added later. The data-field attribute tells it which property to update.

The preview redraw is delayed with drawPreviewSoon(), which you'll write later, so it runs once when the user pauses typing rather than on every letter.

Durations are stored in seconds and shown as 4.5 s under a minute or 1:10 from one minute up:.

The Up and Down buttons, and the Delete button, are handled by one click listener:.

splice(from, 1) removes the frame, and splice(to, 0, frame) puts it back at its upcoming position.

Recent findings suggest that for mouse users, dragging a thumbnail onto another card moves it there. The HTML5 drag and drop API needs preventDefault() in dragover, or the browser won't allow the drop:.

stopPropagation() in the drop handler stops the document-level drop handler from treating the move as a fresh file drop.

Keep the Up and Down buttons even with drag and drop. Drag and drop doesn't work with a keyboard, and it's awkward on touch screens.

Industry observers note that deleting a frame that has a long description typed into it is painful if it was a mistake. So the tool keeps the last deleted frame and its position:.

Math.min(index, state.frames.length) puts the frame back at the end if the list got shorter in the meantime.

All settings are read into state.opts in one place, with the number fields limited to a sensible range:.

Sources indicate that any change goes back to the first sheet and redraws the preview. The board title is saved as a draft too, because it's part of the user's work.

It has been revealed that the four layouts change only the arrangement. The frame data stays the same, so consumers can switch layouts freely without losing anything.

Industry observers note that this is the heart of the tool. Before drawing anything, the code works out where every box goes, in PDF points from the top-left corner of the sheet.

Keeping layout separate from drawing means the same layout is used for the small preview on screen and for the 300 dpi PDF. They can't drift apart.

Industry observers note that the paper sizes are stored once. Landscape just swaps the short and long sides.

Here's what happens step by step:.

Each cell ends up with an img box and a text box, and that's all the drawing code needs to know.

Sources indicate that A cell is rarely the same shape as the picture. Stretching would distort faces and products, and cropping might cut off what matters. So the picture is scaled to fit inside the box, keeping its proportions, and centered:.

According to recent reports, this is the same idea as object-fit: contain in CSS. The smaller of the two scale factors wins, so the whole picture always fits.

Canvas has no automatic line wrapping. fillText draws one line, however long it is. So you measure words with measureText and build the lines yourself:.

If the description is longer than the lines available, the last line ends with an ellipsis, so the user can see that text was cut.

The parameter k is the scale from points to pixels. All positions come from the layout in points and are multiplied by k just before drawing. That's what lets the same function draw a 600-pixel preview and a 300 dpi PDF page.

The duration is drawn first, right-aligned, and the space it takes is subtracted from the room left for the label and title. That way a long title never runs into the duration.

drawSheet draws the heading, then each frame on the sheet:.

The mode parameter is the key trick here:.

It has been revealed that you'll see why in the PDF section. For the film strip, the dark band and the sprocket holes are drawn first, and the picture sits in the middle of the band.

The preview draws the current sheet at the canvas's on-screen width, multiplied by the device pixel ratio so it stays sharp on high-density screens:.

The device pixel ratio is capped at 2. A 3× phone screen would otherwise create a canvas nine times the size of the CSS box, which is slow and adds little you can see.

Writing descriptions for 30 frames takes time. Losing that work to an accidental reload is frustrating, so the tool saves a draft as the user works.

According to recent reports, localStorage won't do here. It only stores strings, and most browsers limit it to about 5 MB, which is less than two phone photos. IndexedDB can store Blob objects directly and allows far more space.

dbRun wraps a transaction in a Promise. It resolves when the transaction completes, so a write is only reported as done once it's actually stored.

It has been revealed that the draft stores the original image files as Blobs, along with the text the user typed. Thumbnails and object URLs aren't stored, because they can be made again from the files.

saveDraftSoon waits until the user pauses for 800 ms, so typing a description doesn't write to the database on every key press.

If saving fails, for example in a private window with storage blocked, the tool tells the user to download the PDF before closing the tab instead of failing silently.

When the page loads, the tool checks for a draft and offers to restore it:.

Each saved Blob goes back through makeFrame, so restored frames get fresh thumbnails, and then the saved text is copied onto them.

Recent findings suggest that the simplest way to make the PDF would be to draw each whole sheet on a canvas, with the pictures, and put that canvas in the PDF as one image. It works, but it forces a choice:.

So the tool uses two layers on each page:.

In a recent development, JPEG is good for photos, and PNG keeps text sharp. This is why drawSheet has the 'overlay' mode that leaves holes where the pictures go.

The picture is decoded again from the original file, not from the thumbnail, so the PDF has full quality.

Here's what happens on each page:.

Note the y coordinate: L.H - rect.y - rect.h. The layout and the canvas measure y from the top of the page, but PDF measures y from the bottom. Forgetting this flip puts every picture upside down in the page, the classic PDF-lib mistake.

Setting c.width = 1 after use frees the canvas memory right away, which matters on phones when there are many sheets.

The file name comes from a text field, cleaned of characters that aren't allowed in file names:.

Sources indicate that the object URL is revoked after a minute, which is long enough for the download to start and frees the memory afterwards. The button is disabled while the PDF is being made, so a double click can't start two exports.

Finally, "Start over" clears the state, the draft and the object URLs. The last two lines of the file read the default settings and check for a saved draft when the page loads:.

Here's the whole workflow in the finished tool.

Drop a folder's worth of images on the page or click Select images. They're sorted by file name, so shot-1, shot-2 … shot-10 land in the right order.

Drag a thumbnail onto another card, or use the Up and Down buttons.

In a recent development, give each frame a title, a description and a duration. The total running time updates as you type.

Pick one frame per page, a grid, panels with notes or a film strip, then set the paper size and orientation.

Use Previous and Next to look at every sheet before you download.

Type a file name, choose the image quality and click Download PDF.

According to recent reports, use thumbnails for everything on screen. The preview redraws often, while the user types and changes settings. Drawing 1000-pixel thumbnails instead of full photos keeps it fast. Only the PDF export touches the original files.

Decode thumbnails once. In drawSheet, each frame keeps its decoded thumbnail in frame.thumbPic, so switching sheets doesn't decode the same image again.

Process images one at a time. Reading or exporting dozens of large photos with Promise.all can use more memory than a phone has. A simple for loop with await keeps only one large image in memory at a time.

It has been revealed that size pictures for the page, not the camera. A picture's pixel size in the PDF should depend on how significant it is on the page and the chosen dpi. That one line in buildPdf is often the difference between a 3 MB file and a 60 MB file.

Industry observers note that release memory as you go. Call close() on an ImageBitmap when you're done with it, set used canvases to width = 1, and revoke object URLs you no longer need.

In a recent development, sideways phone photos. If you read an image's size or draw it without applying EXIF orientation, portrait photos come out landscape. Use createImageBitmap(blob, { imageOrientation: 'from-image' }).

Stretched pictures. Drawing an image straight into a cell with drawImage(img, x, y, cellW, cellH) stretches it. Always fit it with a "contain" calculation like fitContain first.

Industry observers note that wrong order of files. The order files arrive from a file picker or a drop isn't guaranteed. Sort them yourself, and use a numeric sort so shot-10 comes after shot-9.

It has been revealed that forgetting to flip the y axis. Canvas y goes down from the top, PDF y goes up from the bottom. Convert with pageHeight - y - height when placing anything with PDF-lib.

It has been revealed that black backgrounds on transparent PNGs. JPEG has no transparency. Fill the canvas with white before drawing a PNG you'll save as JPEG.

According to recent reports, rebuilding the list while the user types. Re-rendering inputs on every key press moves the cursor and loses focus. Enhancement the state from the input event and only rebuild the list when the order changes.

It has been revealed that canvases that are too large. Browsers limit canvas size, and phones have tight limits. An A3 page at 300 dpi is about 4960 × 3508 pixels, which is fine, but don't multiply that by the device pixel ratio as well.

In this tutorial, you built a browser-based tool that turns a set of images into storyboard sheets and a print-ready PDF.

You learned how to apply phone photo rotation with createImageBitmap, sort file names numerically, keep layout math in PDF points so the preview and the PDF always match, wrap text on a canvas, save a draft of images and text in IndexedDB, and build a two-layer PDF with sharp text and compact photos using PDF-lib.

All of it runs locally in the browser, so the images stay on the user's device.

You can try the full version of this tool, with more options such as sheet colors, a handwritten font, one PDF per frame and PNG export, at Image Storyboard to PDF.

Why Don't Military Vehicles Use 'Lifetime' Sealed Transmissions?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Some military vehicles look and function very much like their civilian counterparts.
  • It has been revealed that since there's the logistical challenge of getting a replacement model to the front lines, it's important to keep these vehicles in action, or at least try to ensure that servicing them is as fast, intuitive, and practical as possible.
  • In a recent development, regular cars and trucks are tools for commuting, and so convenience is enormously crucial.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some military vehicles look and function very much like their civilian counterparts. Others, of course, do not — sporting armor, weaponry, and advanced technology that civilian models don't need. Along with these features can come a need for specialized experience and maintenance knowledge. After all, these vehicles help their occupants survive in the most hostile of environments and are means of transportation just as much as military tools. Typically, ground models have conventional transmissions to maintain.

It has been revealed that since there's the logistical challenge of getting a replacement model to the front lines, it's important to keep these vehicles in action, or at least try to ensure that servicing them is as fast, intuitive, and practical as possible. As such, you might think that a "lifetime" sealed transmission is a more practical choice, as it could reduce the amount of maintenance. However, there are some considerable downsides to this specific type of transmission for military models, including maintenance experience and the fact that they're not as "lifetime" guaranteed as the name suggest. Because of this, military vehicles don't tend to use sealed transmissions, unlike so many modern cars.

In a recent development, regular cars and trucks are tools for commuting, and so convenience is enormously crucial. To facilitate this, many have sealed transmissions that purport to be good for a "lifetime." As such, you'd be forgiven for thinking that a sealed transmission doesn't need to be serviced, but that's not entirely the case. In fact, when these transmissions do require servicing, it can be more complicated because of how they are designed. Sealed transmissions don't have a dipstick or any of the conventional means of access, and this can create a huge potential matter in military use.

In a recent development, unfortunately, the reality of supplying, maintaining, and running a lot of sophisticated military technologies is that some of them will inevitably have issues that can take them out of action. To reduce pressure on servicepeople, the military must utilize systems that don't require specialized knowledge to manage. This, then, can be a primary reason as to why sealed transmissions aren't a focus on military vehicles.

Sources indicate that when care for sealed transmissions is needed in the civilian world, it's often the case that a mechanic with the required knowledge and tools is not far away. Meanwhile, militaries may be dispatched to more remote locations where the key to survival is self-reliance, and while there are some experienced mechanics, they cannot be everywhere. Using systems that are easy to service on the go reduces logistical challenges, and a sealed transmission could compromise that.

Sources indicate that A lot of military vehicles are rugged powerhouses that are expected to transport personnel and certain equipment loads across what could be challenging terrain. Because of this, they're built to be hard-wearing and versatile. They have to be designed with the practicality of maintenance in mind while remaining multi-purpose in terms of operation.

For example, the Humvee 4-CT was designed with a four-speed automatic transmission, but it is far from the only military model to be an automatic, though. For instance, in March 2023, Allison Transmission noted in a press release that its 2500 Specialty Series transmission had been chosen for the Joint Light Tactical Vehicle's A2 variant, after eight years of supplying the transmission for the JLTV A1.

According to recent reports, automatic transmissions are also in a wide range of other prominent military ground vehicles. Take the ever-imposing tank, for instance. For some time, automatic transmissions have been essential components of tracked vehicles, including the Turkish Altay, Malaysian PT-91M, and Indian Arjun main battle tanks. Typically, though, these are not sealed transmissions. Neither are the specialized ones developed for military vehicles, such as Allison Transmission's eGen Force electric hybrid system, which the manufacturer notes is "scalable to 75-ton tracked vehicles, making it capable of meeting future Main Battle Tank requirements." The needs for these vehicles can be very different, so sealed transmissions do not broadly fit here.

'It would make me think twice about applying': Workers are pushing back at companies who insist on AI interviews

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Seven in 10 UK workers say they'd feel uncomfortable if their interview was conducted by an AI assisted, new Careerminds research has revealed, while not even a third say they'd continue without hesitation.
  • But the reality is a stark contrast, because as many as half (47%) of UK job seekers have already been interviewed by AI, per a separate Greenhouse study.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Seven in 10 UK workers say they'd feel uncomfortable if their interview was conducted by an AI assisted, new Careerminds research has revealed, while not even a third say they'd continue without hesitation.

But the reality is a stark contrast, because as many as half (47%) of UK job seekers have already been interviewed by AI, per a separate Greenhouse study.

According to recent reports, but despite hesitation, where workers sit can vary quite widely. Around one-third (33%) would continue but feel uncomfortable and a quarter (25%) say it would depend on the role or salary – only 11% say they would withdraw entirely.

Of those 11%, only 5.5% would definitely withdraw, with the other 5.7% probably considering withdrawing. Still, the figures confirm that recruiters could be losing access to vital human talent if they use AI avatars to interview candidates.

The Greenhouse study put the figure much higher, at 30% of UK candidates abandoning the hiring process because of an AI interview, stressing that four in five (82%) weren't even told beforehand that they'd be answering questions with an AI avatar.

Unsurprisingly, older generations would be more likely to withdraw, Careerminds found, highlighting the challenges that older workers could face when looking for a job change.

Resident careers expert Amanda Augustine stressed that interviews serve as a crucial first point of contact for many workers, and they can influence how that candidate goes on to perceive the employer.

One worker cited in the study described his AI interview as "surreal, strange and impersonal." He noted that the whole experience "felt like a one-way process.".

Augustine remarked the best fit for AI is actually in helping recruiters to process the administrative side of the job, such as trawling through applications and refining the pool. "Let the technology handle the administrative tasks so your team has more time for the human conversations that help both sides decide whether the role is the right fit," she added.

The sentiment isn't universal, though, and there are some Gemini defenders speaking up.

Tech Report: Raising the quality of insights in agentic analytics

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, in just a few years, generative AI has changed the face of enterprise analytics, notably by making analytics accessible to users across the organization.
  • According to recent reports, fewer than half of agent-generated insights at the organizations surveyed for this report lead to business improvement.
  • Recent findings suggest that failure to produce insights that improve the business deprives organizations of their desired return on investment in agentic analytics.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in just a few years, generative AI has changed the face of enterprise analytics, notably by making analytics accessible to users across the organization. Agentic AI promises to do even more, by automating entire workflows and taking actions based on agent insights. But there is a problem: The quality of insights that agents at the moment generate leaves much to be desired.

According to recent reports, fewer than half of agent-generated insights at the organizations surveyed for this report lead to business improvement. And while most respondents praise the quality of their agents’ descriptive insights, reviews of their prescriptive insights—those on which actions are based—are decidedly mixed.

Recent findings suggest that failure to produce insights that improve the business deprives organizations of their desired return on investment in agentic analytics. Worse, flawed insights that trigger incorrect actions can cause reputational or financial damage. This report gauges how companies view the quality of the outputs produced by their analytics agents and explores how organizations are seeking to boost insight quality and get their agents working harder for the business.

Some key findings from the report include the following:.

Agentic analytics is only just starting to deliver. On average, 48% of insights generated by analytics agents at the surveyed companies lead to actions that improve the business. That is a marked advance from the 37% average the respondents say generated such actions one year ago. But it means that more than half of the insights generated by analytics agents today are still failing to help businesses.

Industry observers note that better quality of insights leads to clear business advantage. At a small cohort of organizations, which we term “insight leaders,” AI agents perform much better than the average. In this group, more than 70% of agent insights lead to actions that improve the business. The insight leaders also give the quality of their agents’ insights higher marks than do the total respondents overall. The quality gap is particularly wide when it comes to prescriptive insights.

Insufficient context reduces insight quality. When analytics agents deliver insights of substandard quality, the main reason is a lack of business context, as cited by 55% of surveyed executives. Fragmented or inaccessible data is the other major factor, according to 45%. Fewer insight leaders say their agents struggle with access to context.

Industry observers note that insight overload further inhibits agent effectiveness. At a majority (52%) of surveyed organizations, analytics agents generate too many insights to be properly evaluated and therefore acted upon. Less than one-quarter (24%) are able to evaluate all agent insights; most do so on a case-by-case basis, and that process is currently human-intensive.

Governance and semantics are areas of focus for improving insights. The surveyed companies are prioritizing initiatives that enable better agent insights by strengthening AI and data governance (cited by 60%). They are also adding a semantic layer to their data architecture (45%). The experts we interviewed agree that the semantic layer is crucial to ensure high-performing agents.

This content was produced by Insights, MIT Technology Review’s custom content arm, not its editorial staff. It was researched and written by humans, with any AI tools that may have been used limited to production processes under human oversight.

5 Disadvantages Of Battery-Powered Video Doorbells

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1120 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashgear

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the sphere of home surveillance tech, video doorbells have become one of the most common devices.
  • According to recent reports, of course, battery-powered video doorbells from multiple substantial brands are already a properly-established spin-off of this tech, and certainly, they bring some extra convenience to the table, particularly for those who rent their homes or aren't comfortable with electrical wiring.
  • It has been revealed that the first thing you'll immediately be made cognizant of when using a battery-powered video doorbell is, of course, the battery.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the sphere of home surveillance tech, video doorbells have become one of the most common devices. They provide a clear view of your home's front door and allow you to interface directly with any visitors, as well as receive notifications in case you don't hear the actual chime, some even without a subscription service. These are all very convenient features, and arguably, the optimal way to make the framework even more convenient would be to eliminate the need to wire the doorbell into your home's power grid.

According to recent reports, of course, battery-powered video doorbells from multiple substantial brands are already a properly-established spin-off of this tech, and certainly, they bring some extra convenience to the table, particularly for those who rent their homes or aren't comfortable with electrical wiring. However, as is often the case when messing with power frameworks, switching to a battery-powered video doorbell over a hard-wired one will definitely bring some changes to your usage of it. Depending on your personal preferences, these changes could make all the difference between that sought-after convenience and an entirely new batch of irritating headaches.

It has been revealed that the first thing you'll immediately be made cognizant of when using a battery-powered video doorbell is, of course, the battery. Rather than needing to be wired directly into your home's power grid, a battery-powered video doorbell runs off an internal rechargeable power source. This is the primary feature that lets you just install it anywhere near your front door. With the use of a rechargeable battery, however, comes the unspoken implication that you need to periodically recharge it.

The good news is that the batteries on a video doorbell are generally pretty hearty, able to last anywhere from several weeks to an entire month before needing to be recharged. That mentioned, you do need to recharge it on a fairly tight window, and if you forget to do so, the doorbell will simply stop working. Some brands of video doorbells may send you automatic push notifications when the battery is running low, which is helpful if you're forgetful, but it can also be annoying to keep receiving these notifications and having to tend to the battery at inopportune times, especially since you'll be without a doorbell while it's charging (and some take many hours to recharge).

Recent findings suggest that the battery on a video doorbell can last for a variable amount of time. The reason that we can't provide an exact lifespan of the battery's single charge is because that lifespan is heavily dependent on what you're doing with the doorbell, not to mention the conditions it's operating in.

According to recent reports, when a battery-powered video doorbell isn't in active operation, it's sleeping in a low-power state, which decreases battery usage. Whenever it starts recording footage or using it's additional features like two-way audio, it turns on and starts consuming battery power at the regular rate. If you're using these features very frequently every day, your battery is naturally going to run down faster, which means more frequent recharges are required. Additionally, certain environmental conditions, like intense heat and cold, may cause greater battery draw than usual, which increases the need for recharges during the peaks of summer and winter.

A battery-powered video doorbell's functions are largely built around the fact that it draws from a battery. In other words, where a hard-wired video doorbell can just keep recording footage in perpetuity without worrying about power, a battery-powered doorbell can't do that, or else it'd run out of juice very promptly. This is why many models of battery-powered video doorbell simply don't offer continuous recording functionality, or at least don't have it as the default setting.

Instead, battery-powered video doorbells may opt instead for "event-based recording." This means the camera only turns on when, for instance, the motion sensor is tripped in its line of sight, or someone walks right up to the camera and presses the chime button. If you only care about recording footage when someone's at the door or an animal is running around on your lawn, that's not the end of the world, but if you were hoping for the full, round-the-clock surveillance experience, you're probably not going to get that here. The only way you could circumvent that is by setting up additional cameras around your property with 24/7 surveillance, but at that point, why even bother with the battery-powered doorbell?

In a recent development, have you ever noticed that, when your phone's battery is running low, it seems to take a little longer to wake up from sleep mode than it normally would? Battery-powered devices allocate portions of their available power in order to run their basic functions, with a little bit expended on every wake-up to kick things in gear. It's not dissimilar to the extra gas that's used up every time you start your car. Naturally, this little quirk also applies to battery-powered video doorbells, but that extra second of wake-up can have annoying knock-on effects.

In a recent development, if your battery doorbell has a low battery, or it's just generally getting old and outdated, it may experience slightly slower response times to stimulus. If you were hoping for the doorbell to immediately capture a motion event, for example, that increased response time could result in the camera missing whatever triggered the event, rendering the entire recording worthless. This is another advantage wired doorbells have over battery-powered ones; because they're always drawing power, they don't have to go to sleep, so they don't experience that reduced response time.

In the same vein as response times and non-continuous recording, even if a battery-powered video doorbell shares some features with its wired counterparts, there's a distinct chance that those features will be slightly diminished or otherwise less effective. The primary perk of a battery doorbell is its flexibility, the fact that you can set it up anywhere with a few screws, but oftentimes, with flexibility comes reduced specialization. "Jack-of-all trades, master of none," as the old saying goes.

For example, both wireless and wired video doorbells often possess facial recognition and recording functionality, but while wired doorbells are supplemented by additional recognition software, battery-powered models don't have the necessary power to run those functions, and so may be less effective. For example, as one Reddit user recounts, not once did their battery-powered doorbell camera manage to successfully record anyone's face despite having the feature; the only footage they ever got of anyone on their doorstep was of people leaving after visiting. If you're hoping to make extensive use of features like facial recognition on your doorbell camera, this is a bit of a cautionary tale.

#65. Industry News: Here’s who is falling in line for Trump’s “Super Intelligence” loyalty test

📅 03 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1192 w)
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Technologyreview

Industry News: Here’s who is falling in line for Trump’s “Super Intelligence” loyalty test

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1192 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • At the end of September, President Trump signed an executive order that contained just one directive, ordering government agencies to rebrand what they had been calling artificial intelligence as “Super Intelligence.” That term beat out other contenders, including “Extreme Intelligence” and “Supreme Intelligence,” offered by the president in a poll on X a couple of weeks earlier.
  • Rebrands are, of course, now a White House tradition: Trump has changed names to project US dominance of certain bodies of water (the Gulf of America and Lake America), to signal new institutional priorities (Department of War), or simply to leave his mark on storied places (see the ongoing fight over renaming the Kennedy Center).
  • The stated reason for this name change is that today’s AI systems “amplify human ingenuity” rather than merely “imitate” intelligence, and the government’s terminology should reflect that.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At the end of September, President Trump signed an executive order that contained just one directive, ordering government agencies to rebrand what they had been calling artificial intelligence as “Super Intelligence.” That term beat out other contenders, including “Extreme Intelligence” and “Supreme Intelligence,” offered by the president in a poll on X a couple of weeks earlier.

Rebrands are, of course, now a White House tradition: Trump has changed names to project US dominance of certain bodies of water (the Gulf of America and Lake America), to signal new institutional priorities (Department of War), or simply to leave his mark on storied places (see the ongoing fight over renaming the Kennedy Center).

The stated reason for this name change is that today’s AI systems “amplify human ingenuity” rather than merely “imitate” intelligence, and the government’s terminology should reflect that. But if this rebrand follows the pattern of others, its effects will extend beyond government.

It will turn a choice of words into a political loyalty test: Those who use the upcoming term demonstrate allegiance to the administration, and those who don’t become marks for attacks (recall that the Trump administration barred the Associated Press from some White House press events after the news outlet did not adopt the term “Gulf of America”).

But most Americans go months without ever pondering what to call the major lake between New York and Canada. AI, on the other hand, is at the center of our national conversation and a technology two-thirds of Americans report interacting with multiple times a week. It might be the boldest rebrand yet.

So one month in, who’s on board?

Let’s start with the government itself. The term “Super Intelligence”—or simply “SI”—now appears more often on government solicitations, like a fresh request by Immigration and Customs Enforcement for companies to build “SI-powered” surveillance for ICE detention facilities. The new term has been swapped in silently on most government websites. Some, including that of the National Institutes of Health, now include a banner warning visitors they might see both the new and the old terms during the transition period.

In a recent development, there have been hiccups. A day after the rebrand order, the Pentagon confirmed an ambitious latest initiative to study the future of warfare, called Project Meridian; it used the old terminology. A Federal Trade Commission press release last week used “superintelligence” instead of the two-word, capitalized version ordered by the president, and recent press releases from Health and Human Services show no sign of the new language.

The term “AI” will likely stick around given the countless AI-related offices, initiatives, and programs that have sprung up in recent years, like the Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office at the Pentagon (the executive order says it doesn’t apply to previously issued regulations or documents).

In a recent development, as for government employees, it appears to be taking time for “SI” rather than “AI” to roll off the tongue. One researcher at a national lab I interviewed a few weeks ago used “AI” repeatedly before sheepishly acknowledging the slip-up. Even Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth used “AI” in an interview on October 3.

But Trump’s other rebrands suggest the goal isn’t merely to change the government’s vocabulary. It’s to change how the rest of us speak, too.

In the past couple of weeks, most of President Trump’s posts on Truth Social have been endorsements for candidates in the midterms. But on October 27 he took a break from electioneering to criticize the Wall Street Journal for not using “Super Intelligence,” “the name which virtually everyone else is using, or soon will be.” He suggested that a new rule will soon go further than the executive order to outright ban “artificial intelligence” from government documents.

But the Wall Street Journal is not alone: Even Newsmax, an outlet whose founder described it as “supportive of the President and his policies,” isn’t using the president’s preferred term.

Are Significant Tech executives falling in line? It’s complicated. The same day that President Trump signed the rebranding order, he also released a nonbinding statement on AI safety, the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, signed by six of the most powerful people in tech: Sundar Pichai of Google, Dario Amodei of Anthropic, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta, Greg Brockman of OpenAI, Elon Musk of xAI, and Jensen Huang of Nvidia.

But even among this group—three members of which attended Trump’s inauguration—the term has not caught on.

Industry observers note that in an analysis of third-quarter earnings calls, CNBC reported that only Zuckerberg and Musk used the term consistently. But Zuckerberg doesn’t quite count: Meta has been saying “superintelligence” since last year anyway. Musk’s companies seem to use the term the most—and he even pledged to rename SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI. Musk himself still mixes SI and AI when posting on X.

Executives from Amazon, Microsoft, and Alphabet used “AI” in their calls, though Microsoft’s recent letter to shareholders referred to the “Super Intelligence era.” Huang has referenced the term but still uses AI too.

One objection to this rebranding project is that it will cost time and taxpayer dollars. It is Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff’s prerogative to decide that SIForce is a better name than AIForce and direct his company to implement that change. But government employees are now spending time writing guides on how departments should navigate the rebrand. And, per the executive order, leaders of federal agencies will be required to put their heads together to draft a fresh legislative definition of “Super Intelligence” to be run by the president by the end of this month.

But I’m more worried about what this does to our national conversation about AI than I am about the potential waste of time and money. Surprisingly often I overhear strangers at a grocery store or coffee shop who have struck up a conversation about AI. The substance of the conversation is rarely uplifting—they most often talk about a jobs apocalypse or AI-powered warfare—but what is heartening is how often I see a widespread desire among people to have a say in how this technology transforms their lives.

People may have wildly different feelings about AI, including outright hostility, but those differences don’t yet map neatly onto the partisan divisions that make it awkward for strangers to discuss immigration or climate change.

If “Super Intelligence” turns into a loyalty test, this will cease to be the case. It’s easy to imagine that two people chatting about, say, whether chatbots are good or bad for our mental health will stop once they realize one of them is saying “super intelligence” and the other “AI.” That would be a shame for us all.

Midterm elections are tomorrow. Americans say AI is more important to them in this election than environmental and climate policy (and Democrats even rank it above abortion and gun policy). We’re only just beginning to have a national conversation about what AI will mean for our lives. Whether or not “Super Intelligence” catches on, turning the terminology itself into a loyalty test will do nothing to advance a national conversation about AI that’s only just getting started.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Recent findings suggest that have you ever tried digging a small trench in your garden or property using nothing but spades and shovels? It's as tough as chopping down a tree with a small handsaw. Fortunately, just like chainsaws make cutting wood easier, there's machinery that can offer a similar level of aid while digging. For vertical holes, you can get by with purchasing a Ryobi auger or something similar, but for trenches, you're much better off trying a handheld trencher that looks and operates like a chainsaw.

According to recent reports, designed for smaller DIY projects, landscaping trenchers are compact with the ability to dig as deep as 27 inches. Much like a larger trencher, a handheld one rips into the dirt with steel teeth on a wheel or a chain. The key difference is the size and easy maneuverability that far exceeds the mobility of more "serious" equipment. However, while it doesn't require training or an elaborate setup (which is undoubtedly its main selling point), a handheld trencher has a few drawbacks you should be aware of. Just like chainsaws are tools with a sizable track record for injuries, handheld trenchers can be equally hazardous.

Sources indicate that for instance, if you hit a rock or any solid object with this tool, the kickback could lead to an injury if your hand slips off the handle. You could also get hurt by the flying debris. The other drawback is the price. Quality handheld trenchers are only marginally more affordable than larger equipment. A sit-on towable backhoe by Harbor Freight and its alternatives sit in the $3,000 range, while a handheld TerraTrencher (despite its size) costs around $2,750.

Sources indicate that you don't have to go back to spades and shovels if the trenching chainsaw isn't the right fit for you. There are plenty of larger (yet still somewhat compact) machines you can purchase for smaller DIY projects. The aforementioned towable backhoe is a small version of an excavator that will do just fine for digging canals, and it's equally as useful for other tasks, such as clearing away stumps or removing larger debris.

Recent findings suggest that alternatively, you can get a walk-behind trencher. It's much easier on your back than a handheld trencher, but as with many models, you'll probably have to slowly walk backwards behind the machine as it digs (not everyone's cup of tea). It's also not considerably cheaper than a backhoe and will end up costing you at least $3,000 or more, which makes the chainsaw trencher the wallet-friendlier option.

Considering the higher admission costs of these machines, you could rent one to avoid the upfront costs. Whether this is right for the project you're doing depends on its length, as rentals for equipment like trenchers land in the $150 to $350 range. It goes without saying that this can add up quite fast, so if your trenching "operation" will take time, or you proposal on starting new projects later, it may be more fiscally reasonable to bite the bullet and buy the $3,000 piece of machinery.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Intel’s latest Pelion board adds another device to Googlebook’s Ocelot lineup. It supports Wildcat Lake hardware and could lead to more affordable laptops with 14-inch displays, flexible storage, and Wi-Fi 7.

Google seems to be getting more serious about its Googlebook. Latest information suggests the firm might expand the laptop beyond the premium market. A newly introduced development board, called Pelion, has been spotted in the Chrome repositories. It adds another device to the growing Ocelot hardware family.

The new board, based on Intel’s Core Series 3 Wildcat Lake platform, was recently surfaced in Chromium Gerrit commits. It confirms that development on Pelion has begun. The product’s initial image and Depthcharge files are reportedly created using Matsu, which is another board in the Ocelot family.

The Ocelot family now has a total of nine boards. The list includes Ojal, Matsu, Kodkod, Ocicat, Helka, Coolum, Blanc, Libra, and the newly introduced Pelion. These projects are associated with five major laptop manufacturers: Acer, HP, ASUS, Lenovo, and Dell. It is not yet clear which manufacturer will build a device based on Pelion. However, since it shared a connection with Matsu, it could just be another design from an existing hardware partner.

The biggest twist with the new Pelion is the possibility of a new Googlebook. The first Googlebook, Acer Googlebook 14, starts at $899. For a project that aims to replace Chromebooks, the price is on the very high side. Using Intel’s Wildlake board could help companies make Googlebook more affordable. It opens doors for more affordable alternatives without much reliance on entry-level hardware.

Of course, adding more development boards does not guarantee that these laptops will reach stores anytime soon. Google also has work to do on its Android 17-based desktop operating system.
