#62. Schema Drift vs. Semantic Drift in Data Pipelines

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3582 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Freecodecamp

Schema Drift vs. Semantic Drift in Data Pipelines

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3582 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Freecodecamp

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, when a column is removed from a source database or dataset, the next pipeline run usually fails, making the problem easy to detect.
  • Industry observers note that this happens because a schema describes the structure of data, not what the values actually represent.
  • As a result, most pipeline checks are designed to catch obvious errors, such as missing columns or incorrect data types, but often fail to detect less obvious problems where the data looks correct but its meaning or values have changed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, when a column is removed from a source database or dataset, the next pipeline run usually fails, making the problem easy to detect. But when a field keeps the same name and data type but its meaning changes (known as semantic drift), the pipeline can continue running normally, allowing the problem to go unnoticed.

Industry observers note that this happens because a schema describes the structure of data, not what the values actually represent. It tells us which fields exist, their data types, and whether they can contain null values, but not whether a timestamp uses UTC, a durability score should range from 10 to 100, or an empty string means something different from null.

As a result, most pipeline checks are designed to catch obvious errors, such as missing columns or incorrect data types, but often fail to detect less obvious problems where the data looks correct but its meaning or values have changed.

In a recent development, I wanted to see how far this limitation reaches in practice, so I built a small lab where I introduced nine types of pipeline failures and tested four detectors against each one. This article looks at what each detector caught and what happened when changes went unnoticed and corrupted the data.

You can find the code here and reproduce the experiment with a few commands.

To follow along and run the lab yourself, you’ll need:.

I intentionally kept the pipeline simple. It reads 1,000 game-inventory records from a JSONL file, flattens the nested stats and attributes objects, loads the data into SQLite, and calculates six metrics: total number of records, unequipped items, item counts by rarity, average attack per category, items acquired per day, and average durability. I also left out defensive checks so that each change could affect the pipeline in the same way it might affect a real pipeline when someone assumes the source data is reliable.

Each drift applies a deterministic function that takes one record and returns a changed one, so every result is repeatable. For instance, the timezone drift shifts each UTC timestamp to UTC+4 wall time and drops the offset:.

It has been revealed that after applying each drift, I ran the pipeline and saved its output in a separate SQLite database. I then compared it with the database generated from the original data, checking each row and column for differences. This step helped identify whether the pipeline had produced correct results, rather than simply checking whether it ran successfully.

The comparison placed each change into one of four categories:.

I tested each drifted file with four detectors. Each detector follows the same structure: it takes the baseline file and the incoming file as input, checks for changes, and returns whether it found a problem along with a message. This shared interface keeps the setup simple and makes it easy to add more detectors.

The rest of this article uses two terms: data shape and data meaning. Data shape refers to the fields in a dataset, their paths, and the types of values they contain. The schema detector captures this information by checking each field and the types found in it.

For the baseline, this returns entries like acquired_at: {'str'}, equipped_slot: {'NoneType', 'str'}, and attributes.durability: {'int'}.Data meaning, however, includes everything the dictionary leaves out including the unit and time zone of a value, its expected range, the set of valid strings, and what a null value represents. This reveals a limitation of any detector that only looks at data shape. Since the schema detector bases its results on the dictionary of field paths and data types, it can't distinguish between datasets that produce the same dictionary but contain values with different meanings.

Industry observers note that three of the nine drifts left this dictionary unchanged: the timezone shift, the latest enum value, and the durability scaling. As a result, the schema detector didn't flag any of them.

Detectors can check data at different levels:.

Recent findings suggest that the four detectors cover the first three levels. The fourth level goes beyond what these detectors can establish because a dataset can pass checks on its structure, individual values, and statistical distributions while its meaning has changed. To know what the data means, we need context that can't be gotten from its values alone.

The results matrix summarizes how each of the four detectors responded to the nine drift scenarios.

It highlights which changes they caught, which they missed, and whether the pipeline failed or continued with incorrect data.

Industry observers note that "Yes (only)” means that detector was the only one to catch the change. “n/a” means the pipeline crashed, so no rows were loaded.

The strict model detected the most changes (7 out of 9), followed by the schema diff (6), the loose model (4), and the statistical profile (2).

But each detector missed some changes. Three drifts were detected by only one detector: the strict model caught the timezone shift, the schema diff caught the level change, and the statistical profile caught the durability scaling.

Five of the nine drifts changed the data structure. These included renaming rarity, removing equipped_slot, adding a guild field, replacing the stats object with an array, and changing level from an integer to a string.

In a recent development, the schema diff detected all five changes. The strict model detected four, and the loose model detected three. This demonstrates that the schema diff was the most effective at detecting structural changes.

The pipeline failed on three of the drifts, but some error messages were more useful than others. Renaming rarity caused a KeyError: 'rarity', which tells us exactly which field is missing. Replacing stats with [attack, defense, speed] caused a TypeError: list indices must be integers or slices, not str. This message explains the type of error but doesn't identify the field involved. To find the cause, the reader has to trace the error back through the transformation code.

The classifier labels the first error loud and the second confusing.It makes this distinction by checking whether the error message mentions a field affected by the drift.

The Pydantic detectors ran on the same file and reported stats: Input should be a valid dictionary, directly identifying the field with the problem.

Sources indicate that the level change reveals another way a structural change can go undetected. Both Pydantic models accepted it because Pydantic's default lax mode converts the string "42" into the integer 42. The pipeline also accepted it because SQLite's INTEGER affinity converts text that looks like a number when inserting it into an INTEGER column. As a result, the database matched the baseline, and the classifier labeled the run passed_clean.

Industry observers note that only the schema diff detected the change because it checks the type of the raw value before any conversion takes place. This shows the limitation of checking data after coercion: once a value has been converted, the original type change is no longer visible. In this case, the simplest detector caught a change that both Pydantic models accepted.

In a recent development, the experiment also indicated that not every detected change causes a problem. Adding guild and changing level from an integer to a string both triggered alerts. The schema diff detected both changes, while the strict model detected only the addition of guild. But neither change corrupted any rows because the load step reads only the fields it expects.

This highlights the need to distinguish between changes that should stop a pipeline and those that only need to be logged. If detectors flag too many harmless changes, customers may start to ignore their warnings.

In a recent development, the remaining drifts didn't change the fields or data types. They changed what the values represented. These changes were harder to detect but had real effects on the results. The table below reveals the impact of each drift and whether it was visible in the pipeline's output.

A major thing I noticed is that most of the numbers still look normal. For example, moving timestamps forward by four hours shifts some items onto the next calendar day. Since four hours is one-sixth of a day, roughly one in six items moves to a different day. Each day loses some items to the next day but also gains items from the previous day.

In a recent development, the total number of items remains 1,000, and the daily counts change very little overall. With an average of about 5.5 items per day, the counts already vary by two or three items. So a drop from 9 items to 6 can easily look like typical variation rather than a data problem.

Sources indicate that the pipeline's total-row-count check still passed because no items were lost. Any check that only compares totals would also miss the problem. The total is correct, but some items are now counted under the wrong day.

According to recent reports, I also looked at why the pipeline didn't report a problem. The original timestamp, 2026-01-02T22:30:00+00:00, changed to 2026-01-03T02:30:00 after the drift. The new timestamp has no timezone offset, so datetime.fromisoformat reads it as a naïve datetime. The isoformat() method then writes it back without an offset. SQLite's DATE() treats this offset-free timestamp as UTC, placing the item on January 3 instead of January 2.

The pipeline processed the timestamp without errors but assigned the item to the wrong day. If the producer had written 2026-01-03T02:30:00+04:00 instead, the timestamp would have represented the same instant as the original. SQLite would have converted it to UTC, and the item would still have been counted on January 2.

The problem was the missing timezone offset. Without it, the pipeline had no way to know which timezone the timestamp represented, so it treated the time as UTC.

The empty-string drift caused a different problem. Replacing null with "" kept the field as a string, so checks that only verify the data type still passed.

The schema diff caught the change because the type set for equipped_slot changed from {'NoneType', 'str'} to {'str'}. The pipeline raised no errors, but the query WHERE equipped_slot IS NULL returned no rows. The dashboard would show 0 unequipped items instead of 205, making it look as though every player had equipped their gear.

According to recent reports, the statistical profile showed what had happened: equipped_slot: null rate 20% -> 0%; equipped_slot='': share 0% -> 20%. The null values had been replaced with empty strings, not real values.

According to recent reports, the new mythic rarity went through the pipeline without an error for a similar reason. The drift changed 20 records to mythic: 10 from common (619 to 609), 9 from uncommon (236 to 227), and 1 from rare (98 to 97). The query GROUP BY rarity accepted the new value without any error. It simply created a new row for mythic and reduced the counts for the other rarities. A dashboard that only knows the five original rarities might hide mythic or group it under "other", depending on how it handles unknown values.

Recent findings suggest that the durability change highlights most clearly how data can keep the same structure but mean something different. In the original data, durability ranges from 10 to 100, so an average of 547.85 is clearly wrong. But the field kept the same name and integer type, so the schema diff didn't detect the change.

Sources indicate that the pipeline also accepted the values because nothing checked them against the expected range. Only a check that knows durability should be between 10 and 100 can catch this problem. To test this, I added a range constraint to the strict Pydantic model:.

It has been revealed that this caught 985 of the 1,000 drifted records. The remaining 15 had an original durability value of 10, which became 100 after scaling by 10. Since 100 still falls within the allowed range, those records passed validation.

The four drifts corrupted 1,000, 205, 20, and 1,000 rows, but each one changed only one of the six metrics the pipeline calculates. The other five metrics stayed the same. Anyone monitoring the pipeline could miss the damage unless they checked the affected metric and knew its expected value.

The main finding is that data can change across many rows without changing most of the results people monitor. People only notice the problem if they check the metric that the drift affects.

To catch changes beyond the data structure, we need checks that examine the values themselves.

Recent findings suggest that the strict model checks whether values follow specific rules. It caught the timezone drift because AwareDatetime rejects timestamps without a timezone offset (acquired_at: Input should have timezone info). It also caught the empty-string slot because its Literal rule only accepts five known slot names and rejects "".

It has been revealed that the loose model has fewer restrictions. It accepts any string for acquired_at, any string or None for equipped_slot, and unknown fields. As a result, it missed the timezone shift, the empty-string slot, and the new column.

The strict model also missed the durability change because I hadn't defined an allowed range for that field. In a separate run, I added Field(ge=10, le=100) to a copy of the model. This caught 985 of the 1,000 changed rows. It missed the remaining 15 because their original durability was 10, which became exactly 100 after scaling and still passed the check.

The statistical profile compares data distributions with the baseline. It was the only detector to catch the durability scaling because it doesn't need a predefined range. It simply detected that the average durability rose from 54.8 to 547.9.

But it may also flag normal changes in the data. To test this, I scaled durability by factors from 1.02 to 1.3 and tried four mean-change thresholds. I also tested the detector on 200 clean files generated with different seeds to see how often it raised false alarms. I excluded the baseline seed because it would produce identical data.

In a recent development, the 2% threshold shows how easily the detector can flag normal variation. Durability is roughly uniform from 10 to 100, so a 1,000-row sample has a standard deviation of about 26. That means the sample mean typically lands within about 0.8 of the true mean, which is roughly 1.5% of its value. A 2% threshold is only a little bigger than that, so it should fire on roughly 18% of clean files. It fired on 37 of 200 (18.5%). This shows a tradeoff that lowering the threshold helps catch small changes but also increases false alarms.

The results also show why one threshold doesn't work for every numeric field. stats.attack, level, and player_id vary more than durability relative to their averages. At a 2% threshold, at least one of these fields triggered an alarm in 188 of 200 clean files. At 5%, they caused all 23 false alarms, while durability caused none. stats.attack caused 15 of those alarms. Even player_id triggered alarms, although its average has no useful meaning.

Using a single threshold treats every numeric field the same, even though some vary more than others and some shouldn't be checked by their average at all.

In a recent development, the category-share check uses a fixed 5-percentage-point threshold, so changing the mean threshold doesn't affect its results. It raised 26 alarms across 22 of the 200 clean files (11%). Seventeen alarms involved equipped_slot, and 16 of those involved chest or off_hand.

Sources indicate that there are two reasons for these alarms. First, the check calculates each slot's share using only the 795 non-null rows, not all 1,000. This gives each share a standard error of about 1.4 percentage points.

It has been revealed that second, my baseline doesn't match the intended shares exactly. chest makes up 17.2% of the baseline instead of the intended 20%. As a result, a clean file only needs to reach 22.2% to trigger an alarm. This happens in roughly 6% of files. off_hand has the opposite problem: its baseline share is higher than intended, at 22.3%. This shows that a baseline can contain its own sampling errors, which then affect every comparison.

In a recent development, one more limitation comes from the detector design, not from a measured result. I didn't test this case, but the code shows why it would go undetected. The strict model caught the timezone drift because the timestamp lost its offset. But a producer could shift the clock and keep the Z suffix. Every detector would then accept the data. The strict model checks only whether a timestamp has an offset, not whether the time is correct. The statistical profile skips timestamp strings because they have too many distinct values to treat as categories and aren't numeric.

According to recent reports, this is a limitation of the fourth layer: the timestamp still looks valid, but it represents the wrong time. None of the detectors checks whether the timestamp matches the actual time it is supposed to represent.

The results suggest that combining all four detectors provides better coverage because each one catches changes the others miss.

Industry observers note that the schema diff is simple and cheap to run on every load. It caught six of the nine drifts, including the level change that both Pydantic models missed because they converted the value before checking it. It also identified the field that caused an error when the pipeline's own error message did not. But it caught only one of the four drifts that corrupted data.

The strict model and statistical profile caught all four harmful drifts between them. I'd use the strict model for fields with known rules, such as timezone-aware timestamps, allowed values, and numeric ranges. I'd use statistical checks for important metrics that have no clear validation rules, setting a separate threshold for each field based on past data.

According to recent reports, the lab demonstrated why one threshold doesn't work for every field. A global 5% mean threshold raised 23 false alarms across 200 clean files, all from fields other than durability. I'd only apply statistical checks to fields where the average is meaningful and set thresholds based on how much each field normally varies.

According to recent reports, the fourth layer requires the producer and consumers to agree on what the data means. If the producer changes a field's unit, time zone, or allowed values without telling anyone, consumers can't interpret it correctly. Both sides should agree on clear rules, such as the unit of measurement, the time zone, and the allowed values.

It has been revealed that this is a recommendation based on what my detectors couldn't catch. I haven't tested this approach in the lab yet.

The data is synthetic and independent, so it's much simpler than real data, which often has seasonal patterns and natural growth. Real-world false-alarm rates may therefore be higher than the ones I measured. I also used one fixed baseline, so any sampling error in that sample affects every comparison. A production system would likely use a rolling baseline instead.

I used the same thresholds across fields. Setting a separate threshold based on how much each field normally varies might work better, but I didn't test this. I also tested only four detectors from a much larger set of available tools. These results show where the detectors have blind spots, not which tools are best.

Finally, I chose to group changes into "shape" and "meaning," but some changes, such as replacing null with an empty string, could fit into either group.

My first threshold test also contained a bug. I used the wrong variable name (SEED instead of seed) in the data generator, which caused all 20 clean files to match the baseline exactly. This produced zero false alarms. A result that good at a 2% threshold seemed unlikely, so I checked the code and found the mistake. I corrected the bug and excluded seed 42, the baseline's own seed, because it would generate identical data and could never trigger an alarm. All results in this article use the corrected run.

The experiment demonstrated that schema changes are not the only source of pipeline failures. The schema diff caught all five structural changes but missed semantic changes that left field names and types untouched. For example, timestamps shifted to the wrong day, null values became empty strings, and durability values increased tenfold. In each case, the pipeline ran successfully but produced incorrect results.

Recent findings suggest that the four detectors caught different types of changes, and using them together improved detection coverage. However, detecting changes is only part of the problem. Pipeline checks also need to validate whether values fall within expected ranges and whether they still represent what downstream calculations assume.

Sources indicate that A pipeline completing successfully doesn't necessarily mean the data is correct. It’s just as key to check that the data retains its intended meaning and that downstream calculations still produce reliable results.

#59. Latest Update: These overlooked storage hogs could be taking up gigabytes on your phone

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (931 w)
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Androidpolice

Latest Update: These overlooked storage hogs could be taking up gigabytes on your phone

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (931 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Androidpolice

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Your phone's storage can fill up surprisingly quickly, even if you don't take many photos, download large games, or save videos.
  • In a recent development, the tricky part is that deleting a few photos or uninstalling unused apps might barely make a dent.
  • However, you don't have to delete crucial photos or sacrifice your favorite apps to reclaim that space.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Your phone's storage can fill up surprisingly quickly, even if you don't take many photos, download large games, or save videos. While it's easy to blame apps and media files, some of the biggest storage hogs are things you might not think about checking.

In a recent development, the tricky part is that deleting a few photos or uninstalling unused apps might barely make a dent. Messaging apps, browser caches, offline maps, streaming downloads, and even files sitting in trash folders can take up more space than you expect.

However, you don't have to delete crucial photos or sacrifice your favorite apps to reclaim that space. You need to know where to look and what you can safely remove.

Android AICore is a Google system service that manages Gemini Nano, the tech giant's on-device AI model, on Android phones running Android 14 or later.

AICore supports several features you might already use without realizing they're powered by on-device AI. These include smart replies in messaging apps through Gboard, advanced proofreading, speech transcription, scam detection, text translation, and audio summarization.

Recent findings suggest that the AI model runs locally, so these features work offline and process information on your device instead of sending it to Google's servers. The downside is that running AI models locally requires storage.

If AICore is taking up an unusually large amount of space, check its storage usage under Settings > Apps > AICore.

Messaging apps are among the biggest contributors to storage clutter on Android phones. Think about how many photos, videos, GIFs, voice notes, and documents you receive every day through Telegram, Messages, or WhatsApp.

You might not save most of them, but these apps can download media automatically. That means files from group chats and individual conversations pile up in your phone's storage.

Messages add to storage clutter through downloaded MMS attachments and RCS conversations containing photos and videos.

You can check the app's auto-download settings for MMS attachments by tapping your profile picture, selecting Messages settings > Advanced, and looking for Auto-download MMS.

Streaming apps make it easy to download movies, TV reveals, music, and podcasts so you can enjoy them offline. A few downloaded movies or entire TV show seasons take up several gigabytes, and they eat space until you remove them.

You can delete individual titles after watching them on Netflix or Amazon Prime Video from the app's Downloads section.

Don't overlook music and podcast apps. Spotify stores downloaded albums, playlists, and podcasts locally, while YouTube Music can automatically download songs based on your listening history through its Smart Downloads feature.

On YouTube Music, tap your profile picture and select Settings > Downloads and storage to review these settings and use Clear downloads to reclaim space.

Spotify has similar controls under Settings and privacy > Data saving and offline.

Sources indicate that finally, check the YouTube app if you download videos for offline viewing. Go to Settings > Downloads > Delete all downloads to remove all of them. You can delete a single video by going to Downloads, tapping the menu icon next to a video, and selecting Delete from downloads.

In a recent development, apps such as Instagram, Facebook, Chrome, and Reddit constantly download images, videos, thumbnails, and other temporary files to make content load faster the next time you open them. These files are stored in a cache, and they can accumulate as you use an app.

If you regularly scroll through these apps, the cached data can take up hundreds of megabytes or even several gigabytes.

Recent findings suggest that you don't have to uninstall these apps to reclaim that space. You can clear an individual app's cache without deleting your account information, settings, or personal files.

Open Settings > Apps > See all apps, select an app, tap Storage and cache (or Storage on some phones), and select Clear cache. Repeat this for other apps that have accumulated substantial temporary data.

In a recent development, you can also check Chrome, which stores cached images and files from websites you visit. Open Chrome, tap the three-dot menu, select Delete browsing data, choose a time range, and select Cached images and files before deleting them.

According to recent reports, deleting photos, videos, and documents doesn't always remove them from your phone immediately. Many Android gallery and file management apps have a Trash or Recycle Bin folder that temporarily holds deleted files, giving you a chance to recover something you removed by mistake.

However, these files can occupy storage until you permanently delete them or the retention period expires.

According to recent reports, if you use Google Photos, open the app, tap Collections > Trash, and review the deleted photos and videos. Google keeps deleted items in Trash for 30 days before permanently removing them. If you don't need them, empty the Trash to reclaim space rather than waiting for automatic deletion.

It's worth checking your phone's file manager for a similar option. Depending on the manufacturer and app, you might find separate trash folders for photos, documents, recordings, and other files.

Industry observers note that when your phone starts running out of storage, uninstalling apps or deleting photos might seem like the obvious solution. But some of the biggest culprits hide in places you probably don't think to check.

Messaging attachments, forgotten streaming downloads, app caches, and files sitting in the trash can consume gigabytes without you realizing it.

You don't need to install a third-party cleaner or perform a major cleanup every week. A little attention to these overlooked settings can help you reclaim space.

#55. Industry News: How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check

📅 03 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1269 w)
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Technologyreview

Industry News: How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1269 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A newly introduced approach known as “reverse game theory” aims to control powerful AI models by designing systems that incentivize them to stick to the rules.
  • As AI models become more capable, safety researchers are scrambling to ensure they are “aligned” with human desires—to make sure, in other words, that rogue agents don’t break the law, hack into unauthorized servers, or release poison gas into major cities and kill us all.
  • Until now, this work has mostly focused on trying to peer into an AI’s “brain” to understand what it is “thinking,” or training models to hew to values that we hold dear.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A newly introduced approach known as “reverse game theory” aims to control powerful AI models by designing systems that incentivize them to stick to the rules.

As AI models become more capable, safety researchers are scrambling to ensure they are “aligned” with human desires—to make sure, in other words, that rogue agents don’t break the law, hack into unauthorized servers, or release poison gas into major cities and kill us all.

Until now, this work has mostly focused on trying to peer into an AI’s “brain” to understand what it is “thinking,” or training models to hew to values that we hold dear. Claude, for instance, has its constitution—a sort of moral code.

The trouble is, these techniques don’t seem to work particularly well: Models have been shown to deliberately underperform on tests, hide their intentions, and mislead their evaluators.

Now some alignment researchers believe that reverse game theory, also known as mechanism design, might get better results. Where game theory tries to predict how rational actors will behave when given a particular set of rules, reverse game theory attempts to design rules that will elicit the kinds of behavior we want to encourage.

An example of mechanism design in the real world might be the classic strategy for splitting a piece of cake in two: One person cuts the cake and the other gets the first choice of pieces. This incentivizes the cutter to make the pieces as even as possible. Other examples include surge pricing in ride-hailing apps, which encourages drivers to be available at busy times, and second-price auctions, where the winning bidder pays the price of the second-highest bid instead of the highest. Platforms use these auctions to sell online advertising because they encourage buyers to bid close to the maximum they are willing to pay.

In AI, mechanism design starts from the premise that we may never be able to understand enough about the internal workings of frontier models to make sure they are aligned. This means we should design mechanisms that incentivize agents to behave in ways that we want, regardless of what’s actually going on under the hood.

A recent preprint paper by Stephen Morris, an economist at MIT, along with colleagues from Yale and Columbia suggested some potential mechanisms that could stop agents from “sandbagging” tests (pretending to be worse than they actually are—for example, to avoid triggering safety mechanisms).

Instead of being rewarded only for how well it does on a test, a model could be rewarded for how well its answers predict what a second model will say. Deliberately playing dumb becomes a losing bet. “AI agents have a very good understanding of what other AI agents can achieve,” Morris claims. “So it does seem like a context where this cross-checking could work more practically.

The paper also suggests pitting agents against each other, creating a competitive dynamic that incentivizes them to perform their best, or pairing agents that are known to be biased in opposite directions and rewarding them depending on how closely their outputs match, thus incentivizing them to reach an optimal answer.

According to recent reports, A second approach, as envisioned by Elad Hazan, a professor of computer science at Princeton, is to design mechanisms that take inspiration from the ways human society keeps people “aligned”: social norms, the justice system, the monetary incentives of free-market capitalism. “We want to align superintelligent AI,” he says. “Why don’t we first talk about humans? How do we align humans?”.

Recent findings suggest that hazan’s suggested mechanism involves having AI models take turns as either “solvers” that tackle problems or “auditors” that check the others’ work. “One agent acts like law enforcement; the other agent acts like the citizen,” he says.

Industry observers note that during training, the models are rewarded depending on outcomes: Solvers that get caught cheating are punished, but so are auditors that fail to catch the cheaters. In situations where there’s a disagreement between auditors and solvers, the case can be sent to “trial”—perhaps a human expert will decide who is right.

There is, Hazan admits, a risk that agents will collude with each other—as auditors have colluded with the businesses they’re meant to be auditing, or corrupt police officers have colluded with criminals. But that problem can be solved by rewarding the auditors well enough, so that being caught isn’t worth the risk (a lot easier in the world of AI training than the real one, where money for police salaries is tight), and by auditing the auditors using techniques akin to employing mystery shoppers.

Hazan points to Nobel Prize–winning work by the economist Gary Becker, who introduced the idea of the “rational offender” in the 1960s. Criminals don’t break the law because they’re inherently bad people, he noted. Instead, they do it when it’s the most rational choice given the incentives on offer. Crime makes sense only when the proceeds outweigh the potential punishment.

Alignment shouldn’t be thought of as a property of a model, he argues, but as a descriptor of its behavior at a particular moment. “You are, like, a nice person,” he states. “Are you aligned? I don’t know. Probably you are aligned most of the time, but there could be a situation where you’re not.”.

According to recent reports, one potential issue with applying mechanism design to AI: It relies on the assumption that AI agents behave rationally. Mechanism design has a mixed record with humans, who often fail to behave the way economic models say they should.

It’s ironic: Economists have spent decades trying to reduce human behavior to mathematics, and now, in large language models, we’ve built mathematical systems that run on human language and could be just as inscrutable. AI models exhibit behaviors that seem more human than machine, and they can be swayed by subtle factors that are difficult to understand and explain. “Is it even reasonable to assume that they will respond to incentives?” asks Helen Qu, a research fellow at the Flatiron Institute, a nonprofit dedicated to advancing scientific discovery through computational methods, who has written about mechanism design and AI safety.

“Obviously, AIs are not rational,” Morris notes. “They’re just algorithms at work.” However, as economists have found with humans, treating them as if they’re rational could still be useful if it helps to predict and control their behavior.

Qu sees mechanism design as just one layer in a “defense in depth” strategy for keeping AI models aligned—alongside interpretability, regulation, and training, not instead of them. But there are a lot of questions to be answered before the approach can be implemented in actual frontier models. It’s unclear, for instance, how these theories will apply to real models, or whether mechanisms designed for one task will carry over to another in practice. Models could find loopholes that no one anticipated. (Anthropic and OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment on whether they are working on this.).

Whatever these mechanisms look like, they will ultimately have to slot into the biggest mechanism of all: the free market. “We play by the rules of economics,” states Hazan. A more aligned model may be good for the world, but if it’s slower or more expensive than a less aligned one, does our current system of rules and regulations actually incentivize any of the frontier labs to release it?

“It’s a mechanism that’s responsible for a lot of prosperity for humankind,” he states of the market, “but it could be ultimately responsible for something very terrible.” Perhaps the entities really in need of a better mechanism design are the labs themselves.

If a hacker can't get the physical device, they likely won't be able to authenticate their dubious login. However, one problem is that these keys can sometimes be a hassle to remember to carry with you. Chances are you won't worry about that with the Yubico YubiKey 5C Nano, since it plugs right into the USB-C port on your computer and goes wherever your PC is.

According to recent reports, yubico's hardware key is widely supported, so it is capable of authenticating your logins on hundreds of popular online platforms. Windows, macOS, Linux, and even ChromeOS are supported operating systems. It also supports the FIDO2 authentication protocol, which is one of the safest available multi-factor authentication options. While hardware keys remain super safe, it's worth keeping in mind that multi-factor authentication can still be bypassed if a hacker is determined enough.

It has been revealed that just like the key to your car, losing your YubiKey (which might be easy considering how small it is) can lock you out of your accounts. To prevent that, Yubico recommends buying a spare. A single one costs $68, so if you take the firm's advice, you're effectively paying that twice over.

Whether you're dealing with brutal summer months or a crowded event with little ventilation, you'll want to keep the temperatures down. A portable fan like Triifon's will help you drive the heat away. It runs off the power of your phone's USB-C port, so don't expect performance akin to a regular-sized fan plugged into the wall. Keep in mind that it pulls its power from your phone's battery, so using it for a long time will likely have an impact on your battery life. If you would rather avoid that, you could plug it right into a power bank.

For $10, you'll get four of these fans, enough to hoard or give out to a few friends. The actual fan blades are made of soft rubber, which is essential for safety as the fan has no grill to stop you from touching the blades. If you have an iPhone with a USB-C port, all you have to do is plug it in and it starts working. The same applies for most Android devices with a USB-C port, but only if it supports the USB OTG feature.

Virtually every smartphone that rolls off the manufacturing line has an LED flash on the back that can be turned on to act as a flashlight. The problem with that option is that it chews through your battery, gets hot, and sometimes it simply isn't bright enough for your needs. That's where the ThruNite Ti mini flashlight comes in.

In a recent development, thruNite's mini flashlight is small enough to go on a keychain, made of aluminum, and IPX6 water-resistant. If you're not aware of what IP numbers mean, a six as the second digit indicates that the flashlight can resist high-pressure jets of water, but not submersion (as you'd get with a IPX7 or IPX8 rating). To help achieve that, the USB-C port comes with an anchored rubber plug that seals the port when the item isn't charging.

Sources indicate that with ThruNite's flashlight, you get adjustable brightness and up to 650 lumens of illumination. Despite the flashlight's size, that's about 10 times brighter than the some of the brightest phone flashes can get. Even when you max out the intensity, you'll get 1 hour and 35 minutes of use and almost 10 hours on the low setting. At $17, you won't need to debate too hard on getting this flashlight or not.

Industry observers note that the AltaMoment detachable kickstand and charger is one of the more unique USB-C devices that exists. Most people who seek out a kickstand for their smartphone get a case that comes with one built-in and rely on that. However, you don't have to have a case to get kickstand functionality. AltaMoment's product finds a way to give your phone a kickstand just by plugging into the USB-C port.

In a recent development, the first thing to know is that you don't relinquish the use of your USB-C port when this is plugged in since it has a port on the side, so you can still connect your phone as needed. It comes with a cable too, with support for up to 240W charging and high-speed data transfer. You're not losing much by plugging this in; you're only gaining a little extra bulk on your phone.

Of course, the kickstand feature is the star, as without it, this device would only exist to give you a right-angled charging port. This gadget has two legs which can be flipped out to help stand the attached smartphone in landscape or portrait orientation. If this sounds like something you need, it goes for $10 on Amazon.

Sources indicate that over the years, smartphone charging has gotten faster (though we may have reached a plateau at the moment). Among the Android players, it is rather common to see devices that can charge at speeds close to or even exceeding 100W. With that kind of charging power, it can be frustrating when you sense that your phone isn't charging as fast as it should be. Thankfully, with DuHeSin's USB-C power meter dongle, you know exactly how much juice your charger is pushing out at any time, and for only $10 for a two-pack.

In a recent development, this dongle has a USB-C plug on one side and a USB-C socket on the other. The tiny display lets you see how many watts, volts, or amperes are passing through the gadget at any time. Once you connect your smartphone or laptop with this dongle, you'll instantly see how much power the device is receiving from the charging brick. You can watch in real-time whether your fast-charging smartphone is drawing as much electricity as it should be.

Using this won't be a detriment to your charging speeds or data transfer. It supports up to 240W of power and it can also handle transfer speeds of up to 40 Gbps. If you use your USB-C connection to project images on a larger display, it is compatible with 8K/60 video output. It is a full-function dongle, so you lose nothing by keeping it on the end of your charging cable.

The Asakuki essential oil diffuser relies on a USB-C connection to keep it powered on. Getting it into action is rather straightforward too. You take off the top, fill it with water to an indicated level, add drops of your preferred essential oils, put the top back on, and turn it on. With those steps, you'll be able to fill your house with your favorite fragrances. The water you add means that it also acts as a humidifier, so the mist it sprays doesn't just make your house smell good, but it keeps the air moist to fight dry weather.

In a recent development, asakuki's diffuser doesn't have a battery, so the water level dictates how long this USB-C gadget runs. It should get anywhere between 8 and 14 hours of operation before the water runs out, depending on the level you choose for the mist. You can set different intensity and emission patterns using the included remote. The diffuser can also provide mood lighting with the choice of seven different colors, including one option that cycles through all of them. If you're looking for something to add a comforting scent to your space, there's a $20 price tag on this product.

There are a lot of strange USB-C gadgets out in the world and this product from Connfiton is certainly one of the more unique options you'll find available. It combines a keychain, carabiner, bottle opener, and USB-C cable all into one package that is rather impressive from a product design perspective.

In a recent development, half of the body is made of plastic but the other half is made of metal, which provides some structural rigidity. It has two holes in its construction. One of them is made to have the included aluminum carabiner looped through it, making it easy to attach it to a bag or use it as a keychain. The other hole is the bottle opener.

According to recent reports, built into its construction is a USB-C cable, arguably the star of the show, that folds neatly into its shape when out of use. To fit into a keychain, it's not surprising that the cable is short, but think of it as for emergencies only. It's really only a cable, so you still have to find a power source, but many people might find it suitable for days where the only thing you're missing to charge or transfer data is the cable. There's a lot of utility here, and all for $7.

In a recent development, if you know people who have dealt with trouble sleeping, many might mention that playing white noise can help them fall asleep quicker. Theoretically, you could just play white noise from your phone, but many people prefer to have a device tailor-made for that purpose. While a lot of them plug into a wall socket, the Dreamegg portable white noise machine is tiny and powered through a USB-C port.

While it is called a white noise machine, Dreamegg's product can emit white, pink, and brown noise, in addition to various ambient and nature sounds. Despite its diminutive build, it packs a 1,000mAh battery, which the manufacturer claims will get you over a day of use out of the product. To make the battery last even longer, you can set a timer for the machine to stop after 30, 60, or 90 minutes so it only stops working once you're sure you'll be asleep.

In a recent development, the machine is small enough to slip into a pocket, as it is smaller than 2 inches in all dimensions and weighs only 1.6 ounces. If you're the kind of person who needs white noise to sleep no matter where you are, it's hard to find a reason not to take this along with you. It is available in multiple colors, each of which is priced differently on Amazon, but it starts at $13 for the cream option.

It has been revealed that the Cooper Ray laser measuring tool is a USB-C gadget intended for anyone who finds themselves needing very precise measurements of distance on a regular basis. If you're a contractor who needs it for work or just a regular person who loves DIY in their spare time, a laser measuring tool can be invaluable. It works by shooting a laser, times how long it takes to come back, and uses that to calculate the distance.

Cooper's laser tool is small enough to be hooked up to a keychain or bag without significant weight. Its body is made of an aluminum alloy for sturdiness, and printed on the side is a ruler, in case you need to make measurements that a laser might not be appropriate for, like making cuts at certain widths.

The tool comes with a screen that lets you immediately read distance after you point and press the button. One cool thing it can do is automatically calculate the area and volume of a space if you point it in more than one dimension, which can be useful for material estimates. As you might expect, it charges via USB-C and will last 5,000 measurements on a single charge. Cooper is asking for $20 when ordered through Amazon.

The average day with a smartphone will have you typing something, whether you're writing out whole documents or just typing a web address into your browser. As long as you're writing out something, you need a keyboard, and for speed and accuracy, few things beat a physical keyboard with tactile keys like this $33 Bluetooth keyboard from Samsers.

What sets this USB-C gadget apart from most other Bluetooth keyboards that you can connect to a phone is that this one folds. Foldable keyboards have pros and cons, but perhaps the most notable (and obvious) advantage is that you can fold it closed when not in use, making it more portable. When unfolded, a small trackpad sits to the right of the keys.

It has been revealed that you can use this keyboard on most devices that support Bluetooth, whether it's a phone, tablet, or computer. You'll get a claimed 48 hours of battery life during continuous use and up to 560 hours of standby time from a full charge. As expected, it charges with USB-C, so you won't need another cable when taking this along with you.

AirTrunk stated in an official LinkedIn announcement on November 13, 2026, that it had signed a memorandum of understanding with Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister Nara Chandrababu Naidu for two proposed data center campuses in India’s Anakapalli district: 400 MW at Rambilli and 1,400 MW at Tootipala.

According to recent reports, the agreement supplies named sites and capacities for the firm’s next phase of Indian expansion. Their combined capacity is 1,800 MW, calculated from the two figures in the announcement. Both campuses remain proposals, and AirTrunk plans to work with government and community partners as they progress.

Recent findings suggest that airTrunk projects that the developments could create more than 3,100 direct operational jobs and 4,700 indirect jobs. It intends to support local access to those opportunities through local hiring, skills development and partnerships with Industrial Training Institutes and polytechnics in Anakapalli.

Carly Wishart, AirTrunk’s Managing Director, Corporate and International, thanked the Andhra Pradesh government for its partnership. “Our focus is on responsible planning and helping people build the skills to take part in the opportunities ahead,” she noted.

Sources indicate that the workforce aims connect the campuses’ potential economic impact with a practical requirement for large data center operations: developing a local pool of trained workers. The employment figures remain projections attached to the proposed projects rather than existing positions.

According to recent reports, the MoU follows AirTrunk’s acquisition of Lumina CloudInfra, revealed on April 20, 2026, which brought the tech giant into the Indian market. The deal provided an approximately 600 MW portfolio of planned capacity across Mumbai, Chennai and Hyderabad, along with existing contracts, relationships and operating capabilities. Blackstone and Canada Pension Proposal Investment Board were to continue providing long-term capital support to the platform.

It has been revealed that airTrunk’s current India portfolio describes its data centers as cloud and AI-ready and lists developments in Mumbai, Chennai and Hyderabad. The Anakapalli proposal would add two locations beyond those markets, extending a pipeline designed to serve the growth of large technology customers.

Recent findings suggest that separately, AirTrunk’s June 5, 2026 investment proposal outlined more than US$30 billion of Indian investment by 2030 and 5 GW of latest data center capacity across multiple states and union territories. The tech giant linked that program to growing demand for cloud and artificial intelligence infrastructure.

In a recent development, the June proposal followed founder and CEO Robin Khuda’s meetings with federal representatives and ministers in Maharashtra and Andhra Pradesh. Their discussions covered reliable and cost-effective power, renewable energy, sustainable water supply, talent development, streamlined approvals and greater coordination between state and federal governments.

Those topics show that AirTrunk’s expansion agenda extends beyond financing and construction. Its own account places energy and water supply, workforce preparation and administrative coordination among the practical requirements for AI-driven infrastructure growth.

For Andhra Pradesh, the MoU turns those broader ambitions into two campus proposals with stated capacities and employment projections. Moving them beyond the proposal stage now depends on the practical work AirTrunk has already identified: establishing suitable power and water arrangements, completing approvals and building the local workforce needed to operate AI-ready infrastructure.

#50. Tech Report: Securing the agentic enterprise with data lineage

📅 04 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (249 w)
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Technologyreview

Tech Report: Securing the agentic enterprise with data lineage

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (249 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A sales representative asks an AI agent for customer pricing, and the agent pulls data from multiple sources: restricted pricing systems, internal communications, and archived quotes.
  • According to recent reports, this scenario illustrates why AI governance needs to evolve, rapidly and dynamically.
  • Consequently, traditional security approaches built solely around applications, systems, networks, or endpoints are no longer sufficient.

A sales representative asks an AI agent for customer pricing, and the agent pulls data from multiple sources: restricted pricing systems, internal communications, and archived quotes. The output looks accurate to the agent, so a second agent uses the data to draft the proposal for the sales rep. No human checks either handoff. When it’s discovered that the proposal includes unapproved, confidential, and sensitive information, no one can trace where the problematic data entered the workflow or how it spread across systems, files, and agents.

According to recent reports, this scenario illustrates why AI governance needs to evolve, rapidly and dynamically. As more enterprises begin to use agentic AI in daily workflows, they’re realizing that they must manage more than static files; they must manage moving and fragmented data that is continuously ingested, copied, summarized, transformed, reused, and redistributed in upcoming forms. In short, AI security isn’t a tool problem; it’s a data visibility problem.

Consequently, traditional security approaches built solely around applications, systems, networks, or endpoints are no longer sufficient. Securing agentic AI at scale requires understanding how data moves. Teams, therefore, need to establish data lineage in order to effectively manage governance, accountability, and trust across human, agentic, and hybrid workflows.

#49. Breaking: How to Speed Up CI in the Age of AI-Written Code

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1636 w)
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Freecodecamp

Breaking: How to Speed Up CI in the Age of AI-Written Code

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1636 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Freecodecamp

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that coding agents now write code faster than most CI pipelines can check it.
  • That second figure demonstrates where all those commits end up: in CI.
  • Most of that delay comes from a few causes, and each has a known fix.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that coding agents now write code faster than most CI pipelines can check it. In April 2026, GitHub COO Kyle Daigle remarked that his platform was handling 275 million commits a week, on pace for 14 billion in the year, up from about 1 billion in 2025. In the same post, he put GitHub Actions at 2.1 billion minutes in a single week, up from 500 million a week in 2023.

That second figure demonstrates where all those commits end up: in CI. A 15-minute pipeline is tolerable if a dev pushes a few times a day. When an agent opens ten PRs in an afternoon, that pipeline turns into a queue. You wait for results, agents wait to retry, and the time saved writing code is lost checking it.

Most of that delay comes from a few causes, and each has a known fix. You can speed up CI in five ways:.

In this article, we'll walk through each fix in order. You’ll learn how to find the slowest steps in your GitHub Actions workflows, cache dependencies and Docker layers with stable keys, and move heavy jobs to faster runners. You’ll also see how to shard tests across a matrix of parallel jobs, and how to skip unneeded work with path filters, affected-only tests, and concurrency groups.

Most teams try to guess which step is slowing things down, and they're often wrong. A job that feels like a test problem may be 90 seconds of installs and 30 seconds of tests.

Sources indicate that start with data you already have. GitHub shows job execution time for every run, with a timing for each step. Open the last ten runs of your slowest workflow and note the three longest steps. Use the median, not the worst case, since one slow run can be a network blip.

Recent findings suggest that also separate waiting from working. Queue time, setup time, and run time need different fixes. If jobs sit in a queue for a minute, no test tuning will help.

In a recent development, the fastest work is work you never repeat. Every run starts on a fresh machine, so without a cache you download the same packages again and again.

Sources indicate that the dependency caching reference explains how actions/cache works. You give it a path and a key. If the key matches a saved cache, the files are restored. If not, the step runs, and the files are saved when the job ends.

Everything depends on that key. The usual pattern hashes your lockfile, so the key changes only when your dependencies change.

The restore-keys line is the part that tends to get skipped. When the exact key misses, it restores the closest older cache. You still install a few newly introduced packages, but not all of them. Be careful with keys that include a timestamp or a commit SHA. Those never match twice, so you save a new cache on every run and never reuse one.

Docker builds need the same thinking. Docker images are built in layers, and a layer is reused only if everything above it is unchanged. Copy your lockfile and install dependencies first, then copy your source code. That way a code change doesn't rebuild the install layer. To keep layers between runs, point BuildKit at the GitHub Actions cache backend with cache-from and cache-to set to type=gha.

One catch is that these caches live in remote storage. Each restore is a network download, which on a big cache can rival the install it replaces.

Caching avoids repeating work. This improvement is different. It runs the work itself on faster machines.

Recent findings suggest that standard GitHub-hosted runners for private repositories have 2 vCPUs and 7 GB of RAM. Avrea is a drop-in replacement for GitHub Actions runners. You change one line, from runs-on: ubuntu-latest to an Avrea label such as runs-on: avrea-ubuntu-latest, and the rest of your workflow stays the same. By Avrea's own numbers, jobs run about 2x faster on hardware alone, and up to 10x faster with cache hits.

Sources indicate that independent numbers point the same way. RunsOn maintains a public runner benchmark that builds three open-source projects on nine runner services with build caches turned off: a Rust test suite, TypeScript typechecks, and a production Docker build of PostHog. In the 4-vCPU x64 category, as of November 2026, Avrea finished all three in about 7 minutes of build time, compared with about 18.5 minutes on GitHub's 4-core runner, not counting runner start-up.

Industry observers note that built-in caching is the other half, and it connects to the section above. Avrea keeps its caches in the same datacenter as its runners, so a restore doesn't cross a slow network. Most of it is pre-configured.

Sources indicate that the GitHub Actions cache and package downloads for npm, pip, Go modules, and Cargo work with no workflow changes. Build caches for tools such as Go, Bazel, Gradle, Turborepo, Nx, and sccache are set up on the runner, and some need a small workflow addition. So a team gets cache hits without writing key logic for each tool.

Other providers take other routes. Depot offers faster GitHub Actions runners and remote Docker builds, and now runs its own CI engine that accepts GitHub Actions workflows. RunsOn is self-hosted: it starts EC2 instances inside your own AWS account, so you pay AWS for compute plus a flat yearly license, instead of a per-minute fee to RunsOn. GitHub's own larger runners, available on Team and Enterprise Cloud prepares, add more CPU, RAM, and disk, plus options like static IPs and GPUs, billed by the minute. Check each provider's site for current details, since all of them change often.

Sources indicate that once each job is fast, make sure jobs don't wait in a line. A long test suite on one runner is the classic bottleneck.

In a recent development, start with independent jobs. Lint, type checks, unit tests, and build rarely need each other. GitHub runs jobs in parallel unless you add needs, so remove any needs line that's only there for habit.

In a recent development, next, use a matrix. A matrix strategy creates one job per combination of values, and they all run at once. Teams often use it for Node versions, but it's also the simplest way to shard tests.

Sources indicate that jest's --shard flag splits the suite across jobs by test file. Four shards can turn a twelve-minute suite into about three, plus setup time, if the files take similar time. If a few files are much heavier, one shard will run long, so split those files up. Setting fail-fast: false lets every shard finish, so you see all failures at once.

According to recent reports, playwright works the same way. Run npx playwright test --shard=1/4 in each matrix job, then merge the reports at the end.

Sharding has a limit. Each shard pays its own setup cost, so past a point more shards add cost without saving time. Inside a single job, tools like pytest-xdist spread tests across the CPUs on the machine.

The last one is the cheapest: don't run what you don't need to run.

Path filters are the easiest start. In the workflow syntax, the paths and paths-ignore keys let a workflow run only when certain files change. A change to the docs folder shouldn't trigger a full backend build.

According to recent reports, one warning: if a required status check never runs because of a path filter, the pull request stays stuck on a pending check. For required checks, let the workflow run and skip the job with an if: condition instead, since GitHub counts a skipped job as passed.

In a monorepo, go further and run only affected tests. Tools such as Nx, Turborepo, and Bazel work out which packages a change touches and skip the rest. In Nx that's nx affected -t test, and in Turborepo it's turbo run test --affected. Both compare your branch against main, so check out enough Git history for that comparison, since actions/checkout fetches a single commit by default.

Most commits touch a small part of a large codebase, so the savings add up. This matters more when agents open many small pull requests, each touching a package or two.

Finally, stop paying for runs that no one needs. When you push twice in a row, the first run is already out of date. A concurrency group cancels it.

In a recent development, this matters more as AI tools push more commits. Agents may update a branch many times an hour, and each push starts a full run. Don't use it on deploy workflows, though. Cancelling a deploy halfway can leave a bad state, so queue those instead.

Measure first, because that indicates which of the other four fixes is worth your time. Cache with stable keys and order your Dockerfile so slow layers stay put. Move heavy jobs to faster runners, and compare providers on your own workflow. Shard tests until setup time dominates. Then cut needless work with path filters, affected-only tests, and cancelled stale runs.

Make one change at a time and re-check your timings after each. Saving two minutes on a job that runs fifty times a day beats a clever fix on a job that runs once.

#48. 3 Disadvantages Of Infrared Space Heaters

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (795 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Slashgear

3 Disadvantages Of Infrared Space Heaters

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (795 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashgear

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When you stand in direct sunlight, the rays warm up your skin and clothing because the heat is hitting you directly.
  • In a recent development, however, the biggest advantage of infrared space heaters also leads to some common problems.
  • Sources indicate that continuing with the sun analogy, it can only keep you warm if you are standing in the direct path of its rays.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When you stand in direct sunlight, the rays warm up your skin and clothing because the heat is hitting you directly. Infrared space heaters work in pretty much the same way, delivering targeted warmth instantly. The energy these heaters emit travels as infrared waves toward a person or object and isn't affected by the surrounding cold. It doesn't matter if you're sitting outside on a patio or in a drafty room; the heat will reach you. For this reason, infrared space heaters are great gadgets for keeping you warm in a freezing office. They also don't mess with your air quality, since they don't dry it out or kick up dust.

In a recent development, however, the biggest advantage of infrared space heaters also leads to some common problems. The warmth is too targeted, meaning there's limited coverage and it only lasts as long as the heater is facing you. There's also a safety concern about what happens if you accidentally come into contact with an infrared space heater while it's operating. This is not to say that you shouldn't buy one; only that knowing its cons helps you temper your expectations and use it for the intended purpose.

Sources indicate that continuing with the sun analogy, it can only keep you warm if you are standing in the direct path of its rays. Step out of its line of sight, or if there's an object blocking its rays, you can get cold really fast because the air around you is still cold. After all, your skin and clothing can only absorb so much heat. That's the same with infrared space heaters. You need to be standing directly in front of them to feel the warmth. These heaters don't heat the air around you through convection, so they aren't an ideal solution for warming an entire room.

Industry observers note that compare this to a convection heater, which is designed to spread warm air around the room. During operation, cold air enters the heater and is warmed by a heating element or ceramic plate. The warm air rises, creating a cycle of hot air leaving the heater and cold air rushing in to replace it. So even in a small room, if you want to make the air around you warmer so you can, for instance, move around without feeling cold, an infrared space heater is a poor choice.

In a recent development, when you turn off an infrared space heater, you can instantly feel cold because there's no lingering heat. This is also a problem with convection heaters. Insulation wouldn't provide much help either in the case of the infrared space heater. The job of insulation is to slow down the rate of heat loss by keeping warm air inside while keeping the cold air outside and vice versa. Since the heater directs most of its warmth at what's in front of it, the rest of the room can still feel cold.

Industry observers note that for lasting heating in a room, an oil-filled space radiator would be a better choice to overcome this major drawback of an infrared space heater. The radiator builds up warmth by slowly heating the oil inside it using an internal heating element. Once the oil gets hot enough, the heating element shuts off, and the radiator releases some of the stored heat gradually. At the same time, it will be warming up the air and keeping it that way. Not only does the warmth last longer, but it can also lead to energy savings that you can see when calculating the cost of running an electric heater. This is especially true if you have good insulation.

Infrared heaters have a grid or mesh in front of them to prevent you from accidentally touching the heating element. It's usually made from metal, which can get extremely hot during operation to the point that it can burn your skin. For this reason, it's not advisable to have an infrared heater near kids and pets. Keep in mind that space heaters in general can be a fire hazard when trying to stay warm during the winter. So it's extremely key to follow other safety precautions, like not plugging it into a power strip.

Sources indicate that to prevent burns, you can look for infrared heaters with a feature known as a cool-touch grille. These are safer against instant burns since the grille doesn't get hot to the touch. Manufacturers usually advertise this as a safety feature, like in the Sharper Image Infrared Cabinet Heater, which costs $229.99. However, if you accidentally touch a cool-touch grille, don't keep your hand there for too long, because it can still eventually burn you since it's close to the heating element.

I told Gemini to track a smartphone price drop and notify me when the price drops below $200.

While Google is happy to pocket more cash from your automated search queries, it's better to narrow your choices and set time limits for scheduled tasks.

I told Gemini to find reliable product links online, and then I cross-checked the website myself.

I wanted to buy these products during the sale, so I told it to set up an automation to run twice a day from the 19th to the 30th of November.

Recent findings suggest that now Gemini runs a scheduled task to check the websites for price drops during the Black Friday sale period. This way, Gemini doesn't burn through my token usage.

You can either set up scheduled tasks per product or set up a single task to run across multiple websites and product pages at a scheduled time and date.

If you don't want the AI to mess up an crucial opportunity, set up a separate automation for the product with multiple websites listing the product.

It's better to first check with Gemini whether it can access the website links you provided, or provide the product name and ask Gemini to search for sale listings on websites it can access.

If you thought the foldable craze got crazy when only Android OEMs were involved, it got even crazier with the Apple iPhone Duo. A recent analytics report for Q3 2026 spells out how crazy things got and what 2027 could have in store.

A report by Smart Analytics Global (SAG) on global foldable shipment performance in Q3 2026 highlights one Android OEM's staggering lead. The report states that global foldable shipments declined 2% YoY, which translates to "over 7.5 million units shipped." However, Samsung saw a 13% YoY increase this past quarter, thanks to the Galaxy Z Fold 8, accounting for 69% of the foldable market share.

This is notable—the form factor, specifically. The Fold 8 is the organization's first wide-foldable. Many other OEMs, such as Chinese companies, have also adopted this wider, often shorter foldable design. SAG's report states Samsung experienced "double-digit shipment growth in both South Korea and Europe," as well. A notable competitor, Huawei, accounts for 14% of the foldable share in Q3.

The Pura X View was a significant contributor, despite the report noting a small YoY decline in shipments.

SAG then flips the script. While the market has struggled, it forecasts "a newly introduced growth cycle" next year. Shipments might grow 55% YoY in 2027. Wide foldables might account for most phone shipments next year, driven by Samsung's device, the Apple iPhone Duo, and others from Chinese makers.

Some of this data is a little interesting. This was a while ago, but in 2024, Huawei topped Samsung in foldable shipments. The Chinese OEM became the world's leader in foldable shipments. This was a "turning point," one could say, for Samsung. It came at a time when many believed Samsung had become complacent with its Galaxy Z series: the Flip and Fold.

Sources indicate that samsung's shipments fell 42% year-over-year in Q1 2024, while Huawei increased by a massive 257% YoY. Presently, you have Huawei's Pura X View, the industry's first wide foldable, which didn't perform as well for the company as the Fold 8 did for Samsung. SAG's 2027 outlook is certainly intriguing, but it will take consumers buying new phones to make it happen.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

In the broader phone market, global shipments plummeted in Q3, marking the lowest level in 14 years. The market dropped 20% YoY. Still, Samsung claimed the top spot because of the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Fold 8 Ultra.

Recent findings suggest that everything is in flux right now. Some analysts foresee a turnaround, while others firmly believe we're in for more trying times in 2027. The main thing is pricing. If phones are priced well and buyers can afford them, things will change. But we've seen how prices have gone. Moto's Signature 27 is $1,599, and that's not even a foldable—it's a standard slab phone. Other foldables are $2,000; I know we were all paying attention to Apple's iPhone Duo launch. Wide foldables are cool (I almost got one), but plenty of variables are getting in the way of a turnaround.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Leatherman is a popular choice in the realm of quality multi-tools. Since Leatherman products are US-made, they command a premium — one that many users are willing to pay. Historically, the Leatherman Sidekick was an affordable starting point, with an asking price of between $30 and $50 in the 2010s. However, the organization has significantly upped its prices, with models like the Micra going from $34 to $49 in the span of a few months. At the time of writing, that same product has climbed to $61. The Sidekick has been no exception to price increases, either; it now sells for around $70. So, is the Leatherman Sidekick still worth getting, considering it's not exactly a "budget-friendly" tool?

Opinions are mixed. Plenty of buyers remain impressed with the Sidekick's versatility and durability, using it as everyday carry for uses including yard work, house work, and even staple removal. Others aren't necessarily critical of the Sidekick but have claimed that there are more durable or more affordable options out there, although many people who bought the Leatherman Raptor were fine with its $79.99 price tag (despite its limited tool set) for its quality and purpose-made design.

Some have suggested that the Sidekick has lesser appeal at its higher price point, with one Reddit user claiming they "liked it a lot more when it was $30." Some users also prefer the Leatherman Wingman, which, at the time of publication, retails for $50. Luckily, though, the Sidekick is known to go on sale at Costco for the very same price, so it may be worth scouting out those deals or otherwise waiting for sales directly on Leatherman's website.

The aforementioned Leatherman Wingman, often suggested as a superior alternative, is worth the $50 at face value. But what's the difference between a Leatherman Sidekick and a Wingman, apart from price? While they have the same number of tools (14, to be exact), the Wingman sports a nifty package opener and spring-action scissors, which are enough to make it the superior tool for several owners who have tried both products.

Sources indicate that another alternative cheaper than the Sidekick is the Leatherman Rev, which retails for around $60, as of this writing. It also has 14 tools and is quite close to the Sidekick in terms of functionality. That remarked, some owners find the pliers on the Sidekick to be better, or that the Sidekick is more aesthetically appealing than the Rev is.

According to recent reports, if you don't put much emphasis on brand names, it's also worth exploring other multi-tools that give Leatherman a run for its money. A good example is the 10-tool Gerber Dime, which retails for $34 and affords you the same functionality that the Leatherman Sidekick does. Or, if you want to get as many tools as possible in a single package, something like the SOG PowerAccess Deluxe may be to your liking. It has 21 tools — seven more than the Leatherman Sidekick has — and sports an $89 price tag.
