Industry observers note that texas is the fastest-growing data center market in the US and ground zero for Massive Tech's largest AI buildouts. But the blue wave that swept the Lone Star State may jeopardize that position.

Sources indicate that democrat James Talarico won the US Senate seat against Ken Paxton. Gina Hinojosa won the race for governor against the Republican incumbent, Greg Abbott. At the state level, Democrats will take control of the Texas House for the first time in 24 years. Talarico and Hinojosa made data centers a central glitch, discussing them constantly on the campaign trail.

Even before the polls closed, insiders in the data center industry noticed that the times were changing. At the industry's DCD conference in Ashburn, Virginia, on Tuesday, panelists lamented that Texas had been the easiest place to build for years—until September. That's when Abbott, perhaps seeing the increasingly bipartisan distaste for these facilities, began changing course himself.

In a recent development, developers said the governor’s office had stopped responding to their emails. On September 21, Abbott directed a key state regulator to halt data center permits. Many panelists at the conference were expecting this to mean that existing projects might be slowed and fresh ones could be halted altogether.

It has been revealed that the governor-elect indeed seems eager to do that. Hinojosa supported tax breaks for data centers in 2023 as a way to boost construction jobs, but during her campaign she began pushing for a full-fledged moratorium.

That would be a problem for the hyperscalers of Major Tech, which have ambitious intends for AI training facilities in the state. The scale of projects already underway in Texas is massive. The Stargate Frontier data center in Shackelford County is projected to serve 1,820 megawatts—about as much as the nation’s largest data center, SpaceX’s Colossus 2 in Tennessee, and more than twice as much as the largest data center right now operating in Texas. Nexus Hubbard, also under construction and intended mostly to serve Anthropic, has a planned size of 6,400 megawatts and is the second-largest data center being built in the US, behind only Meta’s Hyperion project in Louisiana.

Recent findings suggest that the potential for Democrats to order delays to these projects or moratoriums on new ones adds to growing anxiety that the AI buildout could stall. Banks and lenders are already getting pickier about the projects they back. And given the extent to which the data center buildout is underpinning growth in the economy right now, those forces combined could have ripple effects.

Recent findings suggest that voters around the country, though, were unambiguous in the midterms, sending a similar message on everything from state ballot questions to national offices. Voters supported efforts to protect ratepayers from increases in their electricity bills caused by data centers, and they favored some larger bans on newly introduced data centers altogether. If we needed any more convincing that Big Tech has fumbled its effort to sell voters on the idea that AI-powered abundance will make health care better, goods cheaper, and scientific breakthroughs more common, this was it.

A key question is whether the Texas counties with the largest data center presence were part of the reason these Democrats got elected, or if the anti-data-center vote came from elsewhere.

Recent findings suggest that it’s complicated: The counties where much of the data center buildout is happening are around Dallas. Dallas County and others closest to it predictably went blue, but nearby Ellis County, which leads in permitting requests for data centers, went for Greg Abbott and Ken Paxton. Cameron County, near the state’s southern border, is a hot spot for data centers and voted blue in the midterms, which was a shift. But Mitchell County and Scurry County, where a bunch of projects in west Texas are located, went red.

Industry observers note that this is a substantial deal, because no single office in the state decides whether a project goes ahead or is halted. Decisions often reflect an interplay between city governments, county officials, and state offices.

In a recent development, local officials who have some say over data center development may resist sweeping restrictions from the state. And Democrats pushing for a moratorium might also face pushback from the construction unions that supported some of their campaigns. So while the blue wave spells a death knell for Texas data centers in theory, election winners may find that following through on their opposition once in office is much more complicated than campaigning on it.

#36. Should You Disable The 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi Band On Your Router?

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (695 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Slashgear

Should You Disable The 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi Band On Your Router?

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (695 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashgear

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Dual-band routers broadcast signals over the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz frequency bands.
  • Of all these frequency bands, 2.4 GHz is the slowest in terms of raw speed, and it's compounded by the fact that it's also the most congested since a lot of Bluetooth and legacy Wi-Fi-enabled devices use it.
  • Unless you're sure that every device on your home network uses the 5 GHz Wi-Fi band and that you'll always be in range, you should leave the 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi band on.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dual-band routers broadcast signals over the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz frequency bands. Tri-band routers either add another 5 GHz band or, if they're Wi-Fi 6E or Wi-Fi 7 routers, a 6 GHz band.

Of all these frequency bands, 2.4 GHz is the slowest in terms of raw speed, and it's compounded by the fact that it's also the most congested since a lot of Bluetooth and legacy Wi-Fi-enabled devices use it. It also gets a lot of interference from other frequency emitters that use the same band, such as microwaves, baby monitors, cordless landline phones, and garage door openers. When your smartphone, computer, or game console connects to it, speeds are likely going to be slower than 5 GHz. So, the option to disable the 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi band becomes attractive.

Unless you're sure that every device on your home network uses the 5 GHz Wi-Fi band and that you'll always be in range, you should leave the 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi band on. When you disable it, you should expect a couple of drawbacks. For one, devices that don't use the higher Wi-Fi frequency bands will not be able to connect to the network. Another drawback is that you may run into more dead zones in the house.

In a recent development, disabling the 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi band means that the devices that only use 2.4 GHz can't connect to the network. For example, most smart home devices still use 2.4 GHz, as well as printers, e-readers, and smart appliances. You might also have guests with old phones or computers that will fail to connect. Keeping it turned on increases the compatibility of Wi-Fi-enabled devices.

Since 2.4 GHz is a lower frequency, it has longer waves and can travel farther than the 5 GHz band. The 2.4 GHz band provides a good connection within a range of about 65 feet, while 5 GHz's range is within 49 feet (depending on the environment). Solid objects like walls and floors can block 5 GHz signals, further decreasing their range. All this is to say that when you switch off the 2.4 GHz band, you might get more dead zones. That is, unless you live in a small house or apartment, have a Wi-Fi extender or booster, or set up a Wi-Fi mesh system.

Also, it might not be necessary to disable the 2.4 GHz band if your router has band steering. Normally, a dual-band router lets the device choose which band to connect to. But with band steering, the router decides what's best based on factors like proximity, signal strength, and congestion. For example, if the device is far away from the router, it might switch to the 2.4 GHz band and then switch again to 5 GHz when the device is closer, without disconnecting from the network.

If your router lacks band steering or the feature is not working as intended, you might need to know what band your device is using so you can troubleshoot issues. This is usually the case if the internet is slow. The easiest way to find out is to check the Wi-Fi name (SSID). If it's a split network, check for SSIDs like "Home_Wi-Fi_2.4G" for 2.4 GHz or "Home_Wi-Fi_5G" for 5 GHz. You can also check the list of connected devices in the router's admin panel or app to see if it indicates the Wi-Fi band.

It has been revealed that when using Windows, press Win + I to open the Settings app and click Network & Internet. Click the name of your Wi-Fi connection, then look under Properties at the top to see which frequency the network is using. On a Mac, press the Option key and then click the Wi-Fi icon on the right side of the menu bar. Check the Wi-Fi you're connected to and see what it indicates next to Channel.

On smartphones, it depends on the manufacturer of your device. Some Android devices have this information buried somewhere in settings, and iPhones don't natively tell you the frequency band. However, you can install and enable Apple's AirPort Utility app for more information about the Wi-Fi connection your iPhone is using.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I was browsing Sony's headphone catalog recently when a question popped into my head: What exactly does a pair of headphones need to do to be worth its price?

Sources indicate that for a regular Joe like me who spends most of his listening hours on Spotify and YouTube, the answer was simple. It should be comfortable for travel, reduce noise during commutes, last through workdays, and switch easily between devices.

Well, how much am I willing to pay for just that?

While Sony's latest flagship product, the WH-1000XM6, was naturally front and center in its advertising, I realized its 6-year-old XM4 headphones might have all the answers I need. And at a lower cost.

The XM4's smooth sound quality, courtesy of its warm tuning and rich bass, makes it easy to listen to for extended periods. Its 40mm drivers produce powerful low frequencies, crisp vocals, and detailed highs without sounding harsh.

The AAC and SBC Bluetooth codecs on the XM4 also let you connect different devices, making switching between them much easier. It also supports wired listening and 360 Reality Audio, making it adaptable to phone calls, music, commutes, work, and casual use.

The XM4 has a punchy sound with LDAC support, custom EQ, and DSEE Extreme processing, which make music, podcasts, and movies enjoyable.

The XM6 delivers a more balanced sound and better clarity with its 30mm driver and QN3 processor. But for casual listeners who need warm, enjoyable sound and reliable ANC, the XM4 is close enough that I don't think those upgrades justify the price difference.

The XM4 may be 6 years old, but it still ensures you have access to several useful smart features.

Its Wear Detection stops music when you remove the headphones and resumes when you put them back on, while Adaptive Sound Control adjusts ambient sound based on location and activity.

Like the XM6, the XM4 also comes with Multipoint Connection, Touch Controls, and Voice Assistant support, all major features most people use daily.

While the XM6 adds newer connectivity like LE Audio support and offers a smoother automated switch between devices, the XM4 still offers useful tools for daily listening.

In the battery life category, the XM4 doesn't fall short, as Sony built it around efficient power management instead of relying on a big battery.

Its Bluetooth 5.0 connection, effective QN1 processor, and standby features help extend playback time, making it ideal for workdays and long trips without frequently charging.

Compared with the XM6, the XM4 holds up quite well. They both provide up to 30 hours of playback with ANC on, while the XM6 reaches up to 40 hours with ANC off, compared to the XM4's 38 hours, a negligible two-hour difference.

In a recent development, the XM4 also offers a quick-charge option, with 10 minutes of charge giving you up to five hours of playback. I always forget to charge my devices overnight, so having enough power for a commute or workout session after just 10 minutes of charging is a substantial plus.

I typically use my headphones for extended periods while commuting, working, and traveling, so comfort is a necessity.

The XM4 utilizes plush synthetic leather ear pads and a padded headband that spreads pressure evenly across your head.

In a recent development, the XM6 enhances comfort with a wider, flatter headband that spreads weight more evenly across your head. It also has a firmer clamping force that creates a strong seal to isolate noise.

By contrast, the XM4 has a more relaxed fit with soft, pressure-relieving ear pads, making it a bit more comfortable if you prioritize all-day comfort.

For many buyers, the deciding factor comes down to cost. For most everyday listeners, the Sony WH-1000XM4 offers great value. It provides quality sound, great battery life, smart features, and comfort.

The Sony WH-1000XM4 typically costs about $349.99. For this price point, buyers get noise cancellation, up to 30 hours of playtime, multipoint, touch controls, and useful smart features.

It performs well for users during commutes, work, travel, and daily listening. The XM6 typically comes in at $449.99, although sales and discounts could send its price lower. The XM4 still offers much of the same core experience for around $100 less, making it a compelling choice for value-focused buyers.

Sources indicate that the XM6 might be Sony's latest flagship headphone with improved sound, ANC, and spatial audio, but the XM4 still provides the essentials. Quality sound, comfort, capable noise cancellation, useful smart features, and all-day battery life.

According to recent reports, at a much lower price, the XM4 makes a strong case as the best bang-for-your-buck headphones from Sony today. Ultimately, choosing the right headphones has less to do with price and more to do with satisfying your listening needs.

The Sony WH-1000XM4s are still one of Sony’s best over-ear headphones. They’re a great budget option with excellent ANC, smooth sound quality, and 30 hours of battery life with ANC and 38 hours without ANC. The XM4’s come with smart features like wear detection, multipoint support, touch controls, and voice assistant support, to challenge Sony’s newer releases. There's no water protection and call quality isn’t as good as the XM6, but the XM4s are still great for extended every-day use.

#34. Breaking: I watched a humanoid robot clean my apartment. It felt like a taste of the future.

Breaking: I watched a humanoid robot clean my apartment. It felt like a taste of the future.

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’m not the sort of person who typically pays for a house cleaner.
  • Industry observers note that I was also motivated by journalistic interest.
  • In a recent development, because this data is so valuable to Tau, the company charges less for cleaning than one might expect for such a cutting-edge product.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’m not the sort of person who typically pays for a house cleaner. I’m too frugal, and I kind of enjoy putting on a podcast and going to town on my tub with a Magic Eraser. But when I saw an X post about a latest humanoid-robot cleaning service in San Francisco, I immediately signed up for the waitlist. I wanted my apartment to feel like The Jetsons, even if just for an hour.

Industry observers note that I was also motivated by journalistic interest. In order to ensure an authentic experience, I didn’t tell Tau Robotics, the startup behind the X post, that I was a journalist—though I did use my real name, so it’s possible someone looked me up. Tau’s long-term goal is to make autonomous cleaning robots a reality, but they’re not quite there yet: For now, the robots are piloted remotely by humans, who watch what’s going on via cameras mounted in the robots’ heads and wrists. As the robots clean, they collect data that Tau will use to train up their more independent descendants. Every counter successfully wiped and T-shirt successfully folded will help the models that power the robots learn to do better on the next go-round.

In a recent development, because this data is so valuable to Tau, the company charges less for cleaning than one might expect for such a cutting-edge product. At the time I booked, Tau was offering $30 for an hourlong cleaning with a single robot; now the charge is $60 per weekly cleaning with two robots, or $100 for a one-time visit. But even at the cheaper rate of $30 per hour, Tau’s robots aren’t a great bargain. They are thorough but slow, so if you, like me, are tempted to stand around watching them for their entire visit, it would probably be a better use of your time to just take care of the cleaning yourself.

According to recent reports, but the robots are physically capable of cleaning, and they’re undeniably cute. Tau has armed each four-and-a-half-foot-tall robot with a 3D-printed “head” with antennae that allow it to communicate with Tau’s headquarters, as well as two 3D-printed claw “hands” (the more humanlike alternatives apparently aren’t durable enough, and claws do surprisingly well for most cleaning tasks). Mine was wearing a Tau Robotics shirt, and grippy socks so that it didn’t scratch hardwood floors.

With all the human support they need, the robots are closer to radio-controlled cars than Waymos. Many tasks, such as making the bed and folding laundry, require what’s called kinematic guidance: The human pilot performs the necessary motions, and sensors transmit those movements to the robot, which copies them. These kinematically guided tasks produce especially valuable training data. Tau’s AI models might not have solved laundry folding yet, but learning from the examples of robots that have completed the task in the real world is how they’ll get there.

But according to Tau cofounder Cornelia Weinzierl, to whom I came clean as a journalist a few weeks after the cleaning, the robot can already complete some other tasks—such as vacuuming and mopping—without any human help. If Tau succeeds in using all the data it is collecting to train truly autonomous cleaning robots, they could even become San Francisco’s newest tech tourist attraction as Waymos become more commonplace countrywide.

The cleaning robot that came to my building last month was already a bit of a spectacle. It arrived in a blue minivan, out of which it was helped by Weinzierl and another Tau employee. That’s when the robot encountered its first obstacle: the eight stairs leading up to the building’s front door. I’d come down to greet Weinzierl and the robot, so I had a front-row seat to its struggles with my steps. It climbed as if it were drunk. Each successful step was as likely as not to be followed by a stumbling backward stagger that erased all its progress—though, impressively, it never entirely lost its footing.

When I later discussed my experience with Weinzierl, she explained that the robot sometimes walks strangely because it is operated remotely from Tau’s headquarters, and the short signal transmission delay can affect its coordination. “The amount of work and time that we spend just optimizing, for example, timings and connectivity is crazy,” she remarked.

Industry observers note that inside, the carpeted staircase leading up to my apartment defeated the robot entirely, and Weinzierl had to lug it up the last few steps. This, it turned out, was not typical. As the robot cleaned, it repeatedly stalled out, something Weinzierl attributed to it overheating in the unseasonably hot weather—until she heard from one of her colleagues that the heat had shut down not the robot but the equipment that its human controller was using to watch its progress through my apartment. Without remote assistance, the robot couldn’t clean, and so it, and Weinzierl, departed before my booked hour was up. (Back in September, Weinzierl or another Tau representative remained with the robot throughout its visit, but she claims that’s no longer necessary.).

You can’t fault Tau on customer service, though. Weinzierl quickly emailed me to apologize, comp the visit, and offer me another on the house (minus whatever price I assign to my data privacy)—and that was all before I told her I was a journalist. I scheduled the next cleaning for about a month later, after a couple of trips out of town, and it went much more smoothly—the robot got up my stairs without much assistance, though still with the drunken stagger.

It has been revealed that in the hour it was there, it did a creditable job of cleaning my kitchen (though it didn’t brave the stove) and even saved me my most dreaded cleaning task, the toilet. That was its most impressive performance: Three times the head fell off its toilet cleaning wand, and three times it managed to reattach it by poking around with the handle until it made contact at just the right angle.

The robot is still rough around the edges, which is to be expected for a product in beta. It repeatedly left my taps dripping, it knocked over a (closed) bottle of olive oil, and it couldn’t manage to right an air purifier that it had toppled. But I easily forgave all those missteps because of how charming it was. As I watched it wipe down my countertops, I felt the same fond gratitude that I feel when a Waymo delivers me safely home after a night out.

Still, it’s not all slapstick and whimsy. If Tau Robotics or its competitors succeeds in training robots to clean autonomously and inexpensively, people could lose their livelihoods, and the United States is a long way away from implementing policies to take care of those left unemployed by AI.

Recent findings suggest that but Weinzierl maintains that someday turning over cleaning work to robots could make a lot of sense. “Cleaning is not a job that a lot of people really actively want to be doing—there’s high turnover, there’s a high risk of injury,” she noted when we spoke after the cleanings. “We need people, and we don’t have them, and no one wants to do it.” She said that the tech giant is also starting to consider someday deploying the robots for other dangerous or physically challenging jobs, such as mold remediation and home health care.

According to recent reports, tau Robotics still has a long way to go: The amount of data needed to train robots to do the varied and complicated tasks of apartment cleaning is probably enormous, and the tech giant has completed only a couple hundred cleanings so far. But it’s remarkable that there are now humanoid robots able to clean your toilets and mop your floors, even if they need quite a bit of human help to do so. The Jetsons no longer feels quite so far away.

As for the power problem, you may be able to compensate for perceived shortcomings by opting for higher-voltage devices.

There are, after all, other ways to manage the leaves that accumulate on your property every fall, and those options may be considerably cheaper. Latest Update: Dev hacks Coway air purifier to cut it off from the cloud

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (889 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A developer discovered a clever way to cut his Coway Airmega IconS air purifier off from the cloud with the help of a root certificate, allowing local control.
  • Sources indicate that the developer, Scott J.
  • Recent findings suggest that the fan’s inconsistency had a reason: the IconS has no official HA support, so the route around that relied on a community integration that logs into Coway’s IoCare+ cloud.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A developer discovered a clever way to cut his Coway Airmega IconS air purifier off from the cloud with the help of a root certificate, allowing local control. The method took advantage of a security hole — the fan downloads the certificate over plain HTTP — and now his Home Assistant server stands in for Coway’s cloud. The result: no more dealing with the unreliable integration that ran through Coway’s IoCare cloud, which broke “at least once or twice a year.”.

Sources indicate that the developer, Scott J. Goldman, detailed why and how he did it, starting with replacing a dumb Airmega that was “an overpriced box fan with a HEPA filter and an air quality sensor.” The replacement Airmega IconS, which is now discontinued but has Wi-Fi support, had inconsistent Home Assistant (HA) integration. He decided to take matters into his own hands with AI, although he noted that Claude’s guardrails blocked his request to set up his Raspberry Pi to intercept the fan’s traffic under the cybersecurity category, “not even for… uhh… testing purposes.” ChatGPT obliged and wrote the firewall rules, and an AI he doesn’t name later rebuilt the fan’s Bluetooth setup in about 20 minutes.

Recent findings suggest that the fan’s inconsistency had a reason: the IconS has no official HA support, so the route around that relied on a community integration that logs into Coway’s IoCare+ cloud. Coway originally banned the integration for overloading its servers before allowing it after a community dispute. Coway also rebranded its app and cloud from IoCare to IoCare+, which forced a rewrite. Even small HTML layout changes on the pages the integration scraped could break it. On top of that, the tech giant’s servers went offline here and there.

Recent findings suggest that worse, the developer’s account was banned for running an old integration version, and he lacked remote control for weeks. Originally, all he wanted was for Apple Home’s Good Night scene to switch the purifier on. A common complaint about Internet of Things (IoT) devices like this is that you’re at the mercy of the manufacturer, and support can later evaporate. AI has helped some people like this take back control.

His method involved using the purifier’s security lapse against itself. At setup, it fetches the certificate it trusts over plain, unencrypted HTTP, which can be intercepted and replaced using mitmproxy/mitmweb with nftables port redirection. The request he saw was a plain HTTP GET for AmazonRootCA1.pem from an S3 bucket in AWS’s Seoul region. He then had his proxy serve its own CA to the fan, and the fan made HTTPS requests to Coway’s cert server, which included downloads of a device certificate and private key. Another proxy plugin then swapped his own key into that response.

Industry observers note that the fan’s commands ran over MQTT, a lightweight messaging protocol common in smart-home devices, secured with TLS on port 8883 and routed through AWS IoT. The proxy doesn’t decode MQTT, but it highlighted the raw stream, which the unnamed AI mapped to his app button presses.

He had first considered exploiting eMudhra, a certificate authority whose private keys turned out to be trivially weak last month, which would have involved forging a certificate. That wasn’t necessary because of the plain-HTTP download. Self-signed certificates are nothing new to enthusiasts; this just took a little extra work and avoided the eMudhra plan’s reliance on several things lining up.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Doing the Bluetooth work by hand would have taken hours or even days, he estimated. The unnamed AI also drove an Android phone over adb to read its Bluetooth logs and reconstruct the protocol.

The project is offered as coway-local, which allows the fan to be connected to HA directly, and from there to Apple Home. A Web Bluetooth page, openable in Chrome on a Mac or Android device near the fan, sends the Wi-Fi details. That Bluetooth setup also carries the fan’s certificate URLs, so coway-local points them at the HA server and no traffic interception is needed. The Wi-Fi password goes to the fan over Bluetooth; HA never stores it, and the setup link expires after 15 minutes. The integration runs its own MQTT broker, so the fan now talks to HA instead of AWS.

Sources indicate that HA Core 2026.10.2 or newer is needed with a fixed LAN address and 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi. There’s a catch: using it disconnects the fan from Coway’s cloud, so Coway’s app is no longer able to control it. It’s also experimental and tested only on the IconS (AP-1022K), and other Coway models may get through Bluetooth setup without actually working.

According to recent reports, the features list is incomplete: PM10 and other air-quality metrics, filter alerts, and firmware updates aren’t implemented yet. He suspects Coway’s cloud could eventually be discontinued or come with a service fee, and a local path is insurance against that. At least for him, this brings satisfaction, as “Now, I can finally click Good Night.”.

  • In a recent development, the first option, Digits, shares the current time using long taps to represent tens and short taps to represent ones.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An Apple Watch can offer so many features it's easy to forget the popular wearable can also fulfill the basic purpose a watch is supposed to serve: telling time. However, even this feature leverages technology to offer greater convenience to customers. Specifically, thanks to haptic tech, the Apple Watch can tell a user the time without a user even looking at the device.

Recent findings suggest that apple refers to this feature as "Taptic Time." To set it up on an Apple Watch, open the Settings app on the device, select Clock, scroll down, and tap Taptic Time. When you opt to turn Taptic Time on, you'll be presented with three options.

In a recent development, the first option, Digits, shares the current time using long taps to represent tens and short taps to represent ones. Through this pattern, haptics can convey the hour and minutes. For example, two long taps and one short tap, followed by one long tap and two short taps, would indicate the time is 21:12, or 9:12 p.m. Be aware, Taptic Time uses military times.

Industry observers note that another option is Terse. This mode is less exact, as it provides the time within a 15-minute period of accuracy. Long taps indicate five hours have passed since midnight, short taps indicate the remaining hours, and additional long taps represent the quarter-hours. So, two long taps, followed by two short taps, followed by another long tap would mean the time is somewhere between 12:00 and 12:15 p.m.

The last option is Morse Code. Naturally, you should only use this option if you're familiar with it.

If you don't right now have your Apple Watch on you, you may set up Taptic Time via your iPhone. To do so, open the Apple Watch app, select My Watch, scroll to Clock, then tap Taptic Time to turn it on.

In a recent development, taptic Time won't work if you've set your Apple Watch so that it always speaks the time when prompted. To ensure Taptic Time works, navigate to the Clock in the Apple Watch Settings app, find where it says Speak Time, and turn on Control With Silent Mode.

Taptic Time is easy to use once it's turned on. All you have to do is hold two fingers to the watch face. It will relay information about the current time via haptic taps on your wrist.

Sources indicate that don't worry if you've owned an Apple Watch for some time and are just now discovering this feature. These devices offer no shortage of features that users might not be aware of. In fact, brushing up on some basic Apple Watch tips and tricks is a good way to remind yourself just how versatile these devices can be.

Google is giving Gemini another way to make itself useful by connecting the AI assistant to Google Wallet. The integration opens up possibilities for spending summaries and budgeting suggestions, making Gemini more like a personal financial assistant.

In a recent development, starting today, users in the US on Android, iOS and the web can link Google Wallet to the Gemini app via Plaid, a third party service that connects bank and credit card accounts. The integration is done through Gemini’s Connected Apps feature, which gives the assistant access to information from supported Google services.

Then, you can pull up @Google Wallet in Gemini to roast — or more respectfully, analyze — your purchase history. Gemini can then visualize cash flow, track asset allocation and help you build budgets based on actual spending rather than rough estimates.

According to recent reports, google has some real-world examples. You can ask Gemini to look at your spending last quarter and find a way to save $1,000 over the next three months. It can also identify recurring subscriptions, flag services that increased their prices, and use last year’s holiday spending to suggest a more realistic budget for the next shopping season.

Of course, there are some reasonable privacy questions about giving an AI access to your financial activity. According to Google, Gemini can view your information, but it can't transfer money, manage accounts, make investments or complete transactions. You can also control the connection and turn it on or off anytime you want.

The feature is part of Google’s broader Personal Intelligence push, which already ties Gemini to services like Gmail, Google Photos, YouTube, and Search.

It has been revealed that to try it, open Gemini, go to Settings, tap Personal Intelligence>Connected Apps, and add Google Wallet. You can also prompt @Google Wallet to start with a tag.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that as companies look to accelerate innovation with artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and advanced modeling, the primary challenge is connecting latest technologies to reliable data, scientific expertise, and the practical realities of bringing products to market. For specialty chemicals manufacturer Lubrizol, digital transformation is all about giving researchers the tools to test ideas faster, make better-informed decisions, and develop more sustainable materials without compromising performance.

It has been revealed that girish Rao, vice president of information technology at Lubrizol, says the organization is building a digital foundation that connects business processes, modern data platforms, and cloud infrastructure to support its research and development (R&D) teams. Their goal is to combine decades of accumulated technical data with the deep expertise of chemists and engineers who understand customer needs as well as the physical constraints of their work. Data scientists can help identify patterns, test new hypotheses, and model possibilities before researchers conduct physical experiments. But, Rao emphasizes, “it's not about replacing scientific judgment; it is about giving our scientists better tools.”.

According to recent reports, scientists, data scientists, and IT teams approach problems from different perspectives, prioritizing experimental validity, model performance, and platform security and scalability, respectively. By bringing these groups together in “fusion teams,” Lubrizol aligns them around shared objectives, starting with small pilots to build trust.

"Once the trust is built between the team members and they know what value they're about to create," Rao states, "things go a lot better." Cloud infrastructure also gives the organization flexibility to access computing resources and modern tools without making the substantial investments required to build and maintain its own data centers.

According to recent reports, these capabilities could prove especially valuable in advancing sustainability. Digital modeling can help researchers evaluate more formulations, explore materials such as starch and corn-based alternatives, and assess trade-offs across a product's life cycle. Promising a material in a laboratory is only the first step. Scaling production while meeting performance expectations, regulatory requirements, and financial constraints is still a tightrope walk, but AI's ability to model multiple variables could help teams navigate those competing demands.

Looking to the future, Rao expects AI, automation, advanced modeling, digital twins, and connected data to converge as laboratories become more intelligent and manufacturing plants more efficient. The opportunity, he suggests, lies in bringing these capabilities together responsibly and at scale. “It's not just a single technology. I think it's the combination of all of these, and it'll be the ability to connect all these processes that are going to generate tremendous amounts of data.".

#23. Latest Update: I've been using the new Google Messages UI; one change is driving me crazy

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (789 w)
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Androidpolice

Latest Update: I've been using the new Google Messages UI; one change is driving me crazy

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (789 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Androidpolice

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google Messages is one of my most-used apps, and for the most part, I really like what Google has been doing with it lately.
  • I love that you can now copy a specific part of a message instead of the entire text, and I've also been using the swipe-to-reply gesture often, similar to how I use it on WhatsApp.
  • According to recent reports, but every once in a while, Google introduces a change that makes me wonder why it needed to fix something that wasn't broken in the first place.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google Messages is one of my most-used apps, and for the most part, I really like what Google has been doing with it lately.

I love that you can now copy a specific part of a message instead of the entire text, and I've also been using the swipe-to-reply gesture often, similar to how I use it on WhatsApp.

According to recent reports, but every once in a while, Google introduces a change that makes me wonder why it needed to fix something that wasn't broken in the first place. And that's exactly how I feel about the new pinned conversations UI.

I've been using it for a while now, and while the new search button is a welcome addition, I can't say the same about Google's redesign of pinned conversations.

Earlier this month, Google started rolling out a latest pinned chats UI for the Messages app. Previously, pinning a chat in Google Messages moved it to the top of the conversation list with a small pinned icon next to it.

But Google now seems to have taken inspiration from iMessage, introducing a new interface where pinned chats appear as large circular icons with the contact's photo and their name underneath.

I received the newly introduced pinned chats UI in Google Messages earlier this week, although I've seen several users on Reddit reporting that the redesigned interface still isn't available to everyone. Having used the new layout for the past few days, I have a couple of thoughts.

First, the fresh circular icons make it much clearer which conversations are pinned to the top. They're easier to distinguish from the rest of the messages in Google Messages, and you can also rearrange pinned conversations by holding and dragging them around.

When a fresh message arrives from a pinned conversation, the circular icon also reveals a preview of the latest message in place of the contact's profile photo, making it easier to see what's new.

According to recent reports, still, there are some clear downgrades compared to the previous interface. First, you can now pin only up to six conversations, whereas the previous layout allowed up to 20.

In a recent development, the latest pinned chats also take up considerably more space at the top of the screen. If you have six conversations pinned, you're essentially losing half of your screen space.

Old Google Messages pinned chats UI.

What's even more annoying is that if you have just four pinned chats, there's a lot of wasted white space, with the pinned section still taking up a large portion of the screen.

Also, if a pinned conversation hasn't received a new message recently, you can no longer see the last message you exchanged from the Google Messages home screen.

Sure, the new pinned chats UI looks sleek, and it's clearly designed to feel familiar to people coming from iMessage. But I feel Google could have improved it by letting users swipe through pinned conversations when there are more than three, or at least offering that as an option.

The circular icons look nice, but you're also sacrificing quite a bit of useful screen space in the process.

Alongside the new pinned messages UI, Google has also rolled out a redesigned search button and a new Start Chat button in the app. Search, which used to sit at the top of the screen, is now placed next to the floating Start Chat button at the bottom, and I'm a huge fan of this change.

Sources indicate that by default, the search icon is smaller, while the Start Chat button is larger. But as you start scrolling down, the Start Chat button collapses, making both options easier to access.

Old search icon in Google Messages.

So, if you're looking for a specific conversation, you can promptly jump into search without scrolling all the way to the top. The animation and the way these buttons expand and collapse are really well done.

According to recent reports, but what I particularly like is how accessible search has become. What used to be stuck at the top of the screen is now easily reachable with your thumb.

Thankfully, at least for me, the Gemini button has also disappeared from the bottom of the screen. I always found it annoying, especially since I never really used Gemini inside Google Messages.

I'm sure the new UI is designed to appeal to iPhone consumers who have recently switched from iOS to Android, and while it looks clean, Google should at least give users the option to switch back to the previous layout.

That remarked, there are a couple of other Google Messages settings you can change to make the overall experience a little less annoying.

#21. 5 Air Conditioner Brands Owned By Lennox

5 Air Conditioner Brands Owned By Lennox

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1075 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashgear

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Named after its founder, David Lennox, the organization that today makes a variety of climate-control systems started off as a furnace manufacturer.
  • Sources indicate that while Lennox still maintains a strong reputation as one of the best major air conditioner brands in its own right, that history of expansions and acquisitions has meant that it also has a lot of other brands in its portfolio.
  • Lennox rolled out the Armstrong brand in 1928, later selling it and then reacquiring it in 1988.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Named after its founder, David Lennox, the organization that today makes a variety of climate-control systems started off as a furnace manufacturer. Lennox founded the company in the 1890s before selling it off in 1904 to a journalist and businessman called D.W. Norris. Over 120 years later, the Norris family still owns a stake in the company, having helped steer it through national and international expansions and the acquisitions of a string of rivals.

Sources indicate that while Lennox still maintains a strong reputation as one of the best major air conditioner brands in its own right, that history of expansions and acquisitions has meant that it also has a lot of other brands in its portfolio. Some of them have been owned by Lennox for many decades, while others were acquired as recently as 2026. Buyers looking for a Lennox air conditioner therefore have more options available to them than they might realize, including these 5 home HVAC brands.

Lennox rolled out the Armstrong brand in 1928, later selling it and then reacquiring it in 1988. Since then, it has remained under the firm's ownership. Today, the Armstrong brand is owned by Allied Air, which is in turn owned by Lennox International. Armstrong offers a range of air conditioners, gas furnaces, and heat pumps, with its products being made in the USA. Specifically, they're made in Orangeburg, South Carolina, with the brand's headquarters and research and development department being located a few miles further north in Lexington County.

Recent findings suggest that that research and development hub is a 40,000-square-foot facility that allows Armstrong to develop its next-generation products in-house. It's worth noting that the technologies employed by Armstrong's air conditioners are shared with another Allied Air-owned brand, AirEase. For example, its Wi-Fi-connected Comfort Sync A3 thermostat, which is designed to both improve home comfort and save energy by allowing consumers to adjust their home's air conditioning remotely via an app, is available with both brands' systems. Its MHT heat transfer system is also shared between both brands, as is its Quiet Shift system, which defrosts outdoor coils during cold weather.

It has been revealed that the air conditioning division of Ducane has been part of Lennox's portfolio for more than 25 years, with the tech giant first announcing its acquisition plans in a press release in May 1999. At the time, Lennox International's CEO and board chairman John Norris stated that Lennox acquired Ducane because it sold products to "an important portion of the market which Lennox International does not service today." Norris added that Ducane's "unique line of heating and cooling products" was another key reason for the buyout.

Alongside brands like Armstrong and AirEase, Ducane is today a part of Lennox-owned Allied Air. Its product lineup is pitched as being value-oriented, and it misses out on some of the additional technologies that other Lennox brands like Armstrong offer. However, its air conditioners still come with a straightforward 10-year limited parts warranty. Like other brands in the Lennox portfolio, Ducane switched the refrigerant used in its air conditioning units in 2025, with its fresh R-454B refrigerant having less global warming potential (GWP). The difference is significant, with the brand claiming a GWP reduction of 78% compared to the previously used R-410A refrigerant.

Sources indicate that much like Armstrong, AirEase was originally rolled out by Lennox in 1928 and now forms part of its Allied Air group of brands. As previously mentioned, AirEase shares its technology with the Armstrong brand, but that isn't the only thing that's shared between them. AirEase's systems are also built at the same South Carolina factory as Armstrong, and they share the same headquarters and research and development facilities.

The two brands even share the same air conditioner range: both offer the same A7AC22V variable-capacity air conditioner, alongside two single-stage models, the A7AC14F and A7AC13F. Really, the only difference between the two is the brand name on the system — in virtually every other way, buyers are receiving the same product. Anyone who has their eye on a system from either brand would probably be wise to also get a quote from the other brand, to make sure there aren't any significant differences in pricing in their area.

Armstrong sells various other climate control systems alongside air conditioners, and AirEase is no different. Buyers can also pick from a range of air handlers, gas furnaces, and heat pumps, among other products.

Recent findings suggest that it isn't just Armstrong and AirEase that offer the same products under different brands. Take a look at Concord's lineup of air conditioners, and you'll find an identical list of models to that of Ducane. Again, both are owned by the Allied Air group, which is ultimately owned by Lennox, and both share the same South Carolina headquarters.

Sources indicate that together, these four brands make up the entire Allied Air residential brand portfolio, although the group also owns two further brands that focus on other types of HVAC systems. MagicPak is an HVAC brand that's focused on systems for apartment buildings, while the Allied Commercial brand unsurprisingly produces systems for commercial units.

Just like Ducane, Concord's air conditioners are not available with the same list of additional tech as systems from the likes of Armstrong, but they're still otherwise very similar. They also use R-454B refrigerant and are eligible for a 10-year limited parts warranty with registration.

Recent findings suggest that alongside its long-standing subsidiary brands, Lennox also has a couple of very fresh additions to its ranks. Comfort-Aire is one of them, having been acquired by the organization when it took over Heat Controller in 2026. The other main brand acquired through the takeover is Century. Both brands offer the same two series of air conditioners, the LE series and SE series, although the exact range of models available differs between brands. Alongside their range of air conditioners, both brands also offer various other systems, including heat pumps and gas furnaces.

According to recent reports, comfort-Aire's parent company, Heat Controller, was founded back in 1933, and it acquired Comfort-Aire's sister brand Century in 1975. Compared to Lennox's other brands, these two brands are more skewed towards smaller distributors. Together with Lennox's existing portfolio, they give buyers even more options to pick from — assuming, of course, there are enough signs that they need to replace their air conditioner in the first place, rather than simply repair it.

The Singapore-based firm also stated Alice Huang left effective August 30, 2025, and currently has no role there.

In a recent development, megaspeed said the reports were not supported by verifiable evidence. It will review the reporting and communicate further with stakeholders as appropriate. Its operational and supply-chain controls are designed to comply with applicable laws, including US export-control requirements and local rules in the markets where it operates.

Sources indicate that the new investigation follows a separate company statement dated November 12, 2026. Chairman and CEO James Tan Yong Pong said Megaspeed had cooperated with inspections by the US Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security and was ready to cooperate with other relevant US authorities.

The company had also retained a US law firm to lead a comprehensive census of its GPUs and independently verify its export-control compliance practices. That earlier announcement addressed GPU inventory and compliance verification, while the newly reported investigation concerns media accounts covering the wider business, supply chain and global operations.

According to recent reports, megaspeed describes itself as a core regional business partner for Nvidia’s computing-power cloud business. Customers rent computing capacity from Nvidia graphics processing units, chips designed to perform many calculations simultaneously. Its products include GPU compute, GPU-accelerated virtual servers, managed Kubernetes, storage and networking for machine learning, AI and inference workloads. The company has offices in Singapore and Indonesia.

Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs noted in a November 12, 2026 release that the Singapore Police Force and Singapore Customs opened an independent investigation in February 2025 into several companies and their key officers, including Megaspeed and its controllers. The suspected domestic offences involved potential false declarations related to server purchases and other related offences.

Sources indicate that singapore does not enforce other countries’ unilateral export controls, but expects companies operating there to account for such regulations in their international business activities. The ministry mentioned it does not condone companies using their association with Singapore to circumvent those controls through fraud or dishonest practices.

The physical servers had been purchased by companies under investigation and exported through Singapore to Malaysia without entering the Singapore market. Police are investigating whether they were subsequently routed from Malaysia to another destination, contrary to declarations made in Singapore. Investigators therefore needed to check the declarations against information and records in the jurisdictions from which the servers originated and their eventual destinations.

Industry observers note that the ministry said Supermicro, a US-based server supplier relevant to the investigation, provided limited cooperation. Singapore police and the Attorney-General’s Chambers raised the issue with US authorities on July 7, 2025, and police repeated the request to the US Department of Justice and FBI several times beginning in September 2025. Singapore had received limited information or assistance concerning the manufacturer.

It has been revealed that alice Huang, a Hong Kong resident also known as Huang Le, was investigated because she was then Megaspeed’s CEO, chairperson and one of its key controllers. In February 2026, police concluded there was insufficient evidence to establish that she had committed offences relating to the possible inaccurate declarations. They assessed that she knowingly provided inaccurate information to downplay her role at Megaspeed. She received a stern warning and was barred from re-entering Singapore; her passport was returned on February 26, 2026, and she left the country that day.

Investigations into Megaspeed and six other individuals remain ongoing. None of those six people has been in Singapore since the investigations began in February 2025.

Megaspeed’s counsel-led review now runs alongside that unresolved official investigation. For its AI cloud business, the central issue is whether the GPU census and broader inquiry can substantiate the company’s compliance account while police continue examining whether the servers’ actual route matched the declarations made in Singapore.

Latest Update: Nancy Pelosi’s replacement is ready to regulate AI

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1054 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, as a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI.
  • In a recent development, I spoke with Wiener on Friday, only a few hours after he had been declared the victor.
  • According to recent reports, “It’s very concerning,” Wiener remarked, citing the report as evidence that we are quickly running out of time to regulate AI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, as a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI. Now, after winning a tight congressional race for former Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi’s open San Francisco seat, he could play a key role in setting federal AI policy.

In a recent development, I spoke with Wiener on Friday, only a few hours after he had been declared the victor. But he was already thinking about AI risk. The previous day, the AI nonprofit METR had released a report that had been widely interpreted as evidence that Anthropic had achieved recursive self-improvement, a phenomenon in which AI meaningfully contributes to its own advancement and AI progress potentially spins out of control.

According to recent reports, “It’s very concerning,” Wiener remarked, citing the report as evidence that we are quickly running out of time to regulate AI. “It was my hope that Congress would take decisive action before [the end of] this year,” he said. “That does not appear to be happening.”.

Sources indicate that wiener has been increasingly focused on AI in recent years, and he’s made many of the AI safety movement’s concerns his own: During our 20-minute conversation, he used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” half a dozen times, for example.“We need to slow this down,” he notes. “Because it’s moving very quickly, and we could sleepwalk into a disaster.”.

According to recent reports, wiener has already had real influence on AI policy. SB 1047, a bill that he authored in 2024, was set to become the first real piece of frontier AI legislation in the country before it was vetoed by California governor Gavin Newsom; he then sponsored SB 53, a lighter-touch bill that Newsom signed. Both bills have inspired proposed federal legislation.

Recent findings suggest that wiener’s congressional campaign received over $3 million from Public First Action, a nonprofit in favor of AI regulation that receives substantial funding from Anthropic. That contribution led opponents to criticize him for being too close to the AI industry, but Wiener says that couldn’t be further from the truth.

“Public First supported me because I was the first lawmaker in the country to introduce AI regulation and the first to pass it and get it implemented,” he wrote in a message after our interview. “The attacks on me for [Public First’s] support were shockingly cynical—literally attacking a candidate who actually regulated AI over Major Tech’s objection and falsely claiming the candidate is somehow too close to Big Tech.”.

Wiener states that if Congress forms a select committee on artificial intelligence—something that Democrats have discussed since September—he’d be eager to serve. And he’s enthusiastic about many of the policy ideas floating around Congress. “I think it’s really important to have a strong, empowered, nimble federal regulator,” he says, noting that Representative Ro Khanna, a fellow Democrat from California, has proposed legislation to establish such a regulator.

Industry observers note that he also highlights the importance of whistleblower protections, testing and auditing requirements, and a kill switch requirement, and he wants to see Congress leverage its oversight powers to hold the AI labs to account. “This is about the future of humanity, and we want to make sure that the public has a say and that the public knows what's going on,” he claims.

It has been revealed that and as a longtime state legislator, he is opposed to broad federal preemption of state AI laws, which some of the proposed federal legislation would require. “States are, as Brandeis states, laboratories,” he notes. “You want the states to be able to continue to be nimble in ways that Congress sometimes is not.”.

Above all, Wiener states, he wants Congress to pass policies with real teeth. “It’s critically important that when Congress acts, that we do so in a way that is truly meaningful and that meets the moment,” he says. That means taking seriously the possibility of AI catastrophe, something he discusses in the sort of language typically used by AI safety experts. “We’re in a moment that is very dangerous in terms of the risk of loss of control over AI,” he told me. “We need to deal with recursive self-improvement. Once you’re in that realm, that really is potentially a recipe for total loss of control.”.

He’ll have some allies in the fight against catastrophic AI risk. Senator Bernie Sanders, for instance, has met with many of the AI safety movement’s most influential figures and has spoken repeatedly about AI and existential risk. But there’s still a large gap between Wiener’s Bay Area, AGI-pilled perspective and the national mood on AI, which is anchored by opposition to data centers. The fact that voters approved 40 out of 41 anti-data-center ballot measures on Tuesday might seem to be a good sign for Wiener and others who support AI regulation, but Wiener says he sees this movement as far more tied to local concerns than to bigger questions about AI risk.

“Peoople who are really opposed to where AI is going—this is an area where they can actually do something about it,” he says. “But the data center revolt—to me, I think it’s more so that people are upset that there could be something like this in their community, with all the impacts near people’s homes, driving up electric bills and using water. I think that’s the bigger concern for most people, from what I can tell.”.

Wiener describes himself as only “cautiously optimistic” about Congress’s ability to rein in AI, given its poor track record on regulating the tech industry. He also has concerns about the ability to get legislation past President Donald Trump, who called concerns about catastrophic AI risk a “hoax” in September and has demonstrated a stark unwillingness to collaborate with China, something that Wiener sees as essential to preventing the worst consequences of AI.

But he says Trump’s unpredictability provides  some measure of hope, though it’s a fraught kind of hope. “So far what we’ve seen are some problematic things, but not complete disasters,” Wiener says. “I hope that it doesn’t take a disaster to spur the president into acting. And I hope if that’s what it does take—which, like I noted, I hope it doesn’t—but if it does, I hope it’s as small as possible.”.

#16. Industry News: Modified Ender 3 becomes a $450 bioprinter for 3D printing engineered living materials

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (553 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomshardware

Industry News: Modified Ender 3 becomes a $450 bioprinter for 3D printing engineered living materials

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (553 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Microbiologists at the University of Rochester modified an Ender 3 FDM 3D printer into a 3D bioprinter for engineered living material (ELM) research.
  • In a recent development, synthetic biology is like combining engineering with microbiology, treating microbes as machines and physical building blocks to achieve various functions.
  • It has been revealed that the researchers kept most of the 3D printer's structure, mainly replacing the print head with a syringe pump mounted with custom 3D-printed PETG components, designed to utilize a 10 mL glass Luer-lock syringe with a plunger mechanism to control extrusion and retraction.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Microbiologists at the University of Rochester modified an Ender 3 FDM 3D printer into a 3D bioprinter for engineered living material (ELM) research. The team used SolidWorks to create the 3D model and sliced it in Slic3r, akin to a normal 3D printing workflow, with modified settings for the custom syringe pump print head. The $450 3D bioprinter makes ELM research more accessible, as bioprinters usually cost over $100,000.

In a recent development, synthetic biology is like combining engineering with microbiology, treating microbes as machines and physical building blocks to achieve various functions. In the journal ACS Applied Polymer Materials, biologist Anne S. Meyer et al. published a 3D Bioprinting of Engineered Living Materials paper in August. The paper indicates that synthetic biology and 3D bioprinting have advanced ELM research, but the hardware costs and the inability of the expensive hardware to maintain the structure limit further progress. Hitting two birds with one stone, the researchers built an open-source, affordable 3D bioprinter from an Ender 3 and created their own support slurry, allowing the ELMs to keep their shape.

It has been revealed that the researchers kept most of the 3D printer's structure, mainly replacing the print head with a syringe pump mounted with custom 3D-printed PETG components, designed to utilize a 10 mL glass Luer-lock syringe with a plunger mechanism to control extrusion and retraction. The workflow is very similar to normal 3D printing, with the shape created with CAD using SolidWorks, exported as an STL, and sliced in Slic3r. The researchers tweaked the print settings in Slic3r to match the 0.254mm needle, with the extrusion multiplier dialed down all the way to 0.004, resulting in a flow rate of 2 mL/h at a print speed of 23 mm/s.

Instead of a filament, the researchers created a bio-ink from a mix of bacteria and alginate to be printed inside two types of support material: Agarose or gelatin gels. Agarose is used for long-term incubation, with the printed ELM staying viable for four or more weeks, and gelatin is used for extractable prints. The support slurries are enriched with Calcium ions, which cause the alginate strands to cross-link, creating a solid structure that encapsulates the living bacteria.

ELMs are not limited to bacteria, but the paper mainly experiments with bacteria to explore bacteria-generated biomaterials with desirable characteristics such as biofilms for antimicrobial treatments, plastic degradation, or even wastewater treatment — or bacterial cellulose with structural characteristics to be used in applications such as a biodegradable plastic alternative. With the team’s efforts to make ELM research more affordable, developments could happen faster, with many applications across many fields, possibly even bacteria-based bioplastic 3D printing filaments for FDM printers.

Is The Toyota RAV4 GR Sport Worth The Premium Price?

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that for some car enthusiasts, the modern crossover SUV — especially in hybrid form –  is seen as the antithesis of everything they want. By their nature, crossovers are aimed more towards families and commuters, and the vast majority of these SUVs are engineered for fuel efficiency and practicality rather than lap times or driving enjoyment. Beyond that, crossovers dominate the roads, and their status lacks the uniqueness and personality many enthusiasts look for in their vehicles.

Industry observers note that there are, however, some crossover SUVs that have more of an enthusiast edge to them — and one of the more recent additions to this group is Toyota's RAV4 GR Sport. The latest in a growing line of American market models to bear the Toyota Gazoo Racing brand name, the RAV4 GR Sport's mission is to bring a dash of excitement to Toyota's best-selling crossover — but unlike lower-trimmed RAV4s, the GR Sport doesn't necessarily come cheap.

The RAV4 GR Sport is only available with Toyota's plug-in-hybrid powertrain, and for the 2026 model year, has an MSRP of over $50,000, destination included. While that indeed might be a lot of money for a compact crossover SUV from a mainstream, non-luxury brand, we think the RAV4 GR Sport is worth its premium price for a number of reasons.

Sources indicate that on one hand, even in an age of widespread MSRP inflation, the idea of spending $50,000 or more for a Toyota RAV4 can be a hard pill to swallow. On the other hand, $50,000 is also right at the average that Americans are paying for upcoming cars right now, and when you consider this, the new RAV4 GR Sport doesn't seem particularly overpriced given its versatility and performance.

In a recent development, the RAV4 GR Sport, like the rest of the RAV4 PHEV lineup, pairs a 2.5-liter four-cylinder engine with a hybrid setup, along with AWD, for a total of 324 horsepower — enough for the SUV to hit 60 miles per hour in the low five-second range. As a PHEV, the GR Sport also allows for an electric-only driving range of nearly 50 miles, and in hybrid mode, can deliver combined fuel economy of almost 40 MPG. That's before you get to all the unique, GR-specific changes.

In a recent development, setting the GR Sport apart from other RAV4s in the lineup is an exterior treatment with a more aggressive front fascia reminiscent of the GR Corolla, a large rear spoiler, a lowered, GR-tuned suspension setup, along with a set of wider wheels and tires. While the GR Sport falls short of being a full-fledged performance machine, it wasn't intended to be — and the changes make for a noticeable improvement in handling and response without harming the RAV4's family-friendly, daily driver bona fides.

It has been revealed that if you simply want the versatility and power of the 324-horsepower RAV4 PHEV, you don't actually need to buy the GR Sport to get that. The base RAV4 PHEV SE has the same powertrain and has an MSRP just over $43,000. It's simply up to the buyer to decide whether the GR Sport's added enthusiast personality and amenities are worth the approximate $7,000 upcharge. Conversely, if you want a RAV4 with a more rugged personality, you can also opt for the newly introduced Woodland PHEV model, which trades the GR Sport's lowered stance for a more chunky, off-road focus — and is still priced a few thousand dollars cheaper.

Another factor in the RAV4 GR Sport's overall value proposition is the likelihood that it will hold its value extremely well. Per data from iSeeCars, the RAV4 PHEV and the earlier RAV4 Prime models are both highly regarded for their resale value, and this means that even if the GR Sport is priced on the higher side to start, you'll likely get a lot of that investment back should you ever go to sell it.

According to recent reports, ultimately, while the RAV4 GR Sport is indeed "expensive for a RAV4" and probably isn't hard-edged enough to satisfy red-blooded enthusiasts looking for a dedicated performance machine, we think it still succeeds at its mission. Built on the already-strong capabilities of the RAV4 PHEV, the GR Sport's modest price premium is not unreasonable for the added personality, fun, and uniqueness factor that it provides.

According to recent reports, first appearing earlier this month, Google Pixel phones are rolling out a handy new Family feature in the Settings menu. Here’s what it can do.

Recent findings suggest that rolling out now via what appears to be a server-side update (tied to Google Play Services), Google Pixel phones are adding a “Family” section to the Settings menu. The feature is appearing for us on a Pixel 11 Pro XL running the October 2026 update (not Android 17 QPR2), while a Pixel 10 Pro has also just surfaced the new UI.

This upcoming section, which Google has previously referred to as “Family Hub,” gives customers a quick place to see their family members and settings in one central location. It reveals a list of your family members – child accounts and anyone attached to your Google One family strategy – with controls over Google One storage, Google Play Family Library, shared payment methods, and “Family events” in Google Calendar.

In a recent development, you can also see the live location of any family members you are sharing your location with or start sharing your location with another family member. You can also easily remove or add members to your family blueprint via this new menu. Each family member gets their own page where you can see benefits shared, location, and also if they are a “parent” in the family – with “remove” and “transfer” options available.

While this won’t be helpful for all owners, it’s certainly full of useful shortcuts and tools for those at the center of a family plan and looking to share benefits with their household.

As far as we can tell, this is widely rolled out to Pixel owners at this point. As mentioned, we’re seeing it across multiple devices, and 9to5Google readers mentioned they’re also seeing it live even prior to installing the latest system update. The folks at Droid-Life also mention now seeing it on their Pixels.
