Locating and purchasing vintage parts is the bane of some auto hobbyists' existence. They comb everything from online marketplaces to ancient junkyards to find the final piece for a restoration or that authentic period touch for a replica racer. Some parts make their name on racing pedigree, others on pure rarity, while still more are part of a thriving aftermarket built around dedicated enthusiasts. Whatever the case, car lovers have been opening their wallets to find the just-right part for their garage queens for as long as cars have existed.

We dug into automotive history to find some vintage car parts (and their re-creations) that are worth more than you might think. They range from specialty performance engines to classic body panels to custom glass windscreens. Woe to the car lover who finds one of these on their to-buy list. Some will be easy to find, but none will be cheap.

It has been revealed that some parts are so unusual and specialized that they demand premium prices whenever they surface for sale. Enter the Horch 853. Founded by August Horch, who was later ousted by a hostile board of directors and went on to create Audi, Horch built German automobiles from 1901 to 1940.

Recent findings suggest that the Horch 853 was the halo car of a organization with decades of experience under its belt. Produced and sold from 1935 to 1940, it is a sleek and sensuous throwback to another age. It's easy to imagine replacement parts costing a fortune, especially after you learn fewer than 1,000 were made. If you find yourself in the rare position of owning one of the relatively few surviving 853s and need one of those graceful fenders, you can expect to pay a premium. Strategy to pony up upward of $25,000 to finally finish that lost 853 you've been waiting to unveil to the world.

The 911 changed everything for Porsche upon its debut at the 1963 Frankfurt Motor Show. It was clearly a new Porsche; the crossover Volkswagen parts were gone. It was a promising step, but Porsche still had to prove it on the track. The Porsche RSR arrived in 1973 as Stuttgart's best foot forward. And those feet needed special shoes. To step up its performance, Porsche chose a set of Otto Fuchs-made aluminum forged wheels.

The same firm shod the debut 911S in 1966, but historical provenance aside, these wheels look like a million bucks. The RSR had a one-year career as a racer sold mostly to racing teams, and today it is a highly sought-after item in a niche market of deep-pocketed collectors like Jerry Seinfeld. If the RSR is worth around $2 million, what might the wheels fetch? Porsche fanatics can put the finishing touch on their RSR replica with these Fuchs racing wheels for about $1,700 per corner.

There once was no replacement for displacement — and then auto manufacturers discovered aerodynamics. One of the earliest and most impactful adopters of aero design is the ultra-classic Dodge Charger Daytona and its running mate, the Plymouth Superbird.

Sources indicate that the ungainly 1969 Dodge Charger Daytona wasn't going to win any beauty contests, but it would win races. The 18-inch steel nose cone sliced through the air, and the 23-inch rear wing provided downforce over the drive wheels. Rudimentary by modern standards, and sinfully ugly, the Daytona upended NASCAR's 1970 season. Driver Buddy Baker broke the 200 mph barrier for the first time on a NASCAR track at Talladega. Chrysler dominated the season, so much so that NASCAR cracked down on the winged cars the following year. The upshot is that those Chargers and Superbirds were built like that for a single model year and have consequently become exceedingly valuable today — to the tune of roughly $200,000 to $3 million.

Industry observers note that part prices for these cars — especially iconic one-year-only aero elements — are through the roof. Say you wanted to turn your Charger into a high-flying winged replica. You can go through aftermarket manufacturers like AAR Quality Fiberglass, which can provide you with a rear wing for $1,100. RPM Productions will build you a nose cone for about $4,700. If nothing less than original will do for your banned baby, expect to pay significantly more, like for this nose cone demanding $8,500 or this rear wing asking nearly $10,000.

The Jaguar E-Type is commonly heralded as the most beautiful car in automotive history, and everything about it is precious. Perhaps its most charming feature is its distinctive wheels. Wire wheels save weight by creating a spindlework of spokes rather than heavy metal. In the case of the E-Type and many others, the design also used a single knock-off nut that pit crews could change in a hurry. Since the E-Type is recognized as a garage queen classic today, it's hard to believe people raced the heck out of these cars.

Recent findings suggest that wire wheels weren't all convenience, though. They required extensive maintenance to remain safe, and knock-off nuts were under enormous pressure as single points of failure holding the wheels on. Fortunately, these wheels proved so popular that there is a thriving aftermarket ready to meet the needs of any British racing enthusiast. Wire wheels are priced from $400 to $700 per shoe. For those who want original equipment, eBay has original Jaguar wire wheels priced from about $90 for a single used wheel up to around $1,700 for a set of four.

Plenty of Ford fans will tell you it kicked off the pony car craze with its 1964 ½ release of the Mustang. But what if we told you there was another contender? The 1964 Plymouth Barracuda was declared on April 1, 1964, a full 16 days before the Mustang's debut at the New York World's Fair, cementing its place in automotive history.

In a recent development, the 'Cuda didn't quite make the same impact as the Mustang. With a design somewhat reminiscent of the Ford, its long hood terminated at a front fascia fit for a previous era, while its curious bubble rear window sloped down to a fastback-ish rear end. And that window costs a surprising amount today.

The 14.4-square-foot wraparound rear window was the biggest piece of auto glass on the market at the time. At one point, a Mopar restorer lamented the inflated cost of obtaining this piece for a restoration, with prices climbing as high as $1,000. The market seems to have calmed down, though, as eBay currently has offerings in the $300 range — without the seals.

It has been revealed that it should be no surprise that one of the most expensive vintage parts finds out there involves the Ferrari 250 GTO. It is one of the most valuable cars in the world, after all. Aside from the Prancing Horse on the fender, many, including us, consider it among the coolest Ferrari designs of all time. Pedigree and rarity make the 250 GTO a premium collector's item. Ferrari built fewer than 40 homologated 250 GTOs (by hand, mind you) between 1962 and 1964. Which brings us to sourcing parts.

According to recent reports, the Gioachino Colombo-designed 3.0-liter V12 drove the GTO to racing glory with 300 horsepower. With an exotic powerplant like that, few owners settle for an LS engine swap. And finding any other parts is nigh on impossible. Ferrari built 36 — plus three 4.0-liter prototypes — and all have survived. It's not precisely the kind of car you find in the wrecking yard.

Sources indicate that that's why a box of miscellaneous parts discovered in a shipping container in 2018 drew enormous interest. The container included pristine parts for the Ferrari 250 SWB, 275, Competition Daytona, F40, 512 LM, and 250 GTO, many of them still in original packaging. The parts included exhaust pipes, radiator grilles, wheels, and more, valued at $1.3 million.

In a recent development, the engine is the most complex part of any car, and when it blows, woe to the owner. Especially if it is a 2017 to 2023 BMW M5. The 616-horsepower super sedan used a twin-turbo 4.4-liter V8 that made 553 lb-ft of torque. This monster drove the Autobahn annihilator to a top (limited) speed of 190 mph.

An engine like that is not going to be fun to replace, unless you happen to own a dealership. Notoriously difficult to work on, it's not as forgiving to home wrenching as, say, an LS2 or LS3 V8. Much of that is due to the twin turbos and all the extra heat and hardware that come with them. Should your F90 M5 engine blow up just past the Munich exit, you have two options. If you're an experienced BMW mechanic, eBay could net you a replacement for $15,000 to $20,000. Then there is always the dealership. One shell-shocked owner posted an invoice for a $56,000 F90 engine replacement.

It has been revealed that toyota's ill-fated Scion offshoot seldom raises any red flags when it comes to expensive parts. It targeted a younger market with an affordable lineup of sedans, hatchbacks, and even a well-regarded sports car in the FR-S.

According to recent reports, the FR-S shared a blueprint with the Subaru BRZ. Hagerty hailed them as a millennial Z-car for the new age. Lithe and light, it was fun, with a plucky 2.0-liter engine good for 200 horsepower. Naturally, pushing that number up was a goal for plenty of owners, but most of them won't have a chance to get their hands on the racing-only supercharger TRD developed for it.

According to recent reports, the racing supercharger could be had — without the management software that anyone wanting to mate it to a factory engine would need — for an asking price of $26,000. And there was a minimum order of two.

#9. The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1186 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Technologyreview

The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1186 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub.
  • In a recent development, driving through it is surreal.
  • According to recent reports, it’s accepted wisdom in Big Tech that the war against data centers must be about something bigger than just data centers themselves.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash now sweeping the country arguably first began taking shape.

In a recent development, driving through it is surreal. Concrete monolithic buildings loom along every major road, with names like Skybox and CloudHQ.

According to recent reports, it’s accepted wisdom in Big Tech that the war against data centers must be about something bigger than just data centers themselves. Two days after the midterms, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, wrote that data centers “have become a proxy for public unease about affordability, corporate power, and people losing control over their futures.” It’s a culture war, in other words.

But spending a few days in Data Center Alley left me wondering if it’s really the proxy that Lehane describes. I came away convinced that the data center backlash is more about electricity than Big Tech admits. The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the physical consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity.

It has been revealed that here’s why. There are two ways to power the sort of data center that AI companies want: connecting to the grid, or generating electricity onsite. In Virginia’s Loudoun County, where data centers are ubiquitous but have been built at a steadier pace than the breakneck expansion now underway elsewhere in the country, most are connected to the existing grid.

In a recent development, one facility I went inside, operated by Equinix, has massive diesel generators onsite for backup but gets its power from the local utility, Dominion Energy. Much of Dominion’s electricity is generated by natural gas (which is cleaner than coal or oil, but worse than renewables).

The average data center operating in this part of Virginia today has a power capacity of 54 megawatts. That’s more than the power draw of the Denver International Airport.

According to recent reports, elena Schlossberg, a prominent activist against data centers in Virginia, told me she’s “always banging my head against the wall” when the industry paints the fight as a culture war. “It was always about power,” she claims—that is, electricity.

In a recent development, some Virginia protesters appear more animated by a broader anti-tech populism than Schlossberg, to be fair. But it’s the particular consequences of drawing so much power from the grid that have done the most to shape how the backlash has played out.

It has been revealed that recent protests have led to new rules from the state that data centers must pay fully for the cost of new transmission lines to the grid and make sure they’re not spread among everyone else. Data center developers told me they’re preparing for new rules that would cut them off from grid power during peak demand. Schlossberg also worries about the downstream effects of a strained grid—for example, that data centers will run more diesel generators or that Dominion Energy will expand fossil fuel inputs rather than renewables to meet demand.

Sources indicate that the overwhelming majority of AI data centers being built elsewhere in the country are not designed this way. The scale desired is so massive that companies are setting up in rural areas where there is virtually no grid infrastructure to connect to. Building there means bringing your own power (so-called “behind the meter” power), in the form of natural-gas-powered turbines. Companies also build diesel generators for backup. Anthropic, for example, has reportedly agreed to pay $3.4 billion for gas turbines in what’s described as the largest power generation purchase by an AI organization.

In a recent development, even if grids were nearby, they’d be unlikely to serve the amount of power demanded. The smallest data centers attractive for AI training are 300 megawatts. It’s a lot of power for one industrial site, but not unprecedented: One data center developer told me he’s eyeing a former steel mill already equipped to draw that much electricity from the grid.

Industry observers note that but the ideal facilities are more like 6,000 megawatts. That’s the estimated draw of the city of Chicago, which is powered by more than 20 power plants within the city alone (and dozens farther out).

In a recent development, the notion of data center companies’ bringing their own power might seem attractive at first, because they wouldn’t be straining the grid. But generating electricity at this scale inevitably affects surrounding communities, and when public utilities build infrastructure of this magnitude, communities have traditionally expected a say in where it goes. Now, private companies are undertaking projects on a similar scale.

Industry observers note that natural-gas turbines of any scale release air pollutants. When diesel generators are used, it’s even worse. And in the unprecedented rush to get these facilities operating, companies have become horrible neighbors (recall that Elon Musk violated air quality laws when he set up dozens of turbines to power a data center in Memphis, according to the Environmental Protection Agency).

Major Tech’s tendency to chalk the backlash up to a culture war obfuscates one simple fact: There’s only so pleasant you can make a small city of computers to live around. Sure, companies can pursue better deals that raise tax revenues, hire local workers, and get more community involvement, as the protests are leading them to do. But if a small town is asked to welcome a Walt Disney World, an international airport, a steel plant, and the power plants to run them all, should we be surprised by its trepidation?

Recent findings suggest that again, that’s not to say this is the sole reason for opposition to data centers. Fears of job losses, existential risks, and concentrated corporate power all fuel the backlash, as does misinformation (most facilities use far less water than many people think). Nor is consuming enormous amounts of electricity inherently bad: Many of the advances that have improved modern life have required just that.

Industry observers note that but as one developer recently told me, industry insiders see their ambitions as constrained less by public opposition than by a lack of electricity. That should tell us something.

According to recent reports, so what happens next? It’s possible that newly elected politicians’ actual stances on data centers won’t be as negative as the ones they campaigned on. But what seems true regardless is that if newly introduced data centers need their own power generated onsite, they’ll go where there are the fewest people able to resist them. That might mean the Permian Basin, where a network of natural-gas lines can be easy for developers to connect to and populations are sparse. Companies might also try their chances abroad; Google, in fact, revealed the day after the elections that it will spend $15 billion on data center projects in Malaysia.

But there’s one place where Big Tech may find virtually no limits at all, as Elon Musk posted just hours after the midterms results came rolling in: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.”.

#6. What Is The DSL Port On Some Internet Routers For?

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (383 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Slashgear

What Is The DSL Port On Some Internet Routers For?

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (383 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Slashgear

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Specifically, the DSL port sits on a device that merges a modem and a router, which is different from an access point, into a single box called a DSL modem router.
  • According to recent reports, supporting DSL also requires a DSL modem, which the average router lacks, so if you do need DSL support, you'd have to hook it up to a separate one instead.
  • That's not to say DSL is alien to the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Specifically, the DSL port sits on a device that merges a modem and a router, which is different from an access point, into a single box called a DSL modem router. The modem part of the device uses the port to communicate with the internet provider over the phone line via signals. These signals are translated into regular Ethernet data, which is then fed to the devices at home via Wi-Fi and LAN ports. That noted, the DSL port itself doesn't carry Ethernet data, so it's incompatible with Ethernet cables. The DSL port takes an RJ11 phone plug, which measures 6 mm by 9.5 mm. It's slightly smaller than the 6 mm by 11 mm RJ45 Ethernet plug.

According to recent reports, supporting DSL also requires a DSL modem, which the average router lacks, so if you do need DSL support, you'd have to hook it up to a separate one instead. Today, very few routers support DSL. Because of these hardware differences, DSL routers are usually labeled as such. A good example is the Asus DSL-AX82U, a Wi-Fi 6 modem router with a DSL port.

That's not to say DSL is alien to the U.S. While the share of copper-line connections is tiny at 5.4% of the country's 135 million fixed connections (as of 2025), according to an FCC report, it still represents a significant number at 7.3 million. However, these connections are declining rapidly. The 7.3 million figure is down from 18.6 million in June 2021, meaning it's fallen a whopping 60% in roughly four years.

It has been revealed that there's a good reason for this. The same FCC report claims that the median download speed on copper lines is just 24 Mbps, which may not match the internet speeds you need for quality HD streaming and gaming. Today, people are increasingly upgrading to fiber and enjoying vastly superior speeds as a result, with a median of 940 Mbps.

At the same time, internet providers are simply winding things down. AT&T stopped taking new DSL customers on October 1, 2020, though it continues to provide existing ones with service. That won't be for long, though, since the carrier prepares to retire most of its copper network by 2029 — one of several substantial changes by AT&T.

Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review in an interview on Thursday, even while an industry group claimed they were “potentially infeasible.”.

Sources indicate that foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, is a cosponsor of the act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify the location of advanced AI chips in order to prevent their smuggling to China. It is one of three chip-security bills under consideration for inclusion in the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, each of which is drawing renewed attention after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and reported affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

Industry observers note that when the Chip Security Act was introduced, in May 2025, lawmakers said the technology to implement it existed, something Nvidia has not publicly confirmed. In March 2026, the Semiconductor Industry Association, of which Nvidia is a member, explicitly opposed the bill and wrote that its mandates for chip tracking were “upcoming, untested, and potentially infeasible.”.

But privately, Nvidia representatives working with Foster told the lawmaker that the tech giant could implement them.

“They never put anything in writing,” Foster indicates, but during technical discussions on the possibility of such safeguards, their reaction was “yeah, of course we can do this.” This private acknowledgment to Foster goes further than anything Nvidia has previously made public.

In a recent development, other technology Nvidia has built for its customers suggests that the organization can indeed offer accurate tracking of its chips’ locations. In December 2025, for example, it confirmed a fresh tool called Fleet Intelligence that would allow customers to monitor how its advanced chips were performing across different data center locations. In doing so, the tool could indicate which country chips were in, Nvidia confirmed to Reuters, but the company would not elaborate on whether this technology could be used to prevent smuggling.

Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment or confirmation of Foster’s characterization.

Industry observers note that in early October, when lawmakers were reportedly increasingly concerned about Nvidia’s role in smuggling, MIT Technology Review asked the company if Fleet Intelligence could be used to prevent the practice. It declined to answer directly, instead sending a statement: “Governments and media have found insignificant diversion of controlled US products—a drop in the bucket compared to the ocean of domestic compute China already has.”.

Recent findings suggest that the recent fallout at Nvidia involves a number of people and companies alleged to be involved in chip smuggling. Alice Huang, with whom Jensen Huang reportedly had an affair, runs Megaspeed, a Singaporean firm now under investigation for smuggling advanced GPUs to China. A US Commerce Department inquiry into the company was reportedly halted after invention by Nvidia. Megaspeed reportedly bought chips from Supermicro, a company that packages Nvidia’s chips onto servers.

The Chip Security Act as drafted would require a mechanism to track the locations of chips, either by inspections of facilities, attestations by companies, or ping-based location mechanisms. The ping-based technique, the hardest option to circumvent, would require the GPU to send a signal of its location when it comes online. In September, the Center for Security and Emerging Technology found it would be the most cost-effective option.

Foster mentioned he did not ask Nvidia’s representatives why they weren’t voluntarily adopting such chip-tracking tools if they could technically do so.

In a recent development, but if the requirements of the bill pass as part of the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, the upcoming tracking mechanisms would only tell investigators where the chips are, not offer a way to disconnect them if it’s revealed they have been smuggled. Foster told MIT Technology Review he intends to introduce new, stricter legislation in the new year that would offer a workaround. The new rule would require licenses to operate advanced GPUs, and before a GPU could connect, its valid license would need to be verified.

In the meantime, the controversy at Nvidia, Foster claims, has fueled support among his colleagues for the rules in the bill: “There will be a lot of political pressure, in the wake of everything that’s happened, on the companies to actually do a very good job of the geographic validation of where the chip actually is.”.
